query.original_query: SemanticLens-style automated concept-level labeling of vision-model components via reference inputs embedded with a frozen CLIP image tower into a shared multi-modal semantic space

sub_queries.semantic_query: Automated concept-level labeling of neurons channels heads in vision models by embedding maximally-activating reference inputs with a frozen foundation encoder such as CLIP into a shared image-text semantic space; Network Dissection MILAN CLIP-Dissect FALCON INVERT DnD SemanticLens; feature visualization activation maximization exemplar reference inputs; per-component semantic vector for interpretability model auditing concept search on ResNet-50 ImageNet
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether individual components of trained vision models such as CNN channels and vision transformer neurons carry concept-specific information that can be recovered without ad hoc human labels. Building on Network Dissection style exemplar analysis and open-vocabulary concept probing with CLIP, we analyze reference-set based labeling: for each component we collect its top activating inputs from ImageNet and embed those inputs with a frozen CLIP image tower to obtain a per-component semantic vector in the joint image-text space. Our analysis relates this vector to concept purity metrics, to text-based descriptions produced by matching in the shared embedding space, and to downstream model auditing tasks including spurious-feature discovery and cross-model neuron alignment. We compare against activation maximization visualizations, MILAN natural-language descriptions, CLIP-Dissect label assignment, FALCON contrastive corpora and INVERT invertible probes, and we characterize how the choice of layer, component granularity, pooling operator, and reference-set size affects concept faithfulness. Results indicate that a small reference set combined with a frozen multi-modal encoder is a strong summary of what a component encodes.

papers.title: CLIP-Dissect: Automatic Description of Neuron Representations in Deep Vision Networks
papers.research_question: How can we automatically describe the function of individual hidden neurons in vision networks without the need for labeled data or human examples?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLIP-Dissect, a method to automatically describe individual neurons in vision networks using multimodal models like CLIP, without requiring labeled data, and shows it is more accurate and efficient than existing methods.
papers.conclusion: CLIP-Dissect is a novel, flexible, and efficient framework for automatically identifying concepts of hidden layer neurons, outperforming previous methods and providing new insights.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP-Dissect provides more accurate descriptions for final layer neurons compared to Network Dissection and MILAN.
CLIP-Dissect is computationally efficient, labeling neurons 10x to 200x faster than existing methods.
CLIP-Dissect can detect concepts even when the probing dataset does not contain images of those concepts.
Neurons connected by high weights tend to represent similar concepts.
The method works on both CNNs and Vision Transformers.
papers.limitation:
Not taking advantage of spatial information of neuron activations, making detecting lower level concepts harder.
Reliance on CLIP, so may not work on tasks requiring highly specific knowledge.
Not all neurons can be described well by simple terms.
future_direction: Extending the method with better multimodal models in the future.
Improving compositional explanations.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose CLIP-Dissect, a new technique to automatically describe the function of individual hidden neurons inside vision networks. CLIP-Dissect leverages recent advances in multimodal vision/language models to label internal neurons with open-ended concepts without the need for any labeled data or human examples. We show that CLIP-Dissect provides more accurate descriptions than existing methods for last layer neurons where the ground-truth is available as well as qualitatively good descriptions for hidden layer neurons. In addition, our method is very flexible: it is model agnostic, can easily handle new concepts and can be extended to take advantage of better multimodal models in the future. Finally CLIP-Dissect is computationally efficient and can label all neurons from five layers of ResNet-50 in just 4 minutes, which is more than 10 times faster than existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/CLIP-dissect. Finally, crowdsourced user study results are available at Appendix B to further support the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Natural Language Descriptions of Deep Visual Features
papers.research_question: Is a richer characterization of neuron-level computation possible? Can we automatically label neurons with open-ended, compositional, natural language descriptions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MILAN, a method for automatically labeling neurons in deep networks with natural language descriptions by maximizing pointwise mutual information between descriptions and image regions where neurons are active.
papers.conclusion: MILAN enables automatic, fine-grained labeling of neurons with natural language descriptions, facilitating analysis, auditing, and editing of deep network models.
papers.key_findings:
MILAN generalizes to new architectures, datasets, and tasks, achieving higher agreement with human annotations than baselines.
MILAN can be used for analyzing feature importance, auditing anonymized models, and editing spurious features to improve robustness.
Neurons described with adjectives or prepositions are more important for model performance, while those with dissimilar concepts are less important.
Blurring faces in training data reduces but does not eliminate neurons selective for faces, and some neurons still detect demographic attributes.
Deleting neurons sensitive to spurious text features can improve adversarial accuracy.
papers.limitation:
MILAN sometimes generates incorrect, vague, or context-mistaking descriptions for neurons, especially when faced with new visual concepts.
Generalization performance varies across different model architectures, datasets, and tasks, with some transfers being more difficult.
future_direction: Extend MILAN to label directions in representation space or clusters of images induced by visual representations.
papers.abstract: Some neurons in deep networks specialize in recognizing highly specific perceptual, structural, or semantic features of inputs. In computer vision, techniques exist for identifying neurons that respond to individual concept categories like colors, textures, and object classes. But these techniques are limited in scope, labeling only a small subset of neurons and behaviors in any network. Is a richer characterization of neuron-level computation possible? We introduce a procedure (called MILAN, for mutual-information-guided linguistic annotation of neurons) that automatically labels neurons with open-ended, compositional, natural language descriptions. Given a neuron, MILAN generates a description by searching for a natural language string that maximizes pointwise mutual information with the image regions in which the neuron is active. MILAN produces fine-grained descriptions that capture categorical, relational, and logical structure in learned features. These descriptions obtain high agreement with human-generated feature descriptions across a diverse set of model architectures and tasks, and can aid in understanding and controlling learned models. We highlight three applications of natural language neuron descriptions. First, we use MILAN for analysis, characterizing the distribution and importance of neurons selective for attribute, category, and relational information in vision models. Second, we use MILAN for auditing, surfacing neurons sensitive to human faces in datasets designed to obscure them. Finally, we use MILAN for editing, improving robustness in an image classifier by deleting neurons sensitive to text features spuriously correlated with class labels.

papers.title: CLIP-MSM: A Multi-Semantic Mapping Brain Representation for Human High-Level Visual Cortex
papers.research_question: How can we construct encoding models that accurately capture brain responses to multiple coexisting semantics in the human high-level visual cortex, and map single voxels to multiple semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CLIP-MSM, a multi-semantic mapping framework for hypothesis-free analysis in human high-level visual cortex, which combines CLIP models with CLIP Dissection to map single brain voxels to multiple semantics and shows improved accuracy over existing methods.
papers.conclusion: CLIP-MSM is a multi-semantic mapping framework for hypothesis-free analysis in the human high-level visual cortex that enables granular examination of concept preferences with a broad range of natural scene categories, showing higher interpretability accuracy than Network Dissection and more precise alignment with ground truth brain activation than CLIP Dissection.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP models (ResNet50_CLIP and ViT-32_CLIP) outperform ImageNet-pretrained models in predicting brain responses.
CLIP-MSM captures more accurate semantic mapping than Network Dissection.
CLIP-MSM enables precise mapping of high-level visual cortex across different categories (faces, bodies, places, words, food).
CLIP-MSM provides more accurate predictions of visual responses compared to CLIP Dissection in hypothesis-free analysis.
The results are validated on two fMRI datasets (NSD and NOD), demonstrating reproducibility.
future_direction: Extend CLIP-MSM to analyze brain responses to more nuanced concepts.
papers.abstract: Prior work employing deep neural networks (DNNs) with explainable techniques has identified human visual cortical selective representation to specific categories. However, constructing high-performing encoding models that accurately capture brain responses to coexisting multi-semantics remains elusive. Here, we used CLIP models combined with CLIP Dissection to establish a multi-semantic mapping framework (CLIP-MSM) for hypothesis-free analysis in human high-level visual cortex. First, we utilize CLIP models to construct voxel-wise encoding models for predicting visual cortical responses to natural scene images. Then, we apply CLIP Dissection and normalize the semantic mapping score to achieve the mapping of single brain voxels to multiple semantics. Our findings indicate that CLIP Dissection applied to DNNs modeling the human high-level visual cortex demonstrates better interpretability accuracy compared to Network Dissection. In addition, to demonstrate how our method enables fine-grained discovery in hypothesis-free analysis, we quantify the accuracy between CLIP-MSM’s reconstructed brain activation in response to categories of faces, bodies, places, words and food, and the ground truth of brain activation. We demonstrate that CLIP-MSM provides more accurate predictions of visual responses compared to CLIP Dissection. Our results have been validated using two large natural image datasets: the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and the Natural Object Dataset (NOD).

papers.title: Does CLIP Bind Concepts? Probing Compositionality in Large Image Models
papers.research_question: To what extent does CLIP encode compositional representations and bind variables in a structure-sensitive way?
papers.core_contribution: CLIP performs well on single-object compositional tasks but fails at tasks requiring concept binding (two-object and relational), and fine-tuning or using compositional models does not solve this issue.
papers.conclusion: CLIP lacks the necessary structure for variable binding, and pretraining methods that account for binding are needed for better compositionality in vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP achieves high accuracy (92.39%) on single-object adjective-noun composition but drops to near chance on two-object (31.40%) and relational (0.00%) tasks.
Fine-tuning CLIP (CLIP-FT) leads to overfitting, with high training accuracy but poor generalization on two-object and relational tasks.
Compositional soft prompting (CSP) shows some improvement but still fails on tasks requiring binding.
Compositional distributional semantics models (CDSMs) also perform poorly, with best performance at chance level in binding tasks.
BLIP shows similar limitations, indicating a general problem in vision-language models.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to CLIP and its variants, and newer visual encoders might perform better.
The datasets are synthetic and may not reflect real-world complexity.
future_direction: Develop pretraining methods for vision-language models that account for binding.
Create more realistic and challenging benchmarks for concept binding.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural network models combining text and images have made incredible progress in recent years. However, it remains an open question to what extent such models encode compositional representations of the concepts over which they operate, such as correctly identifying "red cube" by reasoning over the constituents "red" and "cube". In this work, we focus on the ability of a large pretrained vision and language model (CLIP) to encode compositional concepts and to bind variables in a structure-sensitive way (e.g., differentiating "cube behind sphere" from "sphere behind cube"). To inspect the performance of CLIP, we compare several architectures from research on compositional distributional semantics models (CDSMs), a line of research that attempts to implement traditional compositional linguistic structures within embedding spaces. We benchmark them on three synthetic datasets - single-object, two-object, and relational - designed to test concept binding. We find that CLIP can compose concepts in a single-object setting, but in situations where concept binding is needed, performance drops dramatically. At the same time, CDSMs also perform poorly, with best performance at chance level.

papers.title: Interpreting ResNet-based CLIP via Neuron-Attention Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we interpret CLIP-ResNet models by decomposing the contributions of neuron-head pairs to the output?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces neuron-attention decomposition, a method for interpreting CLIP-ResNet by decomposing output contributions into neuron-head pairs, which are found to be interpretable and useful for downstream tasks like semantic segmentation and monitoring dataset distribution shifts.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-attention decomposition is an effective interpretability method for CLIP-ResNet, uncovering interpretable units that can be utilized for downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron-head pairs can be approximated by a single direction in the joint image-text embedding space.
Only a sparse set of neuron-head pairs contribute significantly to the output value.
Neuron-head pairs often represent sub-concepts of the concepts represented by the corresponding neurons.
The method enables training-free semantic segmentation with CLIP-ResNet, outperforming previous methods.
Neuron-head pair contributions can track dataset distribution shifts, correlating with ground truth concept prevalence.
papers.limitation:
The approach is only applicable to the last layer of the ResNet.
Neuron-head pairs remain polysemantic.
future_direction: Scale and automate the assignment of fine-grained labels to components like neuron-head pairs.
papers.abstract: We present a novel technique for interpreting the neurons in CLIP-ResNet by decomposing their contributions to the output into individual computation paths. More specifically, we analyze all pairwise combinations of neurons and the following attention heads of CLIP's attention-pooling layer. We find that these neuron-head pairs can be approximated by a single direction in CLIP-ResNet's image-text embedding space. Leveraging this insight, we interpret each neuron-head pair by associating it with text. Additionally, we find that only a sparse set of the neuron-head pairs have a significant contribution to the output value, and that some neuron-head pairs, while polysemantic, represent sub-concepts of their corresponding neurons. We use these observations for two applications. First, we employ the pairs for training-free semantic segmentation, outperforming previous methods for CLIP-ResNet. Second, we utilize the contributions of neuron-head pairs to monitor dataset distribution shifts. Our results demonstrate that examining individual computation paths in neural networks uncovers interpretable units, and that such units can be utilized for downstream tasks.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
papers.research_question: How can we automatically explain features in image representations using natural language concepts? Also, which features in the representation space are explainable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces FALCON, an automatic framework for explaining image representation features using natural language concepts. It also shows that interpretable subspaces are often composed of feature groups rather than individual features.
papers.conclusion: FALCON provides an effective way to automatically explain features in image representations. The study reveals that interpretable subspaces often consist of feature groups, and the extracted concepts can be used for debugging and transfer.
papers.key_findings:
FALCON can automatically extract human-understandable concepts for features without human intervention.
Individual features are often not interpretable, but groups of features are more interpretable.
FALCON concepts are validated by human evaluation with high precision and recall.
Concepts can be used to explain failures in downstream tasks.
Concepts can be transferred across representation spaces via a linear transformation.
papers.limitation:
The quality of explanations is dependent on the captioning dataset and the vision-language model.
The method may not capture very high-level abstract concepts that are not well-represented in the captioning data.
future_direction: Extending FALCON to other modalities like text and audio.
Improving the concept extraction to handle more abstract features.
Exploring the use of FALCON for model editing and improving model robustness.
papers.abstract: We propose Automatic Feature Explanation using Contrasting Concepts (FALCON), an interpretability framework to explain features of image representations. For a target feature, FALCON captions its highly activating cropped images using a large captioning dataset (like LAION-400m) and a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP. Each word among the captions is scored and ranked leading to a small number of shared, human-understandable concepts that closely describe the target feature. FALCON also applies contrastive interpretation using lowly activating (counterfactual) images, to eliminate spurious concepts. Although many existing approaches interpret features independently, we observe in state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised models, that less than 20% of the representation space can be explained by individual features. We show that features in larger spaces become more interpretable when studied in groups and can be explained with high-order scoring concepts through FALCON. We discuss how extracted concepts can be used to explain and debug failures in downstream tasks. Finally, we present a technique to transfer concepts from one (explainable) representation space to another unseen representation space by learning a simple linear transformation. Code available at https://github.com/NehaKalibhat/falcon-explain.

papers.title: DISCOVER: Making Vision Networks Interpretable via Competition and Dissection
papers.research_question: How can we make vision networks interpretable by using competition-based activations and network dissection to generate textual descriptions of neuron functionality?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a framework for interpretable vision networks using competition-based activations (stochastic LWTA) and network dissection to generate textual descriptions of neuron functionality, achieving high sparsity and improved interpretability without sacrificing accuracy.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER provides an effective framework for interpretable vision networks through competition and dissection, yielding highly interpretable neuron functionality with sparse activations.
papers.key_findings:
Competitive Vision Networks (CVNs) with stochastic LWTA layers achieve comparable or better classification accuracy than conventional networks, even with high sparsity (as low as 4% active neurons).
CVNs yield more interpretable neuron descriptions, as measured by higher cosine similarity between neuron descriptions and ground truth labels.
The sparsity induced by competition allows for per-example analysis of a small subset of active neurons, facilitating practical concept interrogation.
CVNs improve neuron identification accuracy compared to conventional networks.
papers.limitation:
CLIP-Dissect disregards spatial information, which could allow for identifying lower-level concepts.
LWTA networks are not yet optimized in popular frameworks due to limited adoption.
future_direction: Exploring block-level and unit-level descriptions in CVNs to capture spatial information.
papers.abstract: Modern deep networks are highly complex and their inferential outcome very hard to interpret. This is a serious obstacle to their transparent deployment in safety-critical or bias-aware applications. This work contributes to post-hoc interpretability, and specifically Network Dissection. Our goal is to present a framework that makes it easier to discover the individual functionality of each neuron in a network trained on a vision task; discovery is performed in terms of textual description generation. To achieve this objective, we leverage: (i) recent advances in multimodal vision-text models and (ii) network layers founded upon the novel concept of stochastic local competition between linear units. In this setting, only a small subset of layer neurons are activated for a given input, leading to extremely high activation sparsity (as low as only $\approx 4\%$). Crucially, our proposed method infers (sparse) neuron activation patterns that enables the neurons to activate/specialize to inputs with specific characteristics, diversifying their individual functionality. This capacity of our method supercharges the potential of dissection processes: human understandable descriptions are generated only for the very few active neurons, thus facilitating the direct investigation of the network's decision process. As we experimentally show, our approach: (i) yields Vision Networks that retain or improve classification performance, and (ii) realizes a principled framework for text-based description and examination of the generated neuronal representations.

papers.title: Concept Visualization: Explaining the CLIP Multi-modal Embedding Using WordNet
papers.research_question: How can we explain the CLIP multi-modal embedding in a task-agnostic way, providing saliency maps for any semantic concept, including those not in the model's training set?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Concept Visualization (ConVis), a novel saliency methodology that uses lexical information from WordNet to explain the CLIP image embedding, generating task-agnostic saliency maps for any semantic concept.
papers.conclusion: Concept Visualization (ConVis) is an effective saliency methodology that exploits WordNet to explain CLIP embeddings, providing task-agnostic explanations and enabling users to gain insight into the model's perception of images.
papers.key_findings:
ConVis performs well on Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection, outperforming baselines like Maximum Logit Score and Isolation Forest.
ConVis achieves comparable performance to other saliency methods on the Weakly Supervised Object Localization (WSOL) benchmark.
A user study demonstrates that users can guess image captions from ConVis saliency maps significantly better than random chance, indicating the method provides insight into CLIP's perception.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in recognizing small objects or objects with low contrast.
Patches from central regions of large objects may lack context for accurate recognition.
Only specific portions of an object may be considered similar to a concept (e.g., for 'person', the model often identifies greater similarity with clothing).
future_direction: Explore the use of WordNet elements other than synset definitions, as well as different knowledge graphs.
Apply ConVis to other Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) frameworks such as BLIP.
Explore Saliency Maps for more abstract concepts beyond physical objects.
Investigate using custom-shaped regions (e.g., via Segment Anything Network) instead of square patches to improve explanation quality.
papers.abstract: Advances in multi-modal embeddings, and in particular CLIP, have recently driven several breakthroughs in Computer Vision (CV). CLIP has shown impressive performance on a variety of tasks, yet, its inherently opaque architecture may hinder the application of models employing CLIP as backbone, especially in fields where trust and model explainability are imperative, such as in the medical domain. Current explanation methodologies for CV models rely on Saliency Maps computed through gradient analysis or input perturbation. However, these Saliency Maps can only be computed to explain classes relevant to the end task, often smaller in scope than the backbone training classes. In the context of models implementing CLIP as their vision backbone, a substantial portion of the information embedded within the learned representations is thus left unexplained. In this work, we propose Concept Visualization (ConVis), a novel saliency methodology that explains the CLIP embedding of an image by exploiting the multi-modal nature of the embeddings. ConVis makes use of lexical information from WordNet to compute task-agnostic Saliency Maps for any concept, not limited to concepts the end model was trained on. We validate our use of WordNet via an out of distribution detection experiment, and test ConVis on an object localization benchmark, showing that Concept Visualizations correctly identify and localize the image's semantic content. Additionally, we perform a user study demonstrating that our methodology can give users insight on the model's functioning.

papers.title: Visual Classification via Description from Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve vision-language models for zero-shot classification by using descriptive features obtained from large language models to gain interpretability, improve accuracy, and adapt to new concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot classification framework that uses descriptive features obtained from large language models instead of just category names, improving interpretability, accuracy across distribution shifts, adaptability to novel concepts, and bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The framework leverages linguistic knowledge from large language models to generate textual descriptors for visual categories, enabling interpretable model decisions, improved performance, adaptation to new knowledge, and bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Improves accuracy over CLIP baseline on ImageNet and other datasets by ~3-5%.
Provides inherent interpretability by showing which descriptors contributed to the classification decision.
Can adapt to recognize novel categories (e.g., Ever Given, Wordle) that CLIP fails on due to training data cutoff.
Descriptor editing can mitigate bias, as demonstrated by making wedding classification more inclusive of different cultures.
Identifies failure modes in descriptor generation (non-visual descriptors, word ambiguity, syntactic errors) and recognition (ambiguous descriptors, interference from reading ability).
papers.limitation:
Failures in descriptor creation: GPT-3 sometimes produces non-visual descriptors (e.g., taste, smell), suffers from word ambiguity (e.g., 'Vespa' as wasp instead of scooter), and occasionally makes syntactic errors.
Failures in recognizing descriptors: CLIP can retrieve unexpected images due to descriptor ambiguity or its reading ability interfering with recognition (e.g., 'stocky cat' activating stock photos).
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have shown promising performance on a variety of recognition tasks using the standard zero-shot classification procedure -- computing similarity between the query image and the embedded words for each category. By only using the category name, they neglect to make use of the rich context of additional information that language affords. The procedure gives no intermediate understanding of why a category is chosen, and furthermore provides no mechanism for adjusting the criteria used towards this decision. We present an alternative framework for classification with VLMs, which we call classification by description. We ask VLMs to check for descriptive features rather than broad categories: to find a tiger, look for its stripes; its claws; and more. By basing decisions on these descriptors, we can provide additional cues that encourage using the features we want to be used. In the process, we can get a clear idea of what features the model uses to construct its decision; it gains some level of inherent explainability. We query large language models (e.g., GPT-3) for these descriptors to obtain them in a scalable way. Extensive experiments show our framework has numerous advantages past interpretability. We show improvements in accuracy on ImageNet across distribution shifts; demonstrate the ability to adapt VLMs to recognize concepts unseen during training; and illustrate how descriptors can be edited to effectively mitigate bias compared to the baseline.

papers.title: Saliency Suppressed, Semantics Surfaced: Visual Transformations in Neural Networks and the Brain
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode low-level (visual saliency) and high-level (semantic similarity) information, and how do these representations compare to those in the human visual cortex?
papers.core_contribution: ResNets are more sensitive to saliency than ViTs, and suppress saliency in early layers (enhanced by CLIP training). CLIP enhances semantic encoding in both architectures. Semantic encoding drives alignment with human visual perception, while saliency suppression is a non-brain-like strategy.
papers.conclusion: Semantic encoding is a primary driver of alignment between neural network representations and the human visual cortex, while the strategy of suppressing salient visual information is unique to artificial networks and not observed in human visual processing.
papers.key_findings:
ResNets are more sensitive to saliency information than Vision Transformers (ViTs) when trained with object classification objectives.
ResNets suppress saliency information in early layers, a process enhanced by natural language supervision (CLIP).
CLIP training enhances semantic encoding in both ResNet and ViT architectures.
Semantic encoding is a key factor in aligning artificial neural network representations with human visual cortex representations, while saliency suppression is not observed in the brain.
ViTs are less sensitive to salient distractors than ResNets, and CLIP reduces the additive effect of saliency on semantic disturbance in ResNets.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of CLIP's impact is limited by its training on a larger and more diverse dataset compared to ImageNet, making it unclear if effects are due to language supervision or exposure to complex visual scenes.
fMRI may have limitations in capturing early visual processes critical for saliency, potentially affecting the measured alignment between saliency and cortical activity.
future_direction: Circuit-level analyses to understand saliency suppression.
Establishing formal links between saliency maps and CNN computations.
Assessing neural network responses to a variety of low-to-mid-level image descriptors beyond saliency.
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms lack human-interpretable accounts of how they transform raw visual input into a robust semantic understanding, which impedes comparisons between different architectures, training objectives, and the human brain. In this work, we take inspiration from neuroscience and employ representational approaches to shed light on how neural networks encode information at low (visual saliency) and high (semantic similarity) levels of abstraction. Moreover, we introduce a custom image dataset where we systematically manipulate salient and semantic information. We find that ResNets are more sensitive to saliency information than ViTs, when trained with object classification objectives. We uncover that networks suppress saliency in early layers, a process enhanced by natural language supervision (CLIP) in ResNets. CLIP also enhances semantic encoding in both architectures. Finally, we show that semantic encoding is a key factor in aligning AI with human visual perception, while saliency suppression is a non-brain-like strategy.

papers.title: NeuroCartography: Scalable Automatic Visual Summarization of Concepts in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we scalably summarize and visualize the concepts collectively encoded by multiple neurons in deep neural networks, moving beyond individual neuron-level interpretation?
papers.core_contribution: NeuroCartography is an interactive system that introduces scalable summarization techniques (neuron clustering and neuron embedding) to automatically discover and visualize groups of neurons that detect the same concepts in deep neural networks, enabling a higher-level understanding of how concepts are collectively encoded.
papers.conclusion: NeuroCartography provides a scalable, interactive approach to summarize and visualize the concepts learned by deep neural networks, moving beyond neuron-level inspection to reveal how concepts are collectively encoded and interact, with demonstrated effectiveness through human evaluation and discovery scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
The system's neuron clustering and embedding techniques can scalably discover neuron groups that represent coherent, human-meaningful concepts, as validated by a large-scale human evaluation.
NeuroCartography scales to large datasets like ImageNet (1.2M images) by using efficient algorithms (Min-Hashing, LSH) with linear time complexity in the number of neurons.
The system enables the discovery of interesting phenomena such as concept cascades (how a concept triggers related concepts across layers) and isolated concepts (e.g., watermark neurons that are unrelated to image content).
The human evaluation showed substantial agreement (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.67) among users in interpreting the discovered neuron clusters, indicating the clusters represent coherent concepts.
The neuron embedding effectively preserves the co-activation relationships between neurons, achieving high AUC scores (0.93-0.99) in predicting neuron relatedness.
papers.limitation:
The approach cannot dissect poly-semantic neurons (neurons activated by multiple unrelated concepts) into separate, concept-specific components.
Concepts represented by neuron groups currently require manual labeling; automatic labeling would increase usability.
The Neuron Projection View presents all neurons in the same plot, potentially mixing concepts at different abstraction levels without user control over layer selection.
future_direction: Tackling the challenge of interpreting poly-semantic neurons.
Integrating NeuroCartography into more applications, such as interpreting model compression techniques or adversarial attacks.
Extending support to other neural network architectures (e.g., ResNets, VGG).
Developing automatic labeling for concepts discovered in neuron groups.
Providing users the ability to select specific layers to investigate in the visualization.
papers.abstract: Existing research on making sense of deep neural networks often focuses on neuron-level interpretation, which may not adequately capture the bigger picture of how concepts are collectively encoded by multiple neurons. We present Neurocartography, an interactive system that scalably summarizes and visualizes concepts learned by neural networks. It automatically discovers and groups neurons that detect the same concepts, and describes how such neuron groups interact to form higher-level concepts and the subsequent predictions. Neurocartography introduces two scalable summarization techniques: (1) neuron clustering groups neurons based on the semantic similarity of the concepts detected by neurons (e.g., neurons detecting "dog faces" of different breeds are grouped); and (2) neuron embedding encodes the associations between related concepts based on how often they co-occur (e.g., neurons detecting "dog face" and "dog tail" are placed closer in the embedding space). Key to our scalable techniques is the ability to efficiently compute all neuron pairs' relationships, in time linear to the number of neurons instead of quadratic time. Neurocartography scales to large data, such as the ImageNet dataset with 1.2M images. The system's tightly coordinated views integrate the scalable techniques to visualize the concepts and their relationships, projecting the concept associations to a 2D space in Neuron Projection View, and summarizing neuron clusters and their relationships in Graph View. Through a large-scale human evaluation, we demonstrate that our technique discovers neuron groups that represent coherent, human-meaningful concepts. And through usage scenarios, we describe how our approaches enable interesting and surprising discoveries, such as concept cascades of related and isolated concepts. The Neurocartography visualization runs in modern browsers and is open-sourced.

papers.title: From Colors to Classes: Emergence of Concepts in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers encode concepts across layers, and do they show a hierarchical feature extraction similar to CNNs?
papers.core_contribution: ViTs encode concepts with increasing complexity across layers, similar to CNNs, despite lacking architectural biases for hierarchical processing. Finetuning shifts concepts to task-relevant categories and reduces concept diversity.
papers.conclusion: ViTs exhibit hierarchical feature extraction similar to CNNs, even without architectural constraints, and finetuning adapts concepts to downstream tasks, suggesting hierarchical processing is beneficial for visual processing.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs encode more universal concepts (colors, textures) in early layers and more specialized concepts (objects, natural elements) in later layers.
The number of different concepts increases across layers.
Neurons in early layers activate on simpler images, while later layers react to more complex images.
Finetuning reduces the number of encoded concepts and shifts concepts to task-relevant categories.
DINOv2 shows distinct behaviors: higher similarity scores, more natural elements, and less change during finetuning.
papers.limitation:
The thresholding procedure (mean-thresholding per layer) may suppress layers with more interpretable neurons.
The categorization of concepts is subjective and may contain errors.
The definition of concepts as neuron labels assumes monosemanticity, which may not hold for all neurons.
future_direction: Investigate catastrophic forgetting using concept-based analysis.
Explore internal structures of models like DINOv2 that enable good generalization and investigate other concept discovery methods.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are increasingly utilized in various computer vision tasks due to their powerful representation capabilities. However, it remains understudied how ViTs process information layer by layer. Numerous studies have shown that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extract features of increasing complexity throughout their layers, which is crucial for tasks like domain adaptation and transfer learning. ViTs, lacking the same inductive biases as CNNs, can potentially learn global dependencies from the first layers due to their attention mechanisms. Given the increasing importance of ViTs in computer vision, there is a need to improve the layer-wise understanding of ViTs. In this work, we present a novel, layer-wise analysis of concepts encoded in state-of-the-art ViTs using neuron labeling. Our findings reveal that ViTs encode concepts with increasing complexity throughout the network. Early layers primarily encode basic features such as colors and textures, while later layers represent more specific classes, including objects and animals. As the complexity of encoded concepts increases, the number of concepts represented in each layer also rises, reflecting a more diverse and specific set of features. Additionally, different pretraining strategies influence the quantity and category of encoded concepts, with finetuning to specific downstream tasks generally reducing the number of encoded concepts and shifting the concepts to more relevant categories.

papers.title: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models Learn Discoverable Visual Concepts
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether pre-trained vision-language models learn visual concepts that can be extracted and used for interpretable object recognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Concept Discovery and Learning (CDL) framework, which discovers shortcut-free and visually discriminative concepts from pre-trained VLMs, demonstrating that these models do learn visual concepts that enable accurate and interpretable object recognition.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained vision-language models do learn visual concepts, and the proposed CDL framework can effectively discover and learn these concepts for accurate and interpretable object recognition.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained VLMs learn visual concepts that can be extracted via their vision-language interface without probing internal representations.
Previous concept-augmented prompting methods are category-biased and contain non-visual concepts, leading to misleading conclusions.
The proposed CDL framework discovers concepts that are more category-agnostic and visually discriminative than prior methods.
CDL improves classification accuracy and interpretability on nine diverse fine-grained object recognition benchmarks.
The discovered concepts are precise, thorough, and generalizable, providing human-interpretable descriptions for recognized objects.
papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) pre-trained to caption an image of a "durian" learn visual concepts such as "brown" (color) and "spiky" (texture) at the same time? We aim to answer this question as visual concepts learned "for free" would enable wide applications such as neuro-symbolic reasoning or human-interpretable object classification. We assume that the visual concepts, if captured by pre-trained VLMs, can be extracted by their vision-language interface with text-based concept prompts. We observe that recent works prompting VLMs with concepts often differ in their strategies to define and evaluate the visual concepts, leading to conflicting conclusions. We propose a new concept definition strategy based on two observations: First, certain concept prompts include shortcuts that recognize correct concepts for wrong reasons; Second, multimodal information (e.g. visual discriminativeness, and textual knowledge) should be leveraged when selecting the concepts. Our proposed concept discovery and learning (CDL) framework is thus designed to identify a diverse list of generic visual concepts (e.g. "spiky" as opposed to "spiky durian"), which are ranked and selected based on visual and language mutual information. We carefully design quantitative and human evaluations of the discovered concepts on six diverse visual recognition datasets, which confirm that pre-trained VLMs do learn visual concepts that provide accurate and thorough descriptions for the recognized objects. All code and models are publicly released.

papers.title: Rosetta Neurons: Mining the Common Units in a Model Zoo
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks, trained for various vision tasks, share some common representations? This paper investigates the existence of common features called 'Rosetta Neurons' across models with different architectures, tasks, and supervision.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the existence of 'Rosetta Neurons'—common units across diverse vision models—and presents a method to mine them, enabling model-to-model translation and image editing without specialized training.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a method for mining and visualizing common representations across different visual models, demonstrating that specific units represent the same concepts in diverse networks and can be utilized for generative tasks via lightweight latent optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Rosetta Neurons, common units expressing shared visual concepts, exist across models with different architectures, tasks (generative and discriminative), and types of supervision.
A method based on correlation and best-buddies matching can mine these neurons without human annotations or semantic labels.
Rosetta Neurons enable visualization of shared concepts through activation maps and a novel inversion technique.
They facilitate model-to-model translation, enabling cross-class alignments, shifting, zooming, and other image manipulations without specialized training.
Guiding image inversion with Rosetta Neurons improves reconstruction quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) compared to using perceptual loss alone.
papers.limitation:
The method cannot calculate GAN-GAN matches directly, only through a discriminative model.
The approach was unsuccessful when applied to diffusion models, likely due to their autoregressive nature.
The method relies on correlations and may mine spurious correlations.
future_direction: Exploring the use of Rosetta Neurons in image retrieval tasks.
Applying Rosetta Neurons to more advanced generative tasks.
Investigating similarities and dissimilarities between models trained for different tasks and architectures.
papers.abstract: Do different neural networks, trained for various vision tasks, share some common representations? In this paper, we demonstrate the existence of common features we call "Rosetta Neurons" across a range of models with different architectures, different tasks (generative and discriminative), and different types of supervision (class-supervised, text-supervised, self-supervised). We present an algorithm for mining a dictionary of Rosetta Neurons across several popular vision models: Class Supervised-ResNet50, DINO-ResNet50, DINO-ViT, MAE, CLIP-ResNet50, BigGAN, StyleGAN-2, StyleGAN-XL. Our findings suggest that certain visual concepts and structures are inherently embedded in the natural world and can be learned by different models regardless of the specific task or architecture, and without the use of semantic labels. We can visualize shared concepts directly due to generative models included in our analysis. The Rosetta Neurons facilitate model-to-model translation enabling various inversion-based manipulations, including cross-class alignments, shifting, zooming, and more, without the need for specialized training.

papers.title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstractions are learned by neurons in deep models? Do compositional explanations give insight into model performance? Can they be used to predictably manipulate model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a procedure for generating compositional logical explanations of individual neurons, which provides more precise and expressive characterizations of neuron behavior than atomic labels, and applies it to analyze vision and NLP models.
papers.conclusion: Compositional explanations offer a more precise and expressive way to characterize neuron behavior, providing insights into model performance and enabling targeted adversarial manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons learn compositional concepts: in image classification, some learn meaningful perceptual abstractions while others are polysemantic; in NLI, shallow heuristics (e.g., based on gender, lexical overlap) are reified in individual neurons.
The interpretability of neurons correlates differently with performance: in image classification, human-interpretable abstractions are positively correlated with accuracy, while in NLI, neurons explained by shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with accuracy.
Compositional explanations enable the creation of simple 'copy-paste' adversarial examples that predictably change model behavior by targeting specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
The method requires technical expertise to implement, limiting usability by non-experts.
It relies on annotated datasets which may be expensive to collect and may be biased in the features they contain or omit.
Neuron-level explanations cannot identify concepts distributed across multiple neurons or establish definitive causal chains between inputs and decisions.
future_direction: Building easier user interfaces for explainability.
Reducing data annotation requirements.
Extending composition operators (e.g., to relations like ABOVE and BELOW) and applying the method to other tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.

papers.title: Understanding the role of individual units in a deep neural network
papers.research_question: How can we understand the learned representations in deep neural networks by identifying the semantics of individual hidden units and their causal roles in network behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces network dissection, an analytic framework to systematically identify the semantics of individual hidden units in image classification and generation networks, and demonstrates that these units correspond to interpretable concepts and have causal roles in network behavior.
papers.conclusion: Systematic analysis of individual units can yield insights into the black box internals of deep networks, and by observing and manipulating units, it is possible to understand the structure of the knowledge that the network has learned and to build systems that help humans interact with these models.
papers.key_findings:
In a scene classification CNN (VGG-16), individual units emerge as detectors for objects, parts, materials, and colors, even without explicit object labels in training.
A small number of units are crucial for classifying specific scene classes; removing them significantly reduces accuracy for that class while leaving overall accuracy largely intact.
In a GAN (Progressive GAN), units also emerge as object and part detectors, and they have causal effects on the generated output (e.g., removing tree units reduces trees in generated images).
The GAN's units are context-sensitive: activating door units only adds doors in appropriate locations (e.g., on buildings) and not in nonsensical locations (e.g., in the sky or on trees).
Network dissection can be applied to understand adversarial attacks (by showing attacks target important units) and to enable semantic image editing by directly manipulating units.
papers.limitation: Network dissection relies on the emergence of disentangled, human-interpretable units during training, which is not guaranteed and is an open problem.
future_direction: Training better disentangled models
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks excel at finding hierarchical representations that solve complex tasks over large datasets. How can we humans understand these learned representations? In this work, we present network dissection, an analytic framework to systematically identify the semantics of individual hidden units within image classification and image generation networks. First, we analyze a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on scene classification and discover units that match a diverse set of object concepts. We find evidence that the network has learned many object classes that play crucial roles in classifying scene classes. Second, we use a similar analytic method to analyze a generative adversarial network (GAN) model trained to generate scenes. By analyzing changes made when small sets of units are activated or deactivated, we find that objects can be added and removed from the output scenes while adapting to the context. Finally, we apply our analytic framework to understanding adversarial attacks and to semantic image editing.

papers.title: Visual Concept Connectome (VCC): Open World Concept Discovery and their Interlayer Connections in Deep Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover human-interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in deep vision models in a fully unsupervised manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Visual Concept Connectome (VCC), a method for unsupervised discovery of human-interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in deep vision models, enabling holistic analysis of network structure and application to tasks like failure debugging.
papers.conclusion: VCCs provide a method for unsupervised discovery of interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections, revealing interesting properties of deep models and enabling applications like failure debugging.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers have more but weaker concepts, while later layers have fewer but stronger concepts.
CNNs and transformers compose concepts differently, with transformers showing more diverse connection strengths in the final layer.
VCCs can be used for debugging model failures by tracing hierarchical concept contributions.
Robust and self-supervised models have fewer low-level concepts and less compositionality than standard models.
The branching factor and number of concepts vary across layers and architectures, converging to about two concepts in the final layer.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Silhouette method for selecting the number of clusters during segmentation, which could yield different results with other methods.
Lack of a method for automatic selection of layers to analyze, which could reveal more focused patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding what deep network models capture in their learned representations is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. We present a new methodology to understanding such vision models, the Visual Concept Connectome (VCC), which discovers human interpretable concepts and their interlayer connections in a fully unsupervised manner. Our approach simultaneously reveals fine-grained concepts at a layer, connection weightings across all layers and is amendable to global analysis of network structure (e.g., branching pattern of hierarchical concept assemblies). Previous work yielded ways to extract interpretable concepts from single layers and examine their impact on classification, but did not afford multilayer concept analysis across an entire network architecture. Quantitative and qualitative empirical results show the effectiveness of VCCs in the domain of image classification. Also, we leverage VCCs for the application of failure mode debugging to reveal where mistakes arise in deep networks.

papers.title: Disentangling Latent Embeddings with Sparse Linear Concept Subspaces (SLiCS)
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle latent embeddings into interpretable concept-specific subspaces to enable concept-filtered image retrieval and generation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SLiCS, a supervised dictionary learning method to disentangle latent embeddings into concept-specific subspaces, enabling interpretable concept-filtered image retrieval and generation.
papers.conclusion: SLiCS enables effective decomposition of latent embeddings into interpretable concept subspaces, improving concept-filtered retrieval across various vision embedding models.
papers.key_findings:
SLiCS improves concept-filtered retrieval performance (mAP@20) over unfiltered retrieval on CLIP, TiTok, and DINOv2 embeddings.
The method works in both supervised (with labels) and unsupervised (via zero-shot pseudo-labels) settings.
Dictionary size (number of atoms per concept) affects the quality of disentanglement and retrieval performance.
Word captions derived from text embeddings provide interpretable descriptions of the learned concept subspaces.
DINOv2 embeddings yield the best concept-filtered retrieval performance after disentanglement, even outperforming CLIP.
papers.abstract: Vision-language co-embedding networks, such as CLIP, provide a latent embedding space with semantic information that is useful for downstream tasks. We hypothesize that the embedding space can be disentangled to separate the information on the content of complex scenes by decomposing the embedding into multiple concept-specific component vectors that lie in different subspaces. We propose a supervised dictionary learning approach to estimate a linear synthesis model consisting of sparse, non-negative combinations of groups of vectors in the dictionary (atoms), whose group-wise activity matches the multi-label information. Each concept-specific component is a non-negative combination of atoms associated to a label. The group-structured dictionary is optimized through a novel alternating optimization with guaranteed convergence. Exploiting the text co-embeddings, we detail how semantically meaningful descriptions can be found based on text embeddings of words best approximated by a concept's group of atoms, and unsupervised dictionary learning can exploit zero-shot classification of training set images using the text embeddings of concept labels to provide instance-wise multi-labels. We show that the disentangled embeddings provided by our sparse linear concept subspaces (SLiCS) enable concept-filtered image retrieval (and conditional generation using image-to-prompt) that is more precise. We also apply SLiCS to highly-compressed autoencoder embeddings from TiTok and the latent embedding from self-supervised DINOv2. Quantitative and qualitative results highlight the improved precision of the concept-filtered image retrieval for all embeddings.

papers.title: Refining Skewed Perceptions in Vision-Language Contrastive Models through Visual Representations
papers.research_question: Does CLIP rely on non-causal background features in decision-making? Is a linear probe sufficient to distill task-specific core features from CLIP's image embeddings? Can language prompts help remove spurious features? Can images help refine skewed perceptions in CLIP visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: Visual representations from CLIP are more effective than text embeddings for debiasing spurious correlations, and a simple linear probe can distill task-specific core features.
papers.conclusion: Text representations in CLIP are contaminated by spurious contextual features, while visual representations are more expressive and effective for extracting core features via linear probes.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP relies on non-causal spurious features for decision-making, yet linear probing is sufficient to extract key features for downstream tasks.
CLIP's text embeddings are contaminated by diverse elements, making text embeddings impractical for debiasing.
Using visual embeddings from CLIP to distill visual representations is highly effective for debiasing, achieving group accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art supervised methods.
future_direction: Enhance fairness in image retrieval by leveraging distilled image embeddings as a surrogate for query embeddings, reducing bias in retrieved results.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language contrastive models (VLCMs), such as CLIP, have become foundational, demonstrating remarkable success across a variety of downstream tasks. Despite their advantages, these models, akin to other foundational systems, inherit biases from the disproportionate distribution of real-world data, leading to misconceptions about the actual environment. Prevalent datasets like ImageNet are often riddled with non-causal, spurious correlations that can diminish VLCM performance in scenarios where these contextual elements are absent. This study presents an investigation into how a simple linear probe can effectively distill task-specific core features from CLIP's embedding for downstream applications. Our analysis reveals that the CLIP text representations are often tainted by spurious correlations, inherited in the biased pre-training dataset. Empirical evidence suggests that relying on visual representations from CLIP, as opposed to text embedding, is more effective to refine the skewed perceptions in VLCMs, emphasizing the superior utility of visual representations in overcoming embedded biases. Our code can be found here.

papers.title: Quantifying Structure in CLIP Embeddings: A Statistical Framework for Concept Interpretation
papers.research_question: How to quantify rotation-sensitive structures in CLIP embeddings and how to decompose embeddings into interpretable concepts with statistical guarantees?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hypothesis testing framework to detect rotation-sensitive structure in CLIP embeddings and a post-hoc concept decomposition method that balances interpretability and reconstruction fidelity with statistical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively quantifies rotation-sensitive structures in embeddings, and the decomposition method achieves both interpretability and high reconstruction fidelity, with applications to spurious correlation removal.
papers.key_findings:
The hypothesis test can distinguish between structured embeddings (e.g., ImageNet) and rotation-invariant noise (e.g., white noise).
The concept decomposition method yields interpretable concepts with high reconstruction fidelity, outperforming SpLiCE in reconstruction quality.
Removing spurious concepts identified by the method improves worst-group accuracy by 22.6% on Waterbirds and triples accuracy on iWildCam.
The method captures analogical relations between concepts, such as transforming 'single dog' to 'group of dogs' and applying to birds.
The method provides a flexible trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction fidelity by varying the number of concepts.
papers.limitation:
Assumes linearity in the embedding decomposition, which may overlook complex non-linear structures.
Interpretability of discovered concepts depends on the quality and scope of available text descriptions, which may introduce biases.
The hypothesis testing procedure does not explicitly handle structured, non-rotational noise patterns.
papers.abstract: Concept-based approaches, which aim to identify human-understandable concepts within a model's internal representations, are a promising method for interpreting embeddings from deep neural network models, such as CLIP. While these approaches help explain model behavior, current methods lack statistical rigor, making it challenging to validate identified concepts and compare different techniques. To address this challenge, we introduce a hypothesis testing framework that quantifies rotation-sensitive structures within the CLIP embedding space. Once such structures are identified, we propose a post-hoc concept decomposition method. Unlike existing approaches, it offers theoretical guarantees that discovered concepts represent robust, reproducible patterns (rather than method-specific artifacts) and outperforms other techniques in terms of reconstruction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that our concept-based decomposition algorithm effectively balances reconstruction accuracy with concept interpretability and helps mitigate spurious cues in data. Applied to a popular spurious correlation dataset, our method yields a 22.6% increase in worst-group accuracy after removing spurious background concepts.

papers.title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
papers.research_question: How faithfully do attributions reflect a component's influence on CLIP predictions? How effective are SAEs for extracting interpretable components? How robust is text-image probing in CLIP and what are typical failure cases? Can we detect spurious behavior in a CLIP-based classifier for melanoma detection?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for instance-wise attribution of latent components in CLIP by combining sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and attribution patching, revealing unexpected semantic reliance and failure modes.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a dual perspective on model behavior by explaining what concepts are encoded and how they influence predictions, highlighting the importance of mechanistic interpretability for reliable and safe deployment of multimodal foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution patching (Act×Grad) provides more faithful instance-wise attributions than the global Logit Lens method.
SAEs extract interpretable latent components from CLIP, with highly activated components being more interpretable.
Many SAE components encode unexpected concepts (e.g., clipart, game rendering, typography) not aligned with expected class labels.
Text embeddings in CLIP are relatively robust to spurious correlations compared to linear classifiers trained on image embeddings, which can amplify hidden shortcuts.
In a melanoma detection case study, the framework identified and mitigated a spurious correlation with red background hue, improving model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on class token embeddings from the final transformer block, potentially missing relevant dynamics in earlier layers.
SAEs may not capture all polysemantic or hidden latent concepts.
Semantic alignment relies on CLIP-Mobile-S2, which may itself be affected by spurious correlations or ambiguous language.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based CLIP models are widely used for text-image probing and feature extraction, making it relevant to understand the internal mechanisms behind their predictions. While recent works show that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) yield interpretable latent components, they focus on what these encode and miss how they drive predictions. We introduce a scalable framework that reveals what latent components activate for, how they align with expected semantics, and how important they are to predictions. To achieve this, we adapt attribution patching for instance-wise component attributions in CLIP and highlight key faithfulness limitations of the widely used Logit Lens technique. By combining attributions with semantic alignment scores, we can automatically uncover reliance on components that encode semantically unexpected or spurious concepts. Applied across multiple CLIP variants, our method uncovers hundreds of surprising components linked to polysemous words, compound nouns, visual typography and dataset artifacts. While text embeddings remain prone to semantic ambiguity, they are more robust to spurious correlations compared to linear classifiers trained on image embeddings. A case study on skin lesion detection highlights how such classifiers can amplify hidden shortcuts, underscoring the need for holistic, mechanistic interpretability. We provide code at https://github.com/maxdreyer/attributing-clip.

papers.title: Interpreting CLIP with Sparse Linear Concept Embeddings (SpLiCE)
papers.research_question: Can we decompose CLIP embeddings into human-interpretable representations of the semantic concepts they encode?
papers.core_contribution: SpLiCE is a method for decomposing CLIP embeddings into sparse, interpretable linear combinations of human-interpretable concepts without training, maintaining downstream performance and enabling applications like spurious correlation detection and model editing.
papers.conclusion: This work shows that CLIP embeddings can be approximated by sparse linear combinations of semantic concepts, and SpLiCE transforms dense CLIP embeddings into human-interpretable sparse concept decompositions.
papers.key_findings:
SpLiCE recovers highly sparse, interpretable representations with high performance on downstream tasks.
SpLiCE embeddings can detect spurious correlations, such as between 'woman' and 'swimwear' in CIFAR100.
SpLiCE enables model editing by removing or adjusting concept weights to improve fairness or remove biases.
SpLiCE representations closely match the semantic content of CLIP embeddings while discarding non-semantic noise.
The method is task-agnostic and does not require training.
papers.limitation:
The concept dictionary is limited to one- and two-word concepts and may not capture all salient concepts; it is built from LAION-5B which has its own biases.
SpLiCE uses an ℓ1 penalty as a relaxation for ℓ0 regularization, which may not be optimal.
future_direction: Expand the concept dictionary to include more than two-word concepts or learn a dictionary over tokens.
Explore alternative relaxations for sparsity or binary concept weights.
papers.abstract: CLIP embeddings have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of multimodal applications. However, these high-dimensional, dense vector representations are not easily interpretable, limiting our understanding of the rich structure of CLIP and its use in downstream applications that require transparency. In this work, we show that the semantic structure of CLIP's latent space can be leveraged to provide interpretability, allowing for the decomposition of representations into semantic concepts. We formulate this problem as one of sparse recovery and propose a novel method, Sparse Linear Concept Embeddings, for transforming CLIP representations into sparse linear combinations of human-interpretable concepts. Distinct from previous work, SpLiCE is task-agnostic and can be used, without training, to explain and even replace traditional dense CLIP representations, maintaining high downstream performance while significantly improving their interpretability. We also demonstrate significant use cases of SpLiCE representations including detecting spurious correlations and model editing.

papers.title: Concept Regions Matter: Benchmarking CLIP with a New Cluster-Importance Approach
papers.research_question: How do CLIP models rely on spurious correlations, particularly background overreliance, and how can we better diagnose and evaluate such vulnerabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cluster-based Concept Importance (CCI), a novel interpretability method for CLIP that identifies semantically coherent image regions driving predictions, and COVAR, a benchmark for systematically evaluating spurious background correlations.
papers.conclusion: CCI provides faithful interpretability for CLIP, and COVAR enables rigorous evaluation of spurious correlations, revealing that background reliance is only one of several factors affecting model robustness.
papers.key_findings:
CCI outperforms existing interpretability methods on faithfulness benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art deletion and insertion AUC scores.
Existing benchmarks like CounterAnimals are limited because accuracy drops are not solely due to background reliance; fine-grained confusions are a major error source.
The proposed COVAR benchmark disentangles the effects of background, viewpoint, scale, and other visual factors on model performance.
Scale and viewpoint variations cause significant accuracy drops and increase background reliance in CLIP models.
Fine-grained confusions remain the dominant source of errors across all evaluated CLIP variants and transformations.
future_direction: Using equivariant attention to reduce over-reliance on 2D context.
Curated pretraining data that decouples objects from typical contexts.
Hierarchical architectures with finer-grained patch granularity to reduce background dependence.
Part-based localization and attention mechanisms to improve fine-grained discrimination.
papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot recognition yet remain vulnerable to spurious correlations, particularly background over-reliance. We introduce Cluster-based Concept Importance (CCI), a novel interpretability method that uses CLIP's own patch embeddings to group spatial patches into semantically coherent clusters, mask them, and evaluate relative changes in model predictions. CCI sets a new state of the art on faithfulness benchmarks, surpassing prior methods by large margins; for example, it yields more than a twofold improvement on the deletion-AUC metric for MS COCO retrieval. We further propose that CCI, when combined with GroundedSAM, automatically categorizes predictions as foreground- or background-driven, providing a crucial diagnostic ability. Existing benchmarks such as CounterAnimals, however, rely solely on accuracy and implicitly attribute all performance degradation to background correlations. Our analysis shows this assumption to be incomplete, since many errors arise from viewpoint variation, scale shifts, and fine-grained object confusions. To disentangle these effects, we introduce COVAR, a benchmark that systematically varies object foregrounds and backgrounds. Leveraging CCI with COVAR, we present a comprehensive evaluation of eighteen CLIP variants, offering methodological advances and empirical evidence that chart a path toward more robust VLMs.

papers.title: LLM-assisted Concept Discovery: Automatically Identifying and Explaining Neuron Functions
papers.research_question: How to automatically provide textual concept-based explanations for neurons in deep neural networks without relying on predefined concepts or manual curation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an automatic method for discovering and validating interpretable concepts for neurons in deep neural networks using multimodal large language models and a novel validation score based on co-hyponyms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method addresses limitations of prior concept-based neuron explanation methods by enabling open-ended concept discovery and providing a validation score, leading to more insightful and distinctive explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method discovers interpretable concepts for neurons without requiring a predefined set of concepts, overcoming limitations of prior work.
The generated concepts are more specific and varied compared to prior methods like FALCON and MILAN, as shown by word frequency analysis.
The proposed validation score quantifies the specificity of a discovered concept by comparing neuron activations on generated examples and non-examples (co-hyponyms).
The method successfully labels neurons in ResNet50 with concepts matching or relating to ImageNet classes, achieving high accuracy.
The method effectively explains neurons in CLIP's vision encoder, discovering detailed concepts such as specific words or subjects in text.
papers.limitation:
Multimodal LLMs can produce unwanted outputs, such as concepts that are too abstract or unhelpful.
Multimodal LLMs have built-in safety mechanisms that may refuse prompts, especially when the exemplar representation does not appear to contain a single identifiable common concept.
LLMs have a limited understanding of concepts compared to humans, which can lead to failures in generating appropriate co-hyponyms.
future_direction: Use the concept validation score as a signal to create a feedback loop for automatically improving the discovery method.
papers.abstract: Providing textual concept-based explanations for neurons in deep neural networks (DNNs) is of importance in understanding how a DNN model works. Prior works have associated concepts with neurons based on examples of concepts or a pre-defined set of concepts, thus limiting possible explanations to what the user expects, especially in discovering new concepts. Furthermore, defining the set of concepts requires manual work from the user, either by directly specifying them or collecting examples. To overcome these, we propose to leverage multimodal large language models for automatic and open-ended concept discovery. We show that, without a restricted set of pre-defined concepts, our method gives rise to novel interpretable concepts that are more faithful to the model's behavior. To quantify this, we validate each concept by generating examples and counterexamples and evaluating the neuron's response on this new set of images. Collectively, our method can discover concepts and simultaneously validate them, providing a credible automated tool to explain deep neural networks.

papers.title: CLIP is All You Need for Human-like Semantic Representations in Stable Diffusion
papers.research_question: Does Stable Diffusion's internal representations during text-to-image generation contain human-like semantic information, and is this due to CLIP or the diffusion process?
papers.core_contribution: The semantic understanding in Stable Diffusion comes from the pretrained CLIP model, not the reverse diffusion process, which instead acts as a visual decoder of CLIP's representations.
papers.conclusion: CLIP is primarily responsible for the human-like semantic representations in Stable Diffusion, and the diffusion process serves as a visual decoder. Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial ones.
papers.key_findings:
Most human attribute ratings can be predicted from Stable Diffusion's latent representations with accuracy significantly below chance.
The semantic representation is most human-like at the output of CLIP, and the reverse diffusion process degrades this alignment.
Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial attributes across all model components.
CLIP can disentangle attributes that humans entangle, while the diffusion process tends to entangle attributes.
Attributes become more difficult to disambiguate from one another during the inverse diffusion process.
