Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Revealing Similar Semantics Inside CNNs: An Interpretable Concept-Based Comparison of Feature Spaces
papers.research_question: How can the similarity of semantic information inside different CNN architectures be estimated and compared?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes unsupervised and supervised methods for comparing the semantic information in CNN feature spaces, revealing that similar concepts are learned across different architectures and emerge at similar relative depths.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods enable the comparison of semantic information across CNN backbones, revealing that layers with similar semantic information can be found and that this information depends on relative layer depth.
papers.key_findings:
Similar semantic concepts are learned regardless of the CNN architecture.
Similar concepts emerge at similar relative layer depth, independent of the total number of layers.
Datasets with high semantic variability can lead to lower quality of automatic concept extraction.
The proposed methods can identify layers with similar semantic information across different networks.
The MobileNetV3 backbone exhibits a distinct pattern of capturing semantic information in two distinct regions.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on high-quality data and the semantic diversity of the test data strongly affects the quality of extracted concepts.
Limitations inherent to using ICE concept masks include differing and low mask resolution and dependence on the binarization threshold.
future_direction: Applying the approach to further large NN architectures, e.g., transformers, and other visual tasks than object detection.
Directly comparing non-binary concept masks to mitigate the dependence on the binarization threshold.
papers.abstract: Abstract Safety-critical applications require transparency in artificial intelligence (AI) components, but widely used convolutional neural networks (CNNs) widely used for perception tasks lack inherent interpretability. Hence, insights into what CNNs have learned are primarily based on performance metrics, because these allow, e.g., for cross-architecture CNN comparison. However, these neglect how knowledge is stored inside. To tackle this yet unsolved problem, our work proposes two methods for estimating the layer-wise similarity between semantic information inside CNN latent spaces. These allow insights into both the flow and likeness of semantic information within CNN layers, and into the degree of their similarity between different network architectures. As a basis, we use two renowned explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques, which are used to obtain concept activation vectors, i.e., global vector representations in the latent space. These are compared with respect to their activation on test inputs. When applied to three diverse object detectors and two datasets, our methods reveal that (1) similar semantic concepts are learned regardless of the CNN architecture , and (2) similar concepts emerge in similar relative layer depth, independent of the total number of layers. Finally, our approach poses a promising step towards semantic model comparability and comprehension of how different CNNs process semantic information.

papers.title: Interpreting CLIP's Image Representation via Text-Based Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we interpret CLIP's image representation by decomposing it into contributions from individual model components (attention heads and image patches) using text-based explanations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to interpret CLIP's image representation via text-based decomposition into attention heads and image patches, enabling improved zero-shot segmentation and reduction of spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Scalable understanding of transformer models is attainable and can be used to repair and improve models.
papers.key_findings:
The direct effect on the output is concentrated in the last 4 MSA layers.
TEXT SPAN reveals property-specific roles for many attention heads (e.g., location, shape, color).
Decomposition into image tokens yields a zero-shot segmenter that outperforms existing methods.
Removing heads associated with spurious cues improves worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 48% to 73%.
Joint decomposition visualizes which image regions contribute to specific text directions, validating the text labels.
papers.limitation:
Only direct effects are analyzed, not indirect effects.
Not all attention heads have clear roles.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other CLIP architectures (e.g., ResNet).
Use insights to design better CLIP image encoders and feature extractors for downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate the CLIP image encoder by analyzing how individual model components affect the final representation. We decompose the image representation as a sum across individual image patches, model layers, and attention heads, and use CLIP's text representation to interpret the summands. Interpreting the attention heads, we characterize each head's role by automatically finding text representations that span its output space, which reveals property-specific roles for many heads (e.g. location or shape). Next, interpreting the image patches, we uncover an emergent spatial localization within CLIP. Finally, we use this understanding to remove spurious features from CLIP and to create a strong zero-shot image segmenter. Our results indicate that a scalable understanding of transformer models is attainable and can be used to repair and improve models.

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
The approach provides a holistic, dataset-wide understanding of model behavior, tracing how concepts are constructed and aggregated from lower to higher layers.
future_direction: Extending the method to other deep learning architectures, such as Transformer models.
More thoroughly investigating the implications of analyzing entire datasets rather than focusing solely on class-specific explanations.
papers.abstract: In the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) in language models, the progression from local explanations of individual decisions to global explanations with high-level concepts has laid the groundwork for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to decode the exact operations. However, this paradigm has not been adequately explored in image models, where existing methods have primarily focused on class-specific interpretations. This paper introduces a novel approach to systematically trace the entire pathway from input through all intermediate layers to the final output within the whole dataset. We utilize Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors. Then, we calculate the relevance between concept vectors with our Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG), enabling a comprehensive, dataset-wide analysis of model behavior. We validate our method of concept extraction and concept attribution in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our approach advances the understanding of semantic significance within image models, offering a holistic view of their operational mechanics.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Visual Features in Artificial and Biological Neural Systems
papers.research_question: Does the activation space of neural networks contain meaningful, interpretable directions that are not aligned with individual neurons? And does this also apply to biological neural systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated method for quantifying visual interpretability using an interpretability index (II) and shows that non-axis aligned directions in activation space, found via methods like K-Means, are more interpretable than individual neurons, with similar findings in biological neural data.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that meaningful, interpretable directions exist in activation space beyond individual neurons in both artificial and biological neural systems, supporting the superposition hypothesis and suggesting universal coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpretability index (II) based on LPIPS similarity correlates with human psychophysics judgments, especially in early layers.
K-Means clusters in activation space yield directions that are more interpretable than individual neurons across low, mid, and high-level semantics.
Pairwise synergies between neurons can produce more interpretable directions, with correlated neurons tending to have higher synergy.
In biological neural data (macaque IT cortex and human fMRI), similar patterns are found, suggesting superposition might be deployed by the brain.
Interpretable directions transfer better across subjects and recording sessions than individual units, indicating greater universality.
papers.limitation: The interpretability metric based on LPIPS matches human judgments well for early layers but has room for improvement, particularly for later layers.
papers.abstract: Single neurons in neural networks are often interpretable in that they represent individual, intuitively meaningful features. However, many neurons exhibit $\textit{mixed selectivity}$, i.e., they represent multiple unrelated features. A recent hypothesis proposes that features in deep networks may be represented in $\textit{superposition}$, i.e., on non-orthogonal axes by multiple neurons, since the number of possible interpretable features in natural data is generally larger than the number of neurons in a given network. Accordingly, we should be able to find meaningful directions in activation space that are not aligned with individual neurons. Here, we propose (1) an automated method for quantifying visual interpretability that is validated against a large database of human psychophysics judgments of neuron interpretability, and (2) an approach for finding meaningful directions in network activation space. We leverage these methods to discover directions in convolutional neural networks that are more intuitively meaningful than individual neurons, as we confirm and investigate in a series of analyses. Moreover, we apply the same method to three recent datasets of visual neural responses in the brain and find that our conclusions largely transfer to real neural data, suggesting that superposition might be deployed by the brain. This also provides a link with disentanglement and raises fundamental questions about robust, efficient and factorized representations in both artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: VITRIX-CLIPIN: Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in CLIP via Instruction Editing Data and Long Captions
papers.research_question: How can we effectively and scalably enrich vision-language models like CLIP with robust fine-grained visual understanding by harnessing data sources that offer explicit, targeted supervision for subtle visual-semantic distinctions, while simultaneously leveraging the contextual richness of descriptive language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLIP-IN, a framework that enhances CLIP's fine-grained visual perception by leveraging instruction editing data as hard negative pairs and incorporating long descriptive captions with Rotary Positional Encodings.
papers.conclusion: CLIP-IN effectively enhances fine-grained visual understanding in CLIP without compromising zero-shot performance, and its integration into MLLMs reduces hallucinations and improves reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP-IN significantly improves fine-grained visual perception on the MMVP benchmark, e.g., +11.9pp average accuracy for ViT-L/14.
CLIP-IN achieves competitive or superior zero-shot performance on ImageNet classification and short/long-text retrieval tasks.
Integrating CLIP-IN's visual representations into Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) reduces visual hallucinations and enhances reasoning abilities.
Instruction editing data and long caption data provide complementary benefits, with their combination yielding the best overall performance.
The symmetric hard negative contrastive loss is more effective than one-directional or triplet loss alternatives.
papers.limitation: The performance gap in long caption retrieval compared to FG-CLIP is attributed to using significantly less long caption training data (18M vs 1B pairs).
papers.abstract: Despite the success of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP in aligning vision and language, their proficiency in detailed, fine-grained visual comprehension remains a key challenge. We present CLIP-IN, a novel framework that bolsters CLIP's fine-grained perception through two core innovations. Firstly, we leverage instruction-editing datasets, originally designed for image manipulation, as a unique source of hard negative image-text pairs. Coupled with a symmetric hard negative contrastive loss, this enables the model to effectively distinguish subtle visual-semantic differences. Secondly, CLIP-IN incorporates long descriptive captions, utilizing rotary positional encodings to capture rich semantic context often missed by standard CLIP. Our experiments demonstrate that CLIP-IN achieves substantial gains on the MMVP benchmark and various fine-grained visual recognition tasks, without compromising robust zero-shot performance on broader classification and retrieval tasks. Critically, integrating CLIP-IN's visual representations into Multimodal Large Language Models significantly reduces visual hallucinations and enhances reasoning abilities. This work underscores the considerable potential of synergizing targeted, instruction-based contrastive learning with comprehensive descriptive information to elevate the fine-grained understanding of VLMs.

papers.title: Investigating the Encoding of Words in BERT’s Neurons Using Feature Textualization
papers.research_question: Can the knowledge encoded in individual neurons of BERT be interpreted and symbolized as words, and how many neurons are needed to encode words?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces feature textualization, an adaptation of activation maximization for language models, and uses it to show that single neurons in BERT do not encode words, but groups of 250-450 neurons can be associated with word-like representations.
papers.conclusion: Feature textualization can reveal information encoded in groups of neurons in language models, showing that single neurons do not encode words but groups of 250-450 neurons can be associated with word-like representations.
papers.key_findings:
Words only utilize about 3% of the theoretical activation potential of single neurons, indicating word-based interpretations are not faithful.
Optimized inputs for single neurons are not semantically similar to word embeddings (average cosine similarity ~0.124).
For groups of 250-450 neurons, optimized inputs become similar to word embeddings (cosine similarity ~0.26) and the target word is the closest word in 67% of cases.
Feature textualization can reveal the information encoded in groups of neurons, helping to locate encoded knowledge in model parameters.
The method is computationally expensive and currently infeasible for very large language models.
papers.limitation:
The method is computationally expensive and infeasible for very large language models.
The interpretations are model-specific and do not generalize.
Non-regularized optimal inputs might be adversarial and lie in uninterpretable parts of the vector space.
future_direction: Investigate what high-level semantic knowledge is encoded within neurons, beyond word-level interpretations.
Develop regularizers to pull optimized inputs towards the populated part of the word embedding space.
Apply the method to other language models, including fine-tuned or larger models, and investigate contextualized inputs.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) form the basis of most state-of-the-art NLP technologies. Nevertheless, they are essentially black boxes: Humans do not have a clear understanding of what knowledge is encoded in different parts of the models, especially in individual neurons. A contrast is in computer vision, where feature visualization provides a decompositional interpretability technique for neurons of vision models. Activation maximization is used to synthesize inherently interpretable visual representations of the information encoded in individual neurons. Our work is inspired by this but presents a cautionary tale on the interpretability of single neurons, based on the first large-scale attempt to adapt activation maximization to NLP, and, more specifically, large PLMs. We propose feature textualization, a technique to produce dense representations of neurons in the PLM word embedding space. We apply feature textualization to the BERT model to investigate whether the knowledge encoded in individual neurons can be interpreted and symbolized. We find that the produced representations can provide insights about the knowledge encoded in individual neurons, but that individual neurons do not represent clear-cut symbolic units of language such as words. Additionally, we use feature textualization to investigate how many neurons are needed to encode words in BERT.

papers.title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we automatically discover and name concepts learned by a model (CLIP) and use them to build interpretable concept bottleneck models for classification?
papers.core_contribution: We propose DN-CBM, a novel concept bottleneck model that first discovers concepts learned by CLIP using sparse autoencoders, then automatically names them via CLIP text embeddings, and finally uses these named concepts for interpretable classification across multiple downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: DN-CBM is an effective method for building interpretable concept bottleneck models by automatically discovering and naming concepts learned by CLIP in a task-agnostic way, leading to performant and interpretable classifiers.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can discover human-interpretable concepts from CLIP vision encoders.
The dictionary vectors of the sparse autoencoder align well with CLIP text embeddings, enabling automated concept naming.
The discovered and named concepts can be used as a task-agnostic concept bottleneck, yielding performant and interpretable classifiers for various downstream datasets.
The approach is efficient as concept discovery is done once in a task-agnostic manner and then reused for multiple classification tasks.
User studies show that the discovered concepts are semantically consistent and accurately named compared to baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The granularity and size of the vocabulary used for naming can limit the accuracy and specificity of assigned concept names.
Some discovered concepts may not be human-interpretable, particularly those with low alignment between dictionary vectors and text embeddings.
The approach is currently limited to vision-language models like CLIP and may not generalize to other model types.
future_direction: Extending the approach to other modalities and model architectures.
Improving the vocabulary for naming to include more fine-grained and diverse concepts.
Investigating and mitigating spurious correlations between concepts that may affect interpretability.
papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) have recently been proposed to address the 'black-box' problem of deep neural networks, by first mapping images to a human-understandable concept space and then linearly combining concepts for classification. Such models typically require first coming up with a set of concepts relevant to the task and then aligning the representations of a feature extractor to map to these concepts. However, even with powerful foundational feature extractors like CLIP, there are no guarantees that the specified concepts are detectable. In this work, we leverage recent advances in mechanistic interpretability and propose a novel CBM approach -- called Discover-then-Name-CBM (DN-CBM) -- that inverts the typical paradigm: instead of pre-selecting concepts based on the downstream classification task, we use sparse autoencoders to first discover concepts learnt by the model, and then name them and train linear probes for classification. Our concept extraction strategy is efficient, since it is agnostic to the downstream task, and uses concepts already known to the model. We perform a comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets and CLIP architectures and show that our method yields semantically meaningful concepts, assigns appropriate names to them that make them easy to interpret, and yields performant and interpretable CBMs. Code available at https://github.com/neuroexplicit-saar/discover-then-name.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: Do Vision-Language Pretrained Models Learn Composable Primitive Concepts?
papers.research_question: Whether vision-language pretrained models automatically learn representations of primitive concepts (e.g., colors, shapes) that can be composed to form composite concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the CompMap framework to measure how well VL models learn primitive concepts, and finds that while the learned concepts are useful for recognition tasks, they are not interpretable in a human-like compositional way.
papers.conclusion: Existing VL pretrained models do not learn interpretable primitive concepts, highlighting the importance of developing pretraining objectives that encourage such learning.
papers.key_findings:
State-of-the-art VL pretrained models learn primitive concepts that are highly useful for fine-grained visual recognition and compositional generalization tasks.
The learned composition models have low interpretability, indicating the model's conceptualization does not align well with human compositional reasoning.
Composition models often rely on spurious correlations between primitive concept activations and composite concepts rather than true primitive concepts.
Larger model sizes improve usefulness but not interpretability of the learned primitive concepts.
The choice of prompt templates has a marginal impact on usefulness but a larger impact on interpretability.
papers.limitation: Existing VL models do not learn interpretable primitive concepts, indicating a limitation in their pretraining.
future_direction: Improve VL pretraining objectives to encourage learning interpretable primitive concepts.
papers.abstract: Vision-language (VL) pretrained models have achieved impressive performance on multimodal reasoning and zero-shot recognition tasks. Many of these VL models are pretrained on unlabeled image and caption pairs from the internet. In this paper, we study whether representations of primitive concepts--such as colors, shapes, or the attributes of object parts--emerge automatically within these pretrained VL models. We propose a two-step framework, Compositional Concept Mapping (CompMap), to investigate this. CompMap first asks a VL model to generate primitive concept activations with text prompts, and then learns to construct a composition model that maps the primitive concept activations (e.g. the likelihood of black tail or red wing) to composite concepts (e.g. a red-winged blackbird). We show that a composition model can be reliably learn from ground truth primitive concepts. We thus hypothesize that if primitive concepts indeed emerge in a VL pretrained model, its primitive concept activations can be used to learn a composition model similar to the one designed by experts. We propose a quantitative metric to measure the degree of similarity, and refer to the metric as the interpretability metric. We also measure the classification accuracy when using the primitive concept activations and the learned composition model to predict the composite concepts, and refer to it as the usefulness metric. Our study reveals that state-of-the-art VL pretrained models learn primitive concepts that are highly useful for fine-grained visual recognition on the CUB dataset, and compositional generalization tasks on the MIT-States dataset. However, we observe that the learned composition models have low interpretability in our qualitative analyses. Our results reveal the limitations of existing VL models, and the necessity of pretraining objectives that encourage the acquisition of primitive concepts.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Textual Explanations via Translating Decision-Critical Features
papers.research_question: How to generate faithful textual explanations for image classifiers by isolating decision-critical features, rather than using global image features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TEXTER, a zero-shot framework that generates textual explanations for image classifiers by isolating decision-critical features via concept images and aligning them with CLIP.
papers.conclusion: TEXTER isolates decision-critical features to generate faithful textual explanations, improving interpretability across CNN and Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
TEXTER generates textual explanations that are more faithful to the model's decision rationale than existing zero-shot methods.
Concept images effectively isolate decision-critical features, as validated by metrics like accuracy and confidence ratio.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) improves concept image interpretability, especially for Transformer models.
TEXTER generalizes across CNN and Transformer architectures.
TEXTER enables class-specific explanations, which can help analyze misclassifications.
papers.abstract: Textual explanations make image classifier decisions transparent by describing the prediction rationale in natural language. Large vision-language models can generate captions but are designed for general visual understanding, not classifier-specific reasoning. Existing zero-shot explanation methods align global image features with language, producing descriptions of what is visible rather than what drives the prediction. We propose TEXTER, which overcomes this limitation by isolating decision-critical features before alignment. TEXTER identifies the neurons contributing to the prediction and emphasizes the features encoded in those neurons -- i.e., the decision-critical features. It then maps these emphasized features into the CLIP feature space to retrieve textual explanations that reflect the model's reasoning. A sparse autoencoder further improves interpretability, particularly for Transformer architectures. Extensive experiments show that TEXTER generates more faithful and interpretable explanations than existing methods. The code will be publicly released.

papers.title: Concept-based Analysis of Neural Networks via Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we leverage vision-language models to enable formal, concept-based analysis and verification of vision-based deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Conspec, a concept-based specification language for vision models, and a verification procedure that uses an affine map between vision model and VLM representations to enable efficient checking of natural-language properties.
papers.conclusion: VLMs enable concept-based analysis and verification of vision models, providing a scalable and human-understandable way to specify and check properties.
papers.key_findings:
The concept representation map implemented using CLIP shows high satisfaction probabilities for strength predicates, indicating it is semantically meaningful.
The affine map between ResNet18 and CLIP representation spaces has low MSE and high R2, but counterexamples show the alignment is not faithful.
Verification of ResNet18 using Conspec specifications can be reduced to solving linear constraints, enabling efficient analysis.
For CLIP, verification shows that while properties may be violated, the violation strength is small for regions close to the mean embedding.
The approach enables formal verification of concept-based properties for vision models, as demonstrated on RIVAL-10.
papers.limitation:
Verification soundness depends on the concept representation map implemented via VLM, which may not perfectly capture human understanding.
The affine map between vision model and VLM representation spaces may not be faithful, leading to potential misalignment.
Verification is restricted to input scopes approximating in-distribution data, as verifying over all inputs is too strong.
future_direction: Exploring aggregate concepts with logical connectives built into the concepts themselves.
Extending the verification approach to handle non-linear heads in neural networks.
Applying the approach to other vision tasks and models beyond image classification.
papers.abstract: The analysis of vision-based deep neural networks (DNNs) is highly desirable but it is very challenging due to the difficulty of expressing formal specifications for vision tasks and the lack of efficient verification procedures. In this paper, we propose to leverage emerging multimodal, vision-language, foundation models (VLMs) as a lens through which we can reason about vision models. VLMs have been trained on a large body of images accompanied by their textual description, and are thus implicitly aware of high-level, human-understandable concepts describing the images. We describe a logical specification language $\texttt{Con}_{\texttt{spec}}$ designed to facilitate writing specifications in terms of these concepts. To define and formally check $\texttt{Con}_{\texttt{spec}}$ specifications, we build a map between the internal representations of a given vision model and a VLM, leading to an efficient verification procedure of natural-language properties for vision models. We demonstrate our techniques on a ResNet-based classifier trained on the RIVAL-10 dataset using CLIP as the multimodal model.

papers.title: When are Lemons Purple? The Concept Association Bias of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do vision-language models like CLIP struggle with tasks requiring fine-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA)? The paper investigates a potential cause called Concept Association Bias (CAB).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the Concept Association Bias (CAB) in vision-language models, showing that models trained with contrastive losses tend to treat input as a bag of concepts and incorrectly fill in missing concepts crossmodally, which hinders performance on tasks like VQA.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Association Bias (CAB) is a prevalent issue in contrastively trained vision-language models, and reducing CAB correlates with improved performance on tasks like VQA, highlighting a brittleness in contrastive objectives.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP and other contrastively trained vision-language models exhibit CAB, leading to errors in zero-shot color and part-whole recognition when multiple objects are present (e.g., predicting a lemon is purple when an eggplant is also in the image).
The strength of CAB is correlated with the association strength between concepts (e.g., 'eggplant' and 'purple').
Models trained solely with autoregressive loss (like OFA) show minimal or no CAB.
Adding a Transformer head for deeper modality interaction and fine-tuning on VQA-v2 reduces CAB and improves VQA performance.
Fine-tuning on VQA may not fundamentally solve the general binding problem of correctly associating objects and attributes.
papers.limitation:
Only explored color and part-whole object-attribute relationships; other relationships like material, shape, and texture were not studied.
Focused on VQA and a limited set of models (CLIP, BLIP, BLIP-2, OFA); other vision-language tasks and models with more extensive modality interactions were not investigated.
future_direction: Explore the effect of CAB on other vision-language tasks (e.g., visual entailment).
Investigate other methods to mitigate CAB.
Study other vision-language models that incorporate more extensive modality interactions (e.g., FLAVA, ALBEF).
papers.abstract: Large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP have shown impressive performance on zero-shot image classification and image-to-text retrieval. However, such performance does not realize in tasks that require a finer-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA). As a potential cause of the difficulty of applying these models to VQA and similar tasks, we report an interesting phenomenon of vision-language models, which we call the Concept Association Bias (CAB). We find that models with CAB tend to treat input as a bag of concepts and attempt to fill in the other missing concept crossmodally, leading to an unexpected zero-shot prediction. We demonstrate CAB by showing that CLIP's zero-shot classification performance greatly suffers when there is a strong concept association between an object (e.g. eggplant) and an attribute (e.g. color purple). We also show that the strength of CAB predicts the performance on VQA. We observe that CAB is prevalent in vision-language models trained with contrastive losses, even when autoregressive losses are jointly employed. However, a model that solely relies on autoregressive loss seems to exhibit minimal or no signs of CAB.

papers.title: Unveiling Backbone Effects in CLIP: Exploring Representational Synergies and Variances
papers.research_question: What are the differences in performance and representations among CLIP backbones (ResNets and Vision Transformers) and how can we effectively combine their predictions to improve zero-shot classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that different CLIP backbones exhibit orthogonal predictions, and introducing a simple parametric method to combine their predictions via learned temperature scaling improves zero-shot classification performance.
papers.conclusion: There is significant orthogonality in CLIP backbone predictions, and combining them with a simple parametric method like neural network combination (NNC) can yield substantial gains in zero-shot classification.
papers.key_findings:
Different CLIP backbones (ResNets and ViTs) exhibit orthogonal predictions, meaning they correctly classify different subsets of images.
Normalization of representations affects performance, with L2 normalization generally performing best.
An oracle that selects the best backbone per image can improve accuracy by over 20% on some datasets.
Combining backbones via learned temperature scaling (using a genetic algorithm or a small MLP) improves over the best single backbone, with up to 6.34% improvement.
The neural network combination (NNC) method is data-efficient, requiring as few as one instance to outperform the best single backbone.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) stands out as a prominent method for image representation learning. Various neural architectures, spanning Transformer-based models like Vision Transformers (ViTs) to Convolutional Networks (ConvNets) like ResNets, are trained with CLIP and serve as universal backbones across diverse vision tasks. Despite utilizing the same data and training objectives, the effectiveness of representations learned by these architectures raises a critical question. Our investigation explores the differences in CLIP performance among these backbone architectures, revealing significant disparities in their classifications. Notably, normalizing these representations results in substantial performance variations. Our findings showcase a remarkable possible synergy between backbone predictions that could reach an improvement of over 20% through informed selection of the appropriate backbone. Moreover, we propose a simple, yet effective approach to combine predictions from multiple backbones, leading to a notable performance boost of up to 6.34\%. We will release the code for reproducing the results.

papers.title: Granular Concept Circuits: Toward a Fine-Grained Circuit Discovery for Concept Representations
papers.research_question: How can we discover fine-grained circuits that represent specific visual concepts in deep image classification models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), a method for automatically discovering fine-grained circuits that represent specific visual concepts in deep image classification models.
papers.conclusion: Introduces Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), a novel method for fine-grained visual concept circuit discovery, contributing to AI interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
GCC can discover multiple distinct concept circuits for a single query, enabling fine-grained interpretation.
GCC is effective across various model architectures (CNNs and Transformers) and datasets.
Ablation of neurons in GCC leads to significant logit/accuracy drops, demonstrating faithfulness and completeness.
User study shows that GCC circuits are perceived as meaningful and diverse by human evaluators.
GCC can be applied to audit misclassifications and identify shared concepts across different classes.
papers.limitation:
Connectivity is evaluated in a model-centric manner, so some strongly associated connections may remain difficult to interpret.
A single concept may be distributed across multiple circuit pathways, especially under strict connectivity thresholds.
papers.abstract: Deep vision models have achieved remarkable classification performance by leveraging a hierarchical architecture in which human-interpretable concepts emerge through the composition of individual neurons across layers. Given the distributed nature of representations, pinpointing where specific visual concepts are encoded within a model remains a crucial yet challenging task. In this paper, we introduce an effective circuit discovery method, called Granular Concept Circuit (GCC), in which each circuit represents a concept relevant to a given query. To construct each circuit, our method iteratively assesses inter-neuron connectivity, focusing on both functional dependencies and semantic alignment. By automatically discovering multiple circuits, each capturing specific concepts within that query, our approach offers a profound, concept-wise interpretation of models and is the first to identify circuits tied to specific visual concepts at a fine-grained level. We validate the versatility and effectiveness of GCCs across various deep image classification models.

papers.title: Interpreting and Analysing CLIP's Zero-Shot Image Classification via Mutual Knowledge
papers.research_question: What concepts do both vision and language CLIP encoders learn in common that influence the joint embedding space, causing points to be closer or further apart?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free, multimodal concept-based approach to interpret CLIP's zero-shot image classification by analyzing the mutual knowledge between vision and language encoders via textual concepts and mutual information.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach offers an effective and human-friendly way to understand zero-shot classification decisions with CLIP by interpreting the mutual knowledge between its vision and language encoders.
papers.key_findings:
Multimodal concept-based explanations outperform trained baselines on several XAI metrics and can boost zero-shot accuracy by up to 3.75%.
Mutual information dynamics (AUC) between vision and language concepts correlate with zero-shot accuracy, indicating stronger shared knowledge in better-performing models.
The method provides human-friendly, fine-grained explanations by identifying shared textual concepts that influence classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) performs zero-shot image classification by mapping images and textual class representation into a shared embedding space, then retrieving the class closest to the image. This work provides a new approach for interpreting CLIP models for image classification from the lens of mutual knowledge between the two modalities. Specifically, we ask: what concepts do both vision and language CLIP encoders learn in common that influence the joint embedding space, causing points to be closer or further apart? We answer this question via an approach of textual concept-based explanations, showing their effectiveness, and perform an analysis encompassing a pool of 13 CLIP models varying in architecture, size and pretraining datasets. We explore those different aspects in relation to mutual knowledge, and analyze zero-shot predictions. Our approach demonstrates an effective and human-friendly way of understanding zero-shot classification decisions with CLIP.

papers.title: TextCAM: Explaining Class Activation Map with Text
papers.research_question: How can Class Activation Mapping (CAM) explanations be enriched with natural-language rationales to provide semantic insight into the visual attributes underlying model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TextCAM, a training-free framework that enriches Class Activation Maps (CAM) with natural-language explanations by combining the spatial localization of CAM with the semantic alignment of vision-language models (e.g., CLIP).
papers.conclusion: TextCAM is a training-free method that couples CAM spatial evidence with CLIP semantics to deliver faithful, concise explanations and concept-grouped saliency, enhancing interpretability for pure vision models.
papers.key_findings:
TextCAM produces faithful and interpretable textual rationales that specify both where a model attends and what visual attributes likely support its decision.
The method can detect spurious correlations (e.g., reliance on background cues) and has been applied to guide debiasing by suppressing color-dominant channels in a shape recognition task.
TextCAM is architecture-agnostic, working with various CNN and transformer backbones and different CAM variants (e.g., Grad-CAM, Layer-CAM) without altering model weights.
Experiments on ImageNet, CLEVR, CUB, and DomainNet show that TextCAM explanations align with human intuition and dataset characteristics (e.g., shape attributes dominate in sketch domains).
The extension to saliency grouping partitions feature channels into semantically coherent groups, yielding fine-grained text-annotated saliency maps.
papers.limitation: Sensitivity of CAM-style weights in some transformer backbones.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across domains but remain difficult to interpret, limiting their trustworthiness in high-stakes applications. This paper focuses on deep vision models, for which a dominant line of explainability methods are Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and its variants working by highlighting spatial regions that drive predictions. We figure out that CAM provides little semantic insight into what attributes underlie these activations. To address this limitation, we propose TextCAM, a novel explanation framework that enriches CAM with natural languages. TextCAM combines the precise spatial localization of CAM with the semantic alignment of vision-language models (VLMs). Specifically, we derive channel-level semantic representations using CLIP embeddings and linear discriminant analysis, and aggregate them with CAM weights to produce textual descriptions of salient visual evidence. This yields explanations that jointly specify where the model attends and what visual attributes likely support its decision. We further extend TextCAM to generate feature channels into semantically coherent groups, enabling more fine-grained visual-textual explanations. Experiments on ImageNet, CLEVR, and CUB demonstrate that TextCAM produces faithful and interpretable rationales that improve human understanding, detect spurious correlations, and preserve model fidelity.

papers.title: What do Vision Transformers Learn? A Visual Exploration
papers.research_question: What do vision transformers learn and how do they differ from convolutional neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a visualization framework for ViTs and finds that ViTs preserve spatial information except in the last layer, use background information more effectively than CNNs, and with language supervision learn semantic concepts.
papers.conclusion: ViTs learn spatial relationships from scratch and their last layer performs token mixing similar to average pooling; ViTs and CNNs share similarities in feature progression but differ in use of background and high-frequency information.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs preserve spatial information in all layers except the last layer, which behaves like a learned global pooling operation.
ViTs make better use of background information than CNNs and are less reliant on high-frequency texture information.
ViTs show a progression from edges/textures to parts to objects in deeper layers, similar to CNNs.
ViTs trained with CLIP learn features corresponding to abstract concepts and linguistic elements (prepositions, adjectives, etc.).
The feed-forward layer in ViTs is more interpretable for visualization than keys, queries, and values.
papers.limitation: Visualization method fails for low-dimensional components like keys, queries, and values due to feature entanglement
papers.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) are quickly becoming the de-facto architecture for computer vision, yet we understand very little about why they work and what they learn. While existing studies visually analyze the mechanisms of convolutional neural networks, an analogous exploration of ViTs remains challenging. In this paper, we first address the obstacles to performing visualizations on ViTs. Assisted by these solutions, we observe that neurons in ViTs trained with language model supervision (e.g., CLIP) are activated by semantic concepts rather than visual features. We also explore the underlying differences between ViTs and CNNs, and we find that transformers detect image background features, just like their convolutional counterparts, but their predictions depend far less on high-frequency information. On the other hand, both architecture types behave similarly in the way features progress from abstract patterns in early layers to concrete objects in late layers. In addition, we show that ViTs maintain spatial information in all layers except the final layer. In contrast to previous works, we show that the last layer most likely discards the spatial information and behaves as a learned global pooling operation. Finally, we conduct large-scale visualizations on a wide range of ViT variants, including DeiT, CoaT, ConViT, PiT, Swin, and Twin, to validate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: AlignedCut: Visual Concepts Discovery on Brain-Guided Universal Feature Space
papers.research_question: How can we discover visual concepts shared across different deep networks by aligning channels using brain fMRI data as guidance?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce AlignedCut, a method that aligns channels across different deep networks using brain fMRI data as guidance and discovers recurring visual concepts through spectral clustering.
papers.conclusion: Our key discovery is that recurring visual concepts exist across networks and layers, corresponding to different levels of objects, from figure-ground to categories, and we quantified the information flow, finding a bifurcation of figure-ground visual concepts.
papers.key_findings:
Shared channel sets, recurring across layers and models, predict response in distinct brain regions and encode visual concepts at various levels of abstraction.
Meaningful object segments (figure-ground separation and fine-grained categories) emerge by tracing channel cluster responses onto images without a supervised decoder.
Figure-ground representation emerges before category representation (e.g., in CLIP, figure-ground at layer-4, categories peak at layer-9/10).
The figure-ground visual concept is class-agnostic and consistent across CLIP, DINO, and MAE models.
A bifurcation of figure and ground pixel representations occurs at the middle layers (e.g., CLIP layer-4, DINO layer-5), showing separate encoding paths.
papers.limitation:
The learned channel align transformation does not preserve all information, leading to a drop in unsupervised segmentation performance.
The Nystrom-like approximation does not produce strictly orthogonal eigenvectors, trading orthogonality for faster computation.
papers.abstract: We study the intriguing connection between visual data, deep networks, and the brain. Our method creates a universal channel alignment by using brain voxel fMRI response prediction as the training objective. We discover that deep networks, trained with different objectives, share common feature channels across various models. These channels can be clustered into recurring sets, corresponding to distinct brain regions, indicating the formation of visual concepts. Tracing the clusters of channel responses onto the images, we see semantically meaningful object segments emerge, even without any supervised decoder. Furthermore, the universal feature alignment and the clustering of channels produce a picture and quantification of how visual information is processed through the different network layers, which produces precise comparisons between the networks.

papers.title: Selectivity considered harmful: evaluating the causal impact of class selectivity in DNNs
papers.research_question: Is class selectivity in individual units necessary and/or sufficient for DNN function?
papers.core_contribution: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can even impair it; reducing selectivity can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can be detrimental. This encourages caution when focusing on single-unit properties and emphasizes distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
Reducing class selectivity can improve test accuracy, e.g., by over 2% for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet.
Class selectivity can be reduced by a factor of 2.5 in ResNet20 on CIFAR10 with no impact on test accuracy, and nearly to zero with only a small drop.
Increasing class selectivity significantly decreases test accuracy across all models and datasets.
The regularizer suppresses selectivity generally, not just by rotating it off-axis, indicating viability of low-selectivity distributed representations.
Networks are at a performance cliff with regard to class selectivity; naturally learned levels are at the limit of what impairs performance.
papers.abstract: The properties of individual neurons are often analyzed in order to understand the biological and artificial neural networks in which they're embedded. Class selectivity-typically defined as how different a neuron's responses are across different classes of stimuli or data samples-is commonly used for this purpose. However, it remains an open question whether it is necessary and/or sufficient for deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn class selectivity in individual units. We investigated the causal impact of class selectivity on network function by directly regularizing for or against class selectivity. Using this regularizer to reduce class selectivity across units in convolutional neural networks increased test accuracy by over 2% for ResNet18 trained on Tiny ImageNet. For ResNet20 trained on CIFAR10 we could reduce class selectivity by a factor of 2.5 with no impact on test accuracy, and reduce it nearly to zero with only a small ($\sim$2%) drop in test accuracy. In contrast, regularizing to increase class selectivity significantly decreased test accuracy across all models and datasets. These results indicate that class selectivity in individual units is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary, and can even impair DNN performance. They also encourage caution when focusing on the properties of single units as representative of the mechanisms by which DNNs function.

papers.title: The Hard Positive Truth about Vision-Language Compositionality
papers.research_question: Are existing benchmarks for vision-language compositionality complete, and does finetuning with hard negatives alone lead to models that are oversensitive and fail to remain invariant to semantic-preserving hard positives?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that existing vision-language compositionality benchmarks are incomplete because they ignore hard positives (semantic-preserving caption perturbations). It shows that finetuning CLIP with only hard negatives induces oversensitivity, harming performance on hard positives. The paper proposes finetuning with both hard positives and hard negatives, leading to more robust improvements in compositionality.
papers.conclusion: Hard positives are a vital component of compositionality evaluation that has been overlooked. Finetuning with both hard positives and hard negatives leads to more robust improvements, but model performance remains far behind human capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP models perform poorly on hard positives, with performance dropping by 12.9% when evaluated with hard positives versus hard negatives alone.
Finetuning CLIP with hard negatives alone significantly degrades performance on hard positives (up to 38.7% drop) and makes models oversensitive, often ranking hard negatives above hard positives.
Finetuning CLIP with both hard positives and hard negatives improves performance on hard positives while largely retaining gains on hard negatives and standard benchmarks.
Oversensitivity from hard-negative finetuning transfers across perturbation types (swap and replace), but improved invariance from hard-positive training does not.
Human performance on the hard positive evaluation is near-perfect (99%), indicating a large gap between model and human compositionality.
papers.limitation:
The work is limited to CLIP-style models and does not evaluate vision-language generation models like Flamingo, BLIP, or GPT-4V.
Model performance on hard positives, while improved, is still far behind human performance.
future_direction: Investigate more rigorously how finetuning methods targeting specific behaviors can cause adverse effects on overall model behavior.
Develop finetuning techniques that do not cause such adverse effects and achieve robust vision-language compositionality.
Evaluate vision-language generation models to isolate the effects of architecture and training objective.
papers.abstract: Several benchmarks have concluded that our best vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) are lacking in compositionality. Given an image, these benchmarks probe a model's ability to identify its associated caption amongst a set of compositional distractors. In response, a surge of recent proposals show improvements by finetuning CLIP with distractors as hard negatives. Our investigations reveal that these improvements have, in fact, been significantly overstated -- because existing benchmarks do not probe whether finetuned vision-language models remain invariant to hard positives. By curating an evaluation dataset with 112,382 hard negatives and hard positives, we uncover that including hard positives decreases CLIP's performance by 12.9%, while humans perform effortlessly at 99%. CLIP finetuned with hard negatives results in an even larger decrease, up to 38.7%. With this finding, we then produce a 1,775,259 image-text training set with both hard negative and hard positive captions. By training with both, we see improvements on existing benchmarks while simultaneously improving performance on hard positives, indicating a more robust improvement in compositionality. Our work suggests the need for future research to rigorously test and improve CLIP's understanding of semantic relationships between related "positive" concepts.

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.research_question: Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes.
papers.core_contribution: LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by natural scenes and provide a representational format that accounts for complex visual information extracted by the brain.
papers.conclusion: LLM embeddings provide a versatile representational format for capturing complex information derived by the brain from visual inputs, paving the way for new research avenues.
papers.key_findings:
LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully predict brain activity across higher-level visual areas.
Linear encoding and decoding models using LLM embeddings can capture region-specific tuning properties and reconstruct accurate scene captions from brain activity.
The alignment derives from LLMs' ability to integrate complex information beyond individual words or object categories.
ANNs trained to predict LLM embeddings from images learn representations better aligned with brain activity than many state-of-the-art models, despite less training data.
papers.limitation: The task of the NSD participants was to report if they had previously seen each presented image. It cannot be fully ruled out that, to perform this continuous recognition task, participants were internally captioning the scenes, and this may have benefitted the LLM caption embeddings as a good model of visual responses.
future_direction: Exploring datasets where prepositions, adjectives and adverbs play a more important role is an intriguing direction for future research.
An interesting future direction of research will spell out whether the rich learning signal derived from language might indeed provide important benefits over other training objectives.
It will be interesting for future work to investigate LLM-based codes under different tasks.
papers.abstract: The human brain extracts complex information from visual inputs, including objects, their spatial and semantic interrelations, and their interactions with the environment. However, a quantitative approach for studying this information remains elusive. Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes. We show that LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by viewing the natural scenes. This mapping captures selectivities of different brain areas and is sufficiently robust that accurate scene captions can be reconstructed from brain activity. Using carefully controlled model comparisons, we then proceed to show that the accuracy with which LLM representations match brain representations derives from the ability of LLMs to integrate complex information contained in scene captions beyond that conveyed by individual words. Finally, we train deep neural network models to transform image inputs into LLM representations. Remarkably, these networks learn representations that are better aligned with brain representations than a large number of state-of-the-art alternative models, despite being trained on orders-of-magnitude less data. Overall, our results suggest that LLM embeddings of scene captions provide a representational format that accounts for complex information extracted by the brain from visual inputs.

papers.title: Linking in Style: Understanding learned features in deep learning models
papers.research_question: How to visualize and systematically analyze learned features in convolutional neural networks for object classification.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a linking network and an automated pipeline to visualize and quantify learned representations in the penultimate layer of CNNs, enabling systematic analysis of features and decision boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enables visualization and systematic analysis of learned representations in CNNs, revealing that single units can encode meaningful, partially disentangled features and that the pipeline can interpret thousands of units simultaneously.
papers.key_findings:
A linear mapping can be established between the classifier's representation space and the GAN's latent space due to high similarity, enabling visualization of learned features.
Individual units in the penultimate layer encode interpretable semantic concepts such as gender, color, and object parts, and some units are class-relevant.
The representation space shows a semantic order with both sparse (disentangled) and distributed (entangled) representations across units.
Perturbing single units can significantly change the classifier's prediction probability, revealing units that are important for specific classes.
Counterfactual examples generated by manipulating activations reveal human-interpretable features that change at the decision boundary, such as ear size or color.
papers.limitation:
The method does not generalize to Vision Transformers (ViTs) because the GAN's latent space is not regionally disentangled.
The analyses rely on generated images rather than real images, as current generative models cannot fully capture the diversity of real data.
The few-shot image segmentation model may produce imprecise masks, though averaging across images mitigates this.
future_direction: Insights about the complete representational space may inspire model architectures or training strategies that constrain the representational geometry.
Extending the approach to other convolutional layers could reveal insights into features represented at different hierarchies in the classifier.
Using the method to find difficult-to-classify images is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn abstract features to perform object classification, but understanding these features remains challenging due to difficult-to-interpret results or high computational costs. We propose an automatic method to visualize and systematically analyze learned features in CNNs. Specifically, we introduce a linking network that maps the penultimate layer of a pre-trained classifier to the latent space of a generative model (StyleGAN-XL), thereby enabling an interpretable, human-friendly visualization of the classifier's representations. Our findings indicate a congruent semantic order in both spaces, enabling a direct linear mapping between them. Training the linking network is computationally inexpensive and decoupled from training both the GAN and the classifier. We introduce an automatic pipeline that utilizes such GAN-based visualizations to quantify learned representations by analyzing activation changes in the classifier in the image domain. This quantification allows us to systematically study the learned representations in several thousand units simultaneously and to extract and visualize units selective for specific semantic concepts. Further, we illustrate how our method can be used to quantify and interpret the classifier's decision boundary using counterfactual examples. Overall, our method offers systematic and objective perspectives on learned abstract representations in CNNs. https://github.com/kaschube-lab/LinkingInStyle.git

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Robust Semantic Interpretability: Revisiting Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: How can concept activation vectors be improved to provide more accurate and robust semantic interpretability for image classification models, quantifying concept sensitivity at both the image and dataset levels?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Robust Concept Activation Vectors (RCAV), a method for semantic interpretability that improves upon TCAV by generalizing to non-linear effects and using stricter permutation testing, and introduces two benchmark datasets with metrics for realistic evaluation of semantic interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: RCAV improves upon previous semantic interpretability methods in accuracy, robustness, and runtime, and the introduced benchmarks address a gap in the interpretability evaluation literature.
papers.key_findings:
RCAV accurately quantifies image-level concept sensitivity for both semantically meaningful and confounding concepts, significantly outperforming TCAV which fails at this task.
RCAV reduces the false positive rate to 0% on tested concepts through improved hypothesis testing (permutation test), whereas TCAV exhibits a 100% false positive rate.
RCAV performs robustly across hyperparameters (layer choice, step size) and datasets (TFMNIST, CAMELYON16, ImageNet), though performance drops when concept encoding is non-linear (e.g., in TFMNIST).
The proposed benchmarks (Textured FMNIST and Biased CAMELYON16) provide ground-truth concept sensitivity for realistic evaluation, exposing the importance of counterfactual augmentation and negative controls.
Permutation testing is necessary for robust hypothesis testing in interpretability; the t-test used in TCAV underestimates variance and leads to false positives.
papers.limitation:
RCAV's performance depends on the linearity of concept encoding in the model's latent space; non-linear encodings (as observed in TFMNIST) limit its effectiveness.
RCAV does not account for non-linearity in the initial layers of the model, as it perturbs activations after layer l.
future_direction: Using RCAV to enhance automatic discovery of prediction-relevant concepts.
Conducting a complete comparison of RCAV to other (including non-linear) semantic interpretability methods.
Applying RCAV to scientific discovery, e.g., to assess the importance of specific properties in domains like molecular similarity.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods for image classification assess model trustworthiness by attempting to expose whether the model is systematically biased or attending to the same cues as a human would. Saliency methods for feature attribution dominate the interpretability literature, but these methods do not address semantic concepts such as the textures, colors, or genders of objects within an image. Our proposed Robust Concept Activation Vectors (RCAV) quantifies the effects of semantic concepts on individual model predictions and on model behavior as a whole. RCAV calculates a concept gradient and takes a gradient ascent step to assess model sensitivity to the given concept. By generalizing previous work on concept activation vectors to account for model non-linearity, and by introducing stricter hypothesis testing, we show that RCAV yields interpretations which are both more accurate at the image level and robust at the dataset level. RCAV, like saliency methods, supports the interpretation of individual predictions. To evaluate the practical use of interpretability methods as debugging tools, and the scientific use of interpretability methods for identifying inductive biases (e.g. texture over shape), we construct two datasets and accompanying metrics for realistic benchmarking of semantic interpretability methods. Our benchmarks expose the importance of counterfactual augmentation and negative controls for quantifying the practical usability of interpretability methods.
