Prior works have associated concepts with neurons based on examples of concepts or a pre-defined set of concepts, thus limiting possible explanations to what the user expects, especially in discovering new concepts. Furthermore, defining the set of concepts requires manual work from the user, either by directly specifying them or collecting examples. To overcome these, we propose to leverage multimodal large language models for automatic and open-ended concept discovery. We show that, without a restricted set of pre-defined concepts, our method gives rise to novel interpretable concepts that are more faithful to the model's behavior. To quantify this, we validate each concept by generating examples and counterexamples and evaluating the neuron's response on this new set of images. Collectively, our method can discover concepts and simultaneously validate them, providing a credible automated tool to explain deep neural networks.

papers.title: CLIP is All You Need for Human-like Semantic Representations in Stable Diffusion
papers.research_question: Does Stable Diffusion's internal representations during text-to-image generation contain human-like semantic information, and is this due to CLIP or the diffusion process?
papers.core_contribution: The semantic understanding in Stable Diffusion comes from the pretrained CLIP model, not the reverse diffusion process, which instead acts as a visual decoder of CLIP's representations.
papers.conclusion: CLIP is primarily responsible for the human-like semantic representations in Stable Diffusion, and the diffusion process serves as a visual decoder. Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial ones.
papers.key_findings:
Most human attribute ratings can be predicted from Stable Diffusion's latent representations with accuracy significantly below chance.
The semantic representation is most human-like at the output of CLIP, and the reverse diffusion process degrades this alignment.
Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial attributes across all model components.
CLIP can disentangle attributes that humans entangle, while the diffusion process tends to entangle attributes.
Attributes become more difficult to disambiguate from one another during the inverse diffusion process.
papers.limitation: The study uses a dataset of text prompts and human attribute ratings, but lacks a corresponding image dataset with attribute labels, limiting the analysis to text-based prompts.
future_direction: Applying the probing technique to other generative models (e.g., GANs, other diffusion models) to compare human alignment.
Creating an image dataset labeled with attribute ratings to generalize results to generated images.
Investigating how well language-only and vision-language models align with human perception.
papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion achieve state-of-the-art results on text-to-image generation tasks. However, the extent to which these models have a semantic understanding of the images they generate is not well understood. In this work, we investigate whether the internal representations used by these models during text-to-image generation contain semantic information that is meaningful to humans. To do so, we perform probing on Stable Diffusion with simple regression layers that predict semantic attributes for objects and evaluate these predictions against human annotations. Surprisingly, we find that this success can actually be attributed to the text encoding occurring in CLIP rather than the reverse diffusion process. We demonstrate that groups of specific semantic attributes have markedly different decoding accuracy than the average, and are thus represented to different degrees. Finally, we show that attributes become more difficult to disambiguate from one another during the inverse diffusion process, further demonstrating the strongest semantic representation of object attributes in CLIP. We conclude that the separately trained CLIP vision-language model is what determines the human-like semantic representation, and that the diffusion process instead takes the role of a visual decoder.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Align with Human Neural Representations in Concept Processing
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models (VLMs) from different families align with human neural representations in concept processing, and how does visual or textual context affect this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Vision-language models (VLMs) align with human neural representations in concept processing, with vision-language encoders showing higher alignment than generative VLMs, and for some VLMs the alignment stems from learning human-like concepts during pretraining rather than just context at inference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs, particularly vision-language encoders, align with human neural representations in concept processing, and their advantage stems from learning multimodal semantic information during pretraining, not just from context at inference.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs outperform language-only models in aligning with human brain responses in both sentence and picture conditions.
Vision-language encoders (VisualBERT, LXMERT) are more brain-aligned than contrastive and generative VLMs.
In the sentence condition, only VisualBERT and LXMERT significantly outperform BERT, while generative VLMs do not outperform their language-only counterparts.
Ablation studies show that for LXMERT and IDEFICS2, brain alignment is less sensitive to input images, indicating learning of human-like concepts during pretraining.
Generative VLMs show lower brain alignment compared to vision-language encoders, despite their superior performance on downstream tasks.
papers.limitation:
VLMs differ along many dimensions (size, architecture, learning objective, training data), making it hard to attribute differences in brain alignment to one specific factor.
The brain regions of interest (ROIs) considered may not capture all regions involved in multimodal integration.
Averaging brain responses across participants may smooth out participant-specific patterns.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that transformer-based vision-language models (VLMs) capture the multimodality of concept processing in the human brain. However, a systematic evaluation exploring different types of VLM architectures and the role played by visual and textual context is still lacking. Here, we analyse multiple VLMs employing different strategies to integrate visual and textual modalities, along with language-only counterparts. We measure the alignment between concept representations by models and existing (fMRI) brain responses to concept words presented in two experimental conditions, where either visual (pictures) or textual (sentences) context is provided. Our results reveal that VLMs outperform the language-only counterparts in both experimental conditions. However, controlled ablation studies show that only for some VLMs, such as LXMERT and IDEFICS2, brain alignment stems from genuinely learning more human-like concepts during pretraining, while others are highly sensitive to the context provided at inference. Additionally, we find that vision-language encoders are more brain-aligned than more recent, generative VLMs. Altogether, our study shows that VLMs align with human neural representations in concept processing, while highlighting differences among architectures. We open-source code and materials to reproduce our experiments at: https://github.com/dmg-illc/vl-concept-processing.

papers.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the function of individual neurons in CLIP when direct and indirect effects fail to capture their role? The paper introduces a 'second-order lens' to analyze the effects of neurons flowing through later attention heads.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the second-order lens to interpret neurons in CLIP, revealing polysemantic behavior and enabling applications in adversarial example generation and zero-shot segmentation.
papers.conclusion: Automated interpretability of neurons in CLIP can reveal model limitations and enable new capabilities, such as model deception and zero-shot segmentation.
papers.key_findings:
Second-order effects of neurons are significant in late layers and are sparse, affecting less than 2% of images.
Each second-order effect can be approximated by a single direction in the joint text-image space of CLIP.
Neurons are polysemantic, with each neuron corresponding to multiple, often unrelated concepts.
Sparse text decompositions of neuron directions can be used to mass-produce semantic adversarial examples that fool CLIP.
Second-order effects enable zero-shot segmentation that outperforms previous methods.
papers.limitation:
Did not analyze the effect of neurons on consecutive queries and keys in the attention mechanism (neuron-attention maps mechanisms).
Did not analyze mutual effects between neurons in the same or across different layers (neuron-neuron mechanisms).
future_direction: Investigate neuron effects on attention queries and keys.
Study dependencies between neurons.
Use generated adversarial images to fine-tune CLIP for improved robustness.
papers.abstract: We interpret the function of individual neurons in CLIP by automatically describing them using text. Analyzing the direct effects (i.e. the flow from a neuron through the residual stream to the output) or the indirect effects (overall contribution) fails to capture the neurons' function in CLIP. Therefore, we present the "second-order lens", analyzing the effect flowing from a neuron through the later attention heads, directly to the output. We find that these effects are highly selective: for each neuron, the effect is significant for <2% of the images. Moreover, each effect can be approximated by a single direction in the text-image space of CLIP. We describe neurons by decomposing these directions into sparse sets of text representations. The sets reveal polysemantic behavior - each neuron corresponds to multiple, often unrelated, concepts (e.g. ships and cars). Exploiting this neuron polysemy, we mass-produce "semantic" adversarial examples by generating images with concepts spuriously correlated to the incorrect class. Additionally, we use the second-order effects for zero-shot segmentation, outperforming previous methods. Our results indicate that an automated interpretation of neurons can be used for model deception and for introducing new model capabilities.

papers.title: Prompt the Unseen: Evaluating Visual-Language Alignment Beyond Supervision
papers.research_question: Can the projection layer in vision-language models effectively transfer visual information of unseen concepts? How does it achieve such generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a benchmark for evaluating projection layer generalization in VLMs, showing that projection layers retain 79-88% performance on unseen classes and operate via key-value memory mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Projection layers demonstrate generalization to unseen labels across rigorous experimental settings, and mechanistic interpretability shows FFNs process vision tokens for both seen and unseen labels consistently, supporting the lightweight projection layer design in VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The projection layer generalizes to unseen labels, retaining 79-88% of seen-class performance across various vision encoders and LLMs.
Generalization is consistent across different vision encoders (CLIP, DINOv2, ViT, MAE) and LLMs, even with a small 0.6B parameter model.
Class diversity in the training data is a key factor enhancing generalization to unseen labels.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that feed-forward networks (FFNs) in the frozen LLM process visual tokens similarly to text tokens, acting as key-value memories.
The key-value memory mechanism operates consistently for both seen and unseen visual labels.
papers.limitation: reliance on a fixed prompt format
future_direction: Extend this investigation to more general visual question-answering tasks.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) combine a vision encoder and a large language model (LLM) through alignment training, showing strong performance on multimodal tasks. A central component in this architecture is the projection layer, which maps visual features into the LLM's embedding space. Despite its importance, its ability to generalize to unseen visual concepts has not been systematically evaluated. To address this, we propose a benchmark for evaluating projection-layer generalization. We adapt object detection datasets (rich in fine-grained annotations) into a prompting format and design train/test splits with disjoint label sets, enabling precise control over seen and unseen concept separation. Experimental results show that the projection layer retains about 79 to 88 percent of the performance on unseen classes compared to seen ones across various settings, suggesting a non-trivial level of generalization even without explicit alignment supervision on those concepts. We further analyze this behavior through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Our findings indicate that the feed-forward network in the projection layer functions like a key-value memory, processing seen and unseen tokens in similar ways. This study introduces a new evaluation framework for alignment generalization and highlights the potential for efficient VLM training with limited aligned data.

papers.title: Finding Shared Decodable Concepts and their Negations in the Brain
papers.research_question: How can we identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data during natural image viewing? The paper proposes a method using contrastive learning and a novel clustering approach to find voxel clusters across participants that represent similar semantic concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive learning and a novel cross-participant DBSCAN clustering to identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data, revealing both known and new visuo-semantic categories.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully identifies shared decodable concepts in the brain, including both previously reported and novel visuo-semantic categories, and the use of negative images aids in interpreting the semantic properties of each cluster.
papers.key_findings:
Identified SDCs for known visual features (e.g., orientation tuning in early visual cortex) and semantic concepts (faces, places, bodies).
Discovered two distinct food-related clusters: one driven by color and another by shape, with negative images revealing grayscale images for the color-driven cluster.
Found body-related clusters for legs/hands, motion, and groups of people in extrastriate body area (EBA).
Discovered a numerosity cluster in right intraparietal sulcus (IPS) associated with repeated elements.
Identified clusters for visual perspective (close/far) and lighting conditions.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the stimulus images used in the NSD experiment, which may bias the model towards over-represented categories.
The use of CLIP may introduce biases, as some brain signal may not be captured by CLIP embeddings.
fMRI has limited temporal resolution, restricting the ability to capture rapid neural activity.
The clustering approach might merge concepts within regions of CLIP space that have relatively uniform densities, potentially missing interesting SDCs.
The method is not a replacement for traditional hypothesis-driven experiments.
future_direction: Utilize larger and more diverse fMRI datasets.
Incorporate higher temporal resolution imaging techniques such as EEG or ECoG.
Explore alternative stimulus representations beyond CLIP.
papers.abstract: Prior work has offered evidence for functional localization in the brain; different anatomical regions preferentially activate for certain types of visual input. For example, the fusiform face area preferentially activates for visual stimuli that include a face. However, the spectrum of visual semantics is extensive, and only a few semantically-tuned patches of cortex have so far been identified in the human brain. Using a multimodal (natural language and image) neural network architecture (CLIP) we train a highly accurate contrastive model that maps brain responses during naturalistic image viewing to CLIP embeddings. We then use a novel adaptation of the DBSCAN clustering algorithm to cluster the parameters of these participant-specific contrastive models. This reveals what we call Shared Decodable Concepts (SDCs): clusters in CLIP space that are decodable from common sets of voxels across multiple participants. Examining the images most and least associated with each SDC cluster gives us additional insight into the semantic properties of each SDC. We note SDCs for previously reported visual features (e.g. orientation tuning in early visual cortex) as well as visual semantic concepts such as faces, places and bodies. In cases where our method finds multiple clusters for a visuo-semantic concept, the least associated images allow us to dissociate between confounding factors. For example, we discovered two clusters of food images, one driven by color, the other by shape. We also uncover previously unreported areas such as regions of extrastriate body area (EBA) tuned for legs/hands and sensitivity to numerosity in right intraparietal sulcus, and more. Thus, our contrastive-learning methodology better characterizes new and existing visuo-semantic representations in the brain by leveraging multimodal neural network representations and a novel adaptation of clustering algorithms.

papers.title: CLIP Under the Microscope: A Fine-Grained Analysis of Multi-Object Representation
papers.research_question: What are the limitations and biases of CLIP models in multi-object scenarios, and what are the origins of these biases?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies and analyzes biases in CLIP's encoders: the text encoder prioritizes first-mentioned objects, and the image encoder favors larger objects. It traces these biases to the training data and model architecture, and shows their impact on multi-object tasks.
papers.conclusion: CLIP's text and image encoders exhibit significant biases that degrade performance in multi-object tasks. Addressing these biases is essential for advancing vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
The text encoder of CLIP shows a bias towards the first object mentioned in a caption.
The image encoder of CLIP shows a bias towards larger objects in an image.
These biases are linked to the training data (larger objects are often mentioned earlier in captions) and the model architecture (ViT's attention mechanism).
The biases lead to performance drops in image-text matching when object size or token order changes.
The biases also affect text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion, where prompt order influences object prominence in generated images.
papers.limitation: The proposed bias mitigation method is heuristic and dataset-specific, limiting its generalizability.
future_direction: Explore counterfactual data augmentation and attention regularization to reduce biases.
Leverage LLMs to automate caption decomposition and modify positional embeddings in the text encoder.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models excel in zero-shot classification, yet face challenges in complex multi-object scenarios. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of CLIP's limitations in these contexts using a specialized dataset, ComCO, designed to evaluate CLIP's encoders in diverse multi-object scenarios. Our findings reveal significant biases: the text encoder prioritizes first-mentioned objects, and the image encoder favors larger objects. Through retrieval and classification tasks, we quantify these biases across multiple CLIP variants and trace their origins to CLIP's training process, supported by analyses of the LAION dataset and training progression. Our image-text matching experiments show substantial performance drops when object size or token order changes, underscoring CLIP's instability with rephrased but semantically similar captions. Extending this to longer captions and text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion, we demonstrate how prompt order influences object prominence in generated images. For more details and access to our dataset and analysis code, visit our project repository: https://clip-oscope.github.io.

papers.title: Language-biased image classification: evaluation based on semantic representations
papers.research_question: Does language-biased image classification in artificial models like CLIP depend on shared semantic representations between words and images, similar to human picture-word interference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to evaluate language-biased image classification in joint vision-language models and finds that CLIP exhibits language bias but without shared semantic representations between words and images.
papers.conclusion: CLIP acquires the ability to recognize visual word forms but does not acquire shared semantic representations for words and images, and the benchmark enables step-by-step evaluation of semantic interactions in joint language-vision learning.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP shows high label switching rates when words are superimposed on images, indicating strong language bias.
The bias occurs even across different category levels (superordinate vs basic).
The bias does not depend on semantic similarity between image and word categories.
Representational similarity analysis shows that word representations in CLIP are not shared with image representations.
The bias is robust to different prompts but can be reduced by explicitly describing the superimposed word in the prompt.
papers.limitation: The study does not investigate how CLIP acquires the biased representations or the role of potential biases in the training data.
future_direction: Investigate how CLIP acquires biased representations and the role of training data biases.
Make biases more human-like by controlling joint learning curricula of language and vision.
papers.abstract: Humans show language-biased image recognition for a word-embedded image, known as picture-word interference. Such interference depends on hierarchical semantic categories and reflects that human language processing highly interacts with visual processing. Similar to humans, recent artificial models jointly trained on texts and images, e.g., OpenAI CLIP, show language-biased image classification. Exploring whether the bias leads to interference similar to those observed in humans can contribute to understanding how much the model acquires hierarchical semantic representations from joint learning of language and vision. The present study introduces methodological tools from the cognitive science literature to assess the biases of artificial models. Specifically, we introduce a benchmark task to test whether words superimposed on images can distort the image classification across different category levels and, if it can, whether the perturbation is due to the shared semantic representation between language and vision. Our dataset is a set of word-embedded images and consists of a mixture of natural image datasets and hierarchical word labels with superordinate/basic category levels. Using this benchmark test, we evaluate the CLIP model. We show that presenting words distorts the image classification by the model across different category levels, but the effect does not depend on the semantic relationship between images and embedded words. This suggests that the semantic word representation in the CLIP visual processing is not shared with the image representation, although the word representation strongly dominates for word-embedded images.

papers.title: Exploiting Text-Image Latent Spaces for the Description of Visual Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we automatically generate textual descriptions for Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to aid in interpreting neural network concepts without requiring human interpretation of representative images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an approach to automatically generate textual descriptions for Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) by mapping receptive fields of relevant images into a joint text-image embedding space, reducing the need for human interpretation and improving concept description for early layers.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method aids in interpreting CAVs by providing textual descriptions and using receptive fields improves the explanation quality for early layers, though the approach is limited by the quality of the joint text-image feature space.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach can generate meaningful textual descriptions for CAVs, as validated on CAVs with known concept labels (e.g., CIFAR10 classes).
Using receptive fields (Fmax and Fmean→max) instead of full images (Fmean) improves the textual descriptions for CAVs from early layers, especially for abstract concepts.
The method can reveal biases in training data, such as the association of 'dark' with cats in a biased dataset.
The performance of the approach depends on the quality of the joint text-image feature space (e.g., CLIP), and limitations arise when the CLIP model fails to match visual concepts with textual descriptions.
The approach reduces redundancy in top-k descriptions by deriving a common concept description from the weighted average of the top-k descriptions.
papers.limitation: The performance of the approach depends on the quality of the joint text-image feature space (e.g., CLIP), and there are cases where the generated textual descriptions do not match the visual concepts due to limitations in CLIP.
future_direction: Exploring other image-to-text projections beyond CLIP.
Evaluating the found textual descriptions regarding human understanding.
Extending concept discovery methods with mismatched data to better understand model behavior.
Fine-tuning text-image embeddings to basic concepts for improved description of specific concepts.
papers.abstract: Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) offer insights into neural network decision-making by linking human friendly concepts to the model's internal feature extraction process. However, when a new set of CAVs is discovered, they must still be translated into a human understandable description. For image-based neural networks, this is typically done by visualizing the most relevant images of a CAV, while the determination of the concept is left to humans. In this work, we introduce an approach to aid the interpretation of newly discovered concept sets by suggesting textual descriptions for each CAV. This is done by mapping the most relevant images representing a CAV into a text-image embedding where a joint description of these relevant images can be computed. We propose utilizing the most relevant receptive fields instead of full images encoded. We demonstrate the capabilities of this approach in multiple experiments with and without given CAV labels, showing that the proposed approach provides accurate descriptions for the CAVs and reduces the challenge of concept interpretation.

papers.title: Disentangling visual and written concepts in CLIP
papers.research_question: Does the image encoder of CLIP encode image text differently from the way it encodes the visual concept described by that same text, and can its spelling capability be separated from its visual processing of natural images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using learned orthogonal projections to disentangle the representation of written text from visual concepts in the CLIP image encoder's vector space.
papers.conclusion: A learned orthogonal projection can disentangle written and visual comprehension in the CLIP image encoding, and orthogonality is crucial for the method's effectiveness in reducing text artifacts in generation and defending against typographic attacks.
papers.key_findings:
The CLIP image encoder can associate natural images with word images, indicating a correlation between written words and their visual meaning.
CLIP can retrieve nonsense strings, suggesting its spelling capability is separate from understanding word meaning.
A learned orthogonal projection can separate text and visual comprehension capabilities in CLIP.
The 'forget to spell' projection reduces text artifacts in CLIP-guided image generation.
The 'forget to spell' projection improves robustness against typographic attacks by reducing the model's sensitivity to text labels.
papers.limitation: The method cannot perfectly avoid text all together when using the 'forget to spell' projection, nor guarantee perfectly written text using the 'learn to spell' projection.
papers.abstract: The CLIP network measures the similarity between natural text and images; in this work, we investigate the entanglement of the representation of word images and natural images in its image encoder. First, we find that the image encoder has an ability to match word images with natural images of scenes described by those words. This is consistent with previous research that suggests that the meaning and the spelling of a word might be entangled deep within the network. On the other hand, we also find that CLIP has a strong ability to match nonsense words, suggesting that processing of letters is separated from processing of their meaning. To explicitly determine whether the spelling capability of CLIP is separable, we devise a procedure for identifying representation subspaces that selectively isolate or eliminate spelling capabilities. We benchmark our methods against a range of retrieval tasks, and we also test them by measuring the appearance of text in CLIP-guided generated images. We find that our methods are able to cleanly separate spelling capabilities of CLIP from the visual processing of natural images.

papers.title: Mammo-CLIP Dissect: A Framework for Analysing Mammography Concepts in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain under-represented.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Mammo-CLIP Dissect, a concept-based explainability framework for dissecting deep learning vision models in mammography, and uses it to analyze how domain-specific training and fine-tuning affect concept learning.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides concept-level insights into how CNNs capture mammography-specific knowledge, moving beyond pixel-level interpretability toward an understanding aligned with radiologists' reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows.
Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but reduces coverage of others (e.g., density-related features).
Neurons show selective responsiveness to distinct mammography features such as implants and calcifications.
Mammo-CLIP Dissect reveals that domain-specific training leads to stronger and more stable alignment with mammography concepts.
The framework identifies under-represented concepts, including architectural distortion and modality-inappropriate terms.
papers.limitation: The concept set includes overlaps and modality-inappropriate concepts (e.g., from ultrasound or MRI) which may confound evaluation.
future_direction: Refining concept sets to reduce ambiguity.
Addressing subtle underrepresented findings.
Developing fine-tuning strategies that preserve general conceptual breadth while enhancing task-relevant features.
papers.abstract: Understanding what deep learning (DL) models learn is essential for the safe deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical settings. While previous work has focused on pixel-based explainability methods, less attention has been paid to the textual concepts learned by these models, which may better reflect the reasoning used by clinicians. We introduce Mammo-CLIP Dissect, the first concept-based explainability framework for systematically dissecting DL vision models trained for mammography. Leveraging a mammography-specific vision-language model (Mammo-CLIP) as a "dissector," our approach labels neurons at specified layers with human-interpretable textual concepts and quantifies their alignment to domain knowledge. Using Mammo-CLIP Dissect, we investigate three key questions: (1) how concept learning differs between DL vision models trained on general image datasets versus mammography-specific datasets; (2) how fine-tuning for downstream mammography tasks affects concept specialisation; and (3) which mammography-relevant concepts remain underrepresented. We show that models trained on mammography data capture more clinically relevant concepts and align more closely with radiologists' workflows than models not trained on mammography data. Fine-tuning for task-specific classification enhances the capture of certain concept categories (e.g., benign calcifications) but can reduce coverage of others (e.g., density-related features), indicating a trade-off between specialisation and generalisation. Our findings show that Mammo-CLIP Dissect provides insights into how convolutional neural networks (CNNs) capture mammography-specific knowledge. By comparing models across training data and fine-tuning regimes, we reveal how domain-specific training and task-specific adaptation shape concept learning. Code and concept set are available: https://github.com/Suaiba/Mammo-CLIP-Dissect.

papers.title: Decomposing and Interpreting Image Representations via Text in ViTs Beyond CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we identify and interpret the roles of various components (e.g., attention heads, MLPs) in arbitrary vision transformers (ViTs) beyond CLIP models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a general framework that automates the decomposition of a ViT's final image representation into contributions from its components (e.g., attention heads, MLPs) and aligns these contributions to CLIP's representation space for text-based interpretation, enabling analysis and applications for diverse ViT architectures.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a way to interpret the internal components of diverse vision transformers via text, revealing insights into feature representation and enabling practical applications like retrieval and bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully decomposes representations and aligns component contributions to CLIP space, allowing interpretation via text.
In ImageNet-trained models, useful features are encoded redundantly across many layers, while in models not trained on ImageNet (e.g., CLIP, DINOv2), the last few layers are critical.
A novel scoring function effectively ranks components by their importance for specific image features (e.g., color, pattern, location).
The method enables applications such as text- and image-based feature-specific image retrieval, visualization of token contributions via heatmaps, and zero-shot mitigation of spurious correlations.
Individual components in larger models like MaxViT and Swin often do not respond strongly to any single feature in isolation but encode features effectively in combination with other components.
papers.limitation: The analysis only considers the direct contributions from the last few layers and does not account for indirect contributions via downstream components.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to include indirect contributions (higher-order terms) from components.
Applying the framework to other model architectures beyond vision transformers.
papers.abstract: Recent work has explored how individual components of the CLIP-ViT model contribute to the final representation by leveraging the shared image-text representation space of CLIP. These components, such as attention heads and MLPs, have been shown to capture distinct image features like shape, color or texture. However, understanding the role of these components in arbitrary vision transformers (ViTs) is challenging. To this end, we introduce a general framework which can identify the roles of various components in ViTs beyond CLIP. Specifically, we (a) automate the decomposition of the final representation into contributions from different model components, and (b) linearly map these contributions to CLIP space to interpret them via text. Additionally, we introduce a novel scoring function to rank components by their importance with respect to specific features. Applying our framework to various ViT variants (e.g. DeiT, DINO, DINOv2, Swin, MaxViT), we gain insights into the roles of different components concerning particular image features. These insights facilitate applications such as image retrieval using text descriptions or reference images, visualizing token importance heatmaps, and mitigating spurious correlations. We release our code to reproduce the experiments at https://github.com/SriramB-98/vit-decompose

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic neurons be disentangled into monosemantic concept vectors that represent distinct features in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into monosemantic concept vectors by clustering activations, showing that meaningful directions in activation space can represent distinct features.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that exploring directions in activation space, rather than individual neurons, can lead to more coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons that encode coherent, human-understandable features.
The concept vectors found have higher similarity (projection and cosine similarity) to the activations of their corresponding images than the original neuron directions.
The method allows for fine-grained concept separation by adjusting a distance threshold parameter in the clustering step.
The majority of neurons analyzed in a later layer (Mixed 7b) of Inception V3 showed some amount of polysemanticity.
The concept vectors are confirmed to be monosemantic through qualitative assessment (maximally activating images and feature visualization) and quantitative evaluation (human experiments).
papers.limitation: The method relies on the data used to generate clusters, and experiments are limited to image data which is easier to visualize.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data
Exploring other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user's desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Explaining Caption-Image Interactions in CLIP Models with Second-Order Attributions
papers.research_question: How do dual encoder models like CLIP compare their two inputs (image and text) by analyzing feature interactions, which first-order attribution methods cannot capture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a second-order attribution method for any differentiable dual encoder that can explain interactions between two inputs, and applies it to CLIP models to show they learn fine-grained correspondences between captions and images.
papers.conclusion: The proposed second-order attribution method provides insights into how CLIP models compare images and text, revealing both their capabilities and limitations in visual-linguistic grounding.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP models learn fine-grained correspondences between parts of captions and regions in images, matching objects and accounting for mismatches.
The visual-linguistic grounding ability varies heavily between object classes and exhibits pronounced out-of-domain effects.
The method can identify individual errors and systematic failure categories in CLIP models.
The second-order attributions outperform first-order and other baseline methods in conditional perturbation and object localization experiments.
Fine-tuning on in-domain data improves grounding ability, but the extent varies across models and object classes.
papers.limitation:
The method requires computing Jacobians, which is computationally expensive (quadratic in embedding dimension) and memory-intensive.
The approximation error depends on the number of integration steps and the choice of reference inputs.
future_direction: Extend the method to other dual encoder architectures and modalities (e.g., audio).
Apply the method to analyze other multi-modal tasks and models.
Investigate the use of different reference inputs and integration paths to improve attribution accuracy.
papers.abstract: Dual encoder architectures like Clip models map two types of inputs into a shared embedding space and predict similarities between them. Despite their wide application, it is, however, not understood how these models compare their two inputs. Common first-order feature-attribution methods explain importances of individual features and can, thus, only provide limited insights into dual encoders, whose predictions depend on interactions between features. In this paper, we first derive a second-order method enabling the attribution of predictions by any differentiable dual encoder onto feature-interactions between its inputs. Second, we apply our method to Clip models and show that they learn fine-grained correspondences between parts of captions and regions in images. They match objects across input modes and also account for mismatches. This intrinsic visual-linguistic grounding ability, however, varies heavily between object classes, exhibits pronounced out-of-domain effects and we can identify individual errors as well as systematic failure categories. Code is publicly available: https://github.com/lucasmllr/exCLIP

papers.title: Text encoders bottleneck compositionality in contrastive vision-language models
papers.research_question: How much information about language is lost in the single-vector bottleneck of contrastive vision-language models? Does text-only recovery performance predict multimodal matching performance?
papers.core_contribution: Text encoders in contrastive vision-language models act as a bottleneck for compositional information; text-only recoverability of a property is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the multimodal model to perform well on that property.
papers.conclusion: Text encoders in vision-language models lose significant compositional information, which affects multimodal performance; future work should design encoders that better generalize to unseen compositions.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP's text encoder struggles to encode compositional inputs like object relationships, attribute-object association, counting, and negations.
Text-only recovery performance on CompPrompts predicts multimodal matching performance on ControlledImCaps, indicating the text encoder is a bottleneck.
Some text encoders (e.g., SBERT, RoBERTa-CLIP) perform significantly better than others, but all underperform a proof-of-concept autoencoder.
Model design choices like text pre-training, hard negatives, and larger size improve encoder quality, but significant information loss remains for compositional inputs.
Text encoders struggle more as inputs become more compositional (e.g., from one object to two objects with attributes).
papers.limitation:
The probing method uses a pre-trained T5 decoder, which may introduce language biases from its pre-training (e.g., predicting more likely word orders).
Only one probing method (generative decoder) is used; complementary methods (e.g., linear probes) could reveal more insights.
Text encoders that perform well on the text-only evaluation may not perform well if plugged into a contrastive VL model if the information is not encoded in a linearly recoverable way.
future_direction: Modify contrastive VL training objectives to encourage text reconstruction or use harder negatives.
Explicitly encourage linear text-text recoverability in the training loss to improve multimodal performance.
Create even more difficult test sets to analyze and evaluate vision-language model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Performant vision-language (VL) models like CLIP represent captions using a single vector. How much information about language is lost in this bottleneck? We first curate CompPrompts, a set of increasingly compositional image captions that VL models should be able to capture (e.g., single object, to object+property, to multiple interacting objects). Then, we train text-only recovery probes that aim to reconstruct captions from single-vector text representations produced by several VL models. This approach does not require images, allowing us to test on a broader range of scenes compared to prior work. We find that: 1) CLIP's text encoder falls short on more compositional inputs, including object relationships, attribute-object association, counting, and negations; 2) some text encoders work significantly better than others; and 3) text-only recovery performance predicts multi-modal matching performance on ControlledImCaps: a new evaluation benchmark we collect and release consisting of fine-grained compositional images and captions. Specifically, our results suggest text-only recoverability is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for modeling compositional factors in contrastive VL models. We release our datasets and code.

papers.title: Concept-pedia: a Wide-coverage Semantically-annotated Multimodal Dataset
papers.research_question: Does ImageNet's coverage remain challenging for modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what is the impact of adding novel and varied concept categories?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept-pedia, a wide-coverage semantically-annotated multimodal dataset, and Concept-10k, a manually-curated benchmark for visual concept recognition, showing that current VLMs struggle on Concept-10k, highlighting the need for more representative benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Concept-pedia and Concept-10k provide a broader and more challenging testbed for VLMs, revealing limited generalization of current models to diverse visual concepts and underscoring the need for more representative benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Current VLMs perform well on ImageNet but struggle on the diverse concepts in Concept-10k, with the best model achieving only 40.3% accuracy.
The performance drop is primarily due to concept diversity rather than image or annotation quality.
Fine-tuning on Concept-pedia improves performance on Concept-10k by an average of 5.2 percentage points without degrading ImageNet performance.
Using multi-label annotations in Concept-pedia for fine-tuning yields better performance than single-label annotations.
Models exhibit a bias towards ImageNet-centric concepts and images.
papers.limitation:
Concept-pedia is based solely on English Wikipedia, potentially introducing cultural bias.
The frequency-based algorithm for concept selection may result in suboptimal class diversity within categories.
future_direction: Expand Concept-pedia to cover a wider range of languages to mitigate cultural bias and increase linguistic diversity.
Incorporate multi-label annotations into the Concept-10k benchmark.
Explore the use of Concept-pedia for other tasks such as Visual Question Answering and Multimodal Entity Linking.
papers.abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP and SigLIP, have become the de facto standard for multimodal tasks, serving as essential building blocks for recent Multimodal Large Language Models, including LLaVA and PaliGemma. However, current evaluations for VLMs remain heavily anchored to ImageNet. In this paper, we question whether ImageNet’s coverage is still sufficiently challenging for modern VLMs, and investigate the impact of adding novel and varied concept categories, i.e., semantically grouped fine-grained synsets. To this end, we introduce Concept-pedia, a novel, large-scale, semantically-annotated multimodal resource covering more than 165,000 concepts. Leveraging a language-agnostic, automatic annotation pipeline grounded in Wikipedia, Concept-pedia expands the range of visual concepts, including diverse abstract categories. Building on Concept-pedia, we also present a manually-curated Visual Concept Recognition evaluation benchmark, Concept-10k, that spans thousands of concepts across a wide range of categories. Our experiments show that current models, although excelling on ImageNet, struggle with Concept-10k. Not only do these findings highlight a persistent bias toward ImageNet-centric concepts, but they also underscore the urgent need for more representative benchmarks. By offering a broader and semantically richer testbed, Concept-10k aims to support the development of multimodal systems that better generalize to the complexities of real-world visual concepts

papers.title: Delving into the Openness of CLIP
papers.research_question: How open are CLIP-like models to vocabulary expansion, and how can we evaluate and improve their extensibility and stability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an evaluation protocol for openness (extensibility and stability) and finds that CLIP-like models are not truly open; it also proposes REPE, a lightweight method to improve openness by enhancing text representations.
papers.conclusion: CLIP-like models are not truly open, and the uniformity of the textual space is critical for extensibility; the proposed REPE method alleviates the openness issue.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP-like models' performance deteriorates as vocabulary expands, indicating overestimated openness.
The overestimation is due to confusion among competing text features, not failure to capture image-text similarity.
Enforcing distinguishability of class features improves stability.
The proposed REPE method improves extensibility and stability by retrieving and ensembling representative captions.
CLIP is vulnerable to adversarial non-target vocabulary, revealing security risks.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation protocol based on incremental vocabulary expansion is an approximation of the real open world.
The study is limited to CLIP-like models and does not cover seq2seq models.
future_direction: Extending the evaluation to seq2seq models for open-vocabulary recognition.
Developing an evolving benchmark for openness.
Studying the influence of abstraction level, naming variation, and data distribution on extensibility.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) formulates image classification as an image-to-text matching task, i.e., matching images to the corresponding natural language descriptions instead of discrete category IDs. This allows for open-vocabulary visual recognition, where the model can recognize images from an open class set (also known as an open vocabulary) in a zero-shot manner. However, evaluating the openness of CLIP-like models is challenging, as the models are open to arbitrary vocabulary in theory, but their accuracy varies in practice. To address this, we resort to an incremental perspective to assess the openness through vocabulary expansions, and define extensibility to measure a model's ability to handle novel classes. Our evaluation shows that CLIP-like models are not truly open, and their performance deteriorates as the vocabulary expands. We further dissect the feature space of CLIP from the perspectives of representation alignment and uniformity. Our investigation reveals that the overestimation of openness is due to confusion among competing text features, rather than a failure to capture the similarity between image features and text features of novel classes. We hope that our investigation and analysis will facilitate future research on the CLIP openness issue.

papers.title: Interpreting the structure of multi-object representations in vision encoders
papers.research_question: Do vision encoders represent multi-object scenes in a structured way, with binding of object information into discrete tokens and segregation of object representations to minimize cross-object entanglement?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes two properties (binding and segregation) to evaluate structured object-wise representations in vision encoders, and uses them to analyze and compare various pre-trained vision encoders, revealing differences in how they represent multi-object scenes.
papers.conclusion: Characterizes and measures the extent to which representations of image encoders are structured in token space, showing that individual objects are represented separately but their representations are entangled.
papers.key_findings:
CLS tokens best model image-level information but prefer main objects, while object-specific tokens in higher layers hold discriminating features about individual objects.
Object-wise token representations are not disentangled; they can decode other objects in the scene with accuracy far above random guesses.
Vision-language models (VLMs) trained on objectives requiring multiple objects have better multi-object representations in the CLS token than ViT encoders trained for image classification.
ViT-based encoders have more entangled object representations than CNN-based CLIP (ResNet X4).
Measures of structured representation (M1, M2) correlate with the retention of object-specific information for background objects, indicating their usefulness for selecting layers and models for downstream tasks.
papers.limitation: High decoding accuracy in tasks with few object classes may be due to the ease of the task rather than rich object representation, and lower accuracy does not necessarily indicate absence of information.
future_direction: Verify the usefulness of the two representation measures on specific datasets for choosing the best layer and network for downstream tasks like semantic segmentation or object localization.
papers.abstract: In this work, we interpret the representations of multi-object scenes in vision encoders through the lens of structured representations. Structured representations allow modeling of individual objects distinctly and their flexible use based on the task context for both scene-level and object-specific tasks. These capabilities play a central role in human reasoning and generalization, allowing us to abstract away irrelevant details and focus on relevant information in a compact and usable form. We define structured representations as those that adhere to two specific properties: binding specific object information into discrete representation units and segregating object representations into separate sets of tokens to minimize cross-object entanglement. Based on these properties, we evaluated and compared image encoders pre-trained on classification (ViT), large vision-language models (CLIP, BLIP, FLAVA), and self-supervised methods (DINO, DINOv2). We examine the token representations by creating object-decoding tasks that measure the ability of specific tokens to capture individual objects in multi-object scenes from the COCO dataset. This analysis provides insights into how object-wise representations are distributed across tokens and layers within these vision encoders. Our findings highlight significant differences in the representation of objects depending on their relevance to the pre-training objective, with this effect particularly pronounced in the CLS token (often used for downstream tasks). Meanwhile, networks and layers that exhibit more structured representations retain better information about individual objects. To guide practical applications, we propose formal measures to quantify the two properties of structured representations, aiding in selecting and adapting vision encoders for downstream tasks.

papers.title: Color in Visual-Language Models: CLIP Deficiencies
papers.research_question: How is color encoded in CLIP, and what are the main deficiencies in its color labeling capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies deficiencies in CLIP's color encoding, including bias against achromatic colors and text prioritization, and analyzes neuron-level representations to explain these issues.
papers.conclusion: CLIP's color deficiencies may stem from training data biases, and progressive training could improve color representation.
papers.key_findings:
Achromatic stimuli are poorly related to the color concept, leading to errors in assigning black, white, or grey labels.
CLIP prioritizes text over visual information, exhibiting a strong Stroop effect where it reads color names instead of perceiving font color.
In global color assignments, CLIP labels the predominant color, except when it is achromatic.
CLIP can attribute color labels to specific image parts when instructed, but fails if the part is achromatic.
Color multi-modal neurons are found in shallow layers of CLIP, which may underlie color understanding.
papers.limitation: The black-box nature of models makes it hard to explain behavior
future_direction: Progressive training to ensure learning from basic to complex concepts
papers.abstract: This work explores how color is encoded in CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) which is currently the most influential VML (Visual Language model) in Artificial Intelligence. After performing different experiments on synthetic datasets created for this task, we conclude that CLIP is able to attribute correct color labels to colored visual stimulus, but, we come across two main deficiencies: (a) a clear bias on achromatic stimuli that are poorly related to the color concept, thus white, gray and black are rarely assigned as color labels; and (b) the tendency to prioritize text over other visual information. Here we prove it is highly significant in color labelling through an exhaustive Stroop-effect test. With the aim to find the causes of these color deficiencies, we analyse the internal representation at the neuron level. We conclude that CLIP presents an important amount of neurons selective to text, specially in deepest layers of the network, and a smaller amount of multi-modal color neurons which could be the key of understanding the concept of color properly. Our investigation underscores the necessity of refining color representation mechanisms in neural networks to foster a more comprehensive comprehension of colors as humans understand them, thereby advancing the efficacy and versatility of multimodal models like CLIP in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Linearly Mapping from Image to Text Space
papers.research_question: To what extent can the conceptual representations learned by frozen text-only language models and vision-only models be mapped to each other through a linear transformation?
papers.core_contribution: A single linear projection is sufficient to transfer visual semantic information from frozen image encoders to a frozen language model as soft prompts, enabling competitive performance on captioning and VQA tasks. The results indicate that language models encode conceptual information structurally similarly to vision-based models.
papers.conclusion: Language models encode conceptual information structurally similarly to vision-based models, even those trained solely on images. Linguistic supervision during an image encoder's pretraining plays a key role in shaping its representation space for effective transfer to language.
papers.key_findings:
Training only a single linear projection to map image representations into a frozen language model's input space achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering compared to models that tune both the image encoder and text decoder.
Image encoders pretrained with linguistic supervision (CLIP, NFRN50) transfer lexical category information more saliently than those without (BEIT), but all pretrained encoders transfer coarse-grained visual property information approximately equally well.
The conceptual representation spaces of text-only language models and vision-only image encoders are structurally similar enough to allow effective transfer via a linear map, with the degree of similarity influenced by the linguistic supervision in the image encoder's pretraining.
papers.limitation:
Due to computational constraints, the prompt length (k) was not controlled for each image encoder.
LM runoff: the language model might generate relevant information due to strong linguistic priors, giving the illusion it recognizes every element in an image.
papers.abstract: The extent to which text-only language models (LMs) learn to represent features of the non-linguistic world is an open question. Prior work has shown that pretrained LMs can be taught to caption images when a vision model's parameters are optimized to encode images in the language space. We test a stronger hypothesis: that the conceptual representations learned by frozen text-only models and vision-only models are similar enough that this can be achieved with a linear map. We show that the image representations from vision models can be transferred as continuous prompts to frozen LMs by training only a single linear projection. Using these to prompt the LM achieves competitive performance on captioning and visual question answering tasks compared to models that tune both the image encoder and text decoder (such as the MAGMA model). We compare three image encoders with increasing amounts of linguistic supervision seen during pretraining: BEIT (no linguistic information), NF-ResNET (lexical category information), and CLIP (full natural language descriptions). We find that all three encoders perform equally well at transferring visual property information to the language model (e.g., whether an animal is large or small), but that image encoders pretrained with linguistic supervision more saliently encode category information (e.g., distinguishing hippo vs. elephant) and thus perform significantly better on benchmark language-and-vision tasks. Our results indicate that LMs encode conceptual information structurally similarly to vision-based models, even those that are solely trained on images. Code is available here: https://github.com/jmerullo/limber

papers.title: Concepts from Representations: Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models via Sparse Decomposition of Visual Representations
papers.research_question: How can we build interpretable concept bottleneck models by automatically extracting visual concepts from pre-trained encoders and using sparse decomposition to reconstruct image representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCBM-ReD, a pipeline that retrofits interpretability onto pretrained opaque models by automatically extracting visual concepts from a pre-trained encoder, using MLLMs to label and filter concepts, and selecting an independent subset via reconstruction-guided optimization, then decomposing image representations into concept embeddings to fit the CBM abstraction.
papers.conclusion: PCBM-ReD is an effective method for building interpretable concept bottleneck models that achieve high accuracy, zero-shot/few-shot capabilities, and built-in interpretability by decomposing visual representations into human-understandable concepts.
papers.key_findings:
PCBM-ReD achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy across 11 image classification tasks, narrowing the performance gap with end-to-end models.
The method exhibits better interpretability through human-understandable concepts and allows for error correction via concept interventions.
PCBM-ReD retains zero-shot and few-shot capabilities similar to the original CLIP model, enabling interpretable few-shot learning.
Human evaluation shows that concepts extracted by PCBM-ReD are visually identifiable and faithfully describe images, with a clear causal link to predictions.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of data-driven concept creation, reconstruction-guided selection, and sparse decomposition for performance.
papers.limitation:
Concept generation relies on MLLMs and LLMs, which can be suboptimal for domain-specific images that general MLLMs cannot describe precisely.
As a post-hoc method, the model's performance depends on the original image encoder.
future_direction: Improving the model by designing better prompts or leveraging more advanced MLLMs.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in image recognition, yet their inherent opacity poses challenges for deployment in critical domains. Concept-based interpretations aim to address this by explaining model reasoning through human-understandable concepts. However, existing post-hoc methods and ante-hoc concept bottleneck models (CBMs), suffer from limitations such as unreliable concept relevance, non-visual or labor-intensive concept definitions, and model or data-agnostic assumptions. This paper introduces Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Model via Representation Decomposition (PCBM-ReD), a novel pipeline that retrofits interpretability onto pretrained opaque models. PCBM-ReD automatically extracts visual concepts from a pre-trained encoder, employs multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to label and filter concepts based on visual identifiability and task relevance, and selects an independent subset via reconstruction-guided optimization. Leveraging CLIP's visual-text alignment, it decomposes image representations into linear combination of concept embeddings to fit into the CBMs abstraction. Extensive experiments across 11 image classification tasks show PCBM-ReD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, narrows the performance gap with end-to-end models, and exhibits better interpretability.

papers.title: Pruning the Paradox: How CLIP's Most Informative Heads Enhance Performance While Amplifying Bias
papers.research_question: How do attention heads with high concept consistency (CCS) in CLIP models contribute to both strong performance and social biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Consistency Score (CCS) to measure concept alignment in CLIP attention heads, and shows that high-CCS heads are essential for performance but also amplify social biases, revealing a performance-bias paradox.
papers.conclusion: CCS provides a holistic view of interpretability, proving the paradox of performance vs social biases in CLIP models.
papers.key_findings:
High-CCS heads are critical for model performance: pruning them leads to significant performance drops.
High-CCS heads are important for out-of-domain detection and concept-specific reasoning.
High-CCS heads are crucial for video retrieval tasks.
High-CCS heads encode spurious correlations that amplify social biases (race and gender).
Pruning high-CCS heads can reduce bias without fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily on CLIP models, not other vision-language models.
Use of LLM models for concept labelling and judging requires robust manual verification and may not scale to larger models.
future_direction: Extending CCS to more vision-language models.
Scaling the work to much bigger models with more layers and heads.
papers.abstract: CLIP is one of the most popular foundation models and is heavily used for many vision-language tasks, yet little is known about its inner workings. As CLIP is increasingly deployed in real-world applications, it is becoming even more critical to understand its limitations and embedded social biases to mitigate potentially harmful downstream consequences. However, the question of what internal mechanisms drive both the impressive capabilities as well as problematic shortcomings of CLIP has largely remained unanswered. To bridge this gap, we study the conceptual consistency of text descriptions for attention heads in CLIP-like models. Specifically, we propose Concept Consistency Score (CCS), a novel interpretability metric that measures how consistently individual attention heads in CLIP models align with specific concepts. Our soft-pruning experiments reveal that high CCS heads are critical for preserving model performance, as pruning them leads to a significantly larger performance drop than pruning random or low CCS heads. Notably, we find that high CCS heads capture essential concepts and play a key role in out-of-domain detection, concept-specific reasoning, and video-language understanding. Moreover, we prove that high CCS heads learn spurious correlations which amplify social biases. These results position CCS as a powerful interpretability metric exposing the paradox of performance and social biases in CLIP models.

papers.title: Data or Language Supervision: What Makes CLIP Better than DINO?
papers.research_question: Does CLIP's superior performance over DINO as a vision encoder for vision-language models stem from its language supervision or its much larger training data?
papers.core_contribution: Through controlled experiments, the paper finds that language supervision, not data scale, is the key factor making CLIP a better vision encoder than DINO for VLMs, as it leads to better high-level semantic representations and improved performance on text-intensive tasks.
papers.conclusion: The controlled study shows that language supervision is the key factor behind CLIP's superior performance in VLMs, providing insights for vision encoder design.
papers.key_findings:
Under controlled training conditions, CLIP and DINO achieve similar ImageNet accuracy, but CLIP significantly outperforms DINO on fine-grained classification tasks.
Embedding analysis reveals CLIP captures high-level semantics (object categories, text) while DINO is more responsive to low-level visual features like colors and styles.
When integrated into VLMs, CLIP excels at text-intensive tasks (e.g., OCR) by 7.5%, while DINO performs slightly better on some vision-centric tasks.
Alternative language supervision objectives (SigLIP loss) or using a pretrained language encoder (Vicuna) do not improve CLIP performance in VLMs.
The advantage of CLIP over DINO in VLMs is attributed to its language-supervised training objective, not its larger training dataset.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a 10M-image subset, and scaling to billion-image datasets is needed to fully understand the interplay between supervision type and data magnitude.
future_direction: Scaling comparisons to billion-image datasets
Exploring hybrid approaches combining self-supervised and language-supervised signals
papers.abstract: CLIP outperforms self-supervised models like DINO as vision encoders for vision-language models (VLMs), but it remains unclear whether this advantage stems from CLIP's language supervision or its much larger training data. To disentangle these factors, we pre-train CLIP and DINO under controlled settings -- using the same architecture, dataset, and training configuration -- achieving similar ImageNet accuracy. Embedding analysis shows that CLIP captures high-level semantics (e.g., object categories, text), while DINO is more responsive to low-level features like colors and styles. When integrated into VLMs and evaluated on 20 VQA benchmarks, CLIP excels at text-intensive tasks, while DINO slightly outperforms on vision-centric ones. Variants of language supervision (e.g., sigmoid loss, pre-trained language encoders) yield limited gains. Our findings provide scientific insights into vision encoder design and its impact on VLM performance.

papers.title: Interpreting Neurons in Deep Vision Networks with Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically describe the roles of hidden neurons in vision networks using complex natural language descriptions, without labeled training data or a predefined concept set?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Describe-and-Dissect (DnD), a training-free method that uses multimodal models (image-to-text, LLM, text-to-image) to generate high-quality natural language descriptions of neurons in vision networks, outperforming prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Describe-and-Dissect is an effective, training-free method for interpreting neurons in deep vision networks, providing high-quality natural language descriptions that outperform existing approaches and offering practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
DnD provides higher quality neuron descriptions than existing methods, as shown in human evaluations where it was selected as the best description over 2x more often than the best baseline.
DnD's descriptions are more complex and semantically coherent, especially for intermediate layer neurons, compared to single-word or fixed-concept-set baselines.
The method is training-free and model-agnostic, allowing it to easily leverage advancements in foundation models.
DnD can be applied to practical use cases, such as interpreting and improving land cover prediction models for sustainability.
Ablation studies show the importance of generative image captioning and concept selection steps in the pipeline.
papers.limitation:
Relatively high computational cost (about 38.8 seconds per neuron on a Tesla V100 GPU).
May not detect purely visual elements (e.g., contrast or spatial patterns) because it converts images to text.
Focuses only on top-k activating images, potentially missing information from lower-activating images.
Challenges in handling polysemantic neurons (neurons representing multiple unrelated concepts).
Evaluation of description quality is complex and depends on choices of probing dataset, activation summarization, and display methods.
future_direction: Optimizing the pipeline for speed, e.g., leveraging multiple GPUs.
Addressing polysemanticity, e.g., by using sparse autoencoders to decompose neuron activations.
Improving the method by incorporating advancements in image-to-text, natural language processing, and text-to-image models.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Describe-and-Dissect (DnD), a novel method to describe the roles of hidden neurons in vision networks. DnD utilizes recent advancements in multimodal deep learning to produce complex natural language descriptions, without the need for labeled training data or a predefined set of concepts to choose from. Additionally, DnD is training-free, meaning we don't train any new models and can easily leverage more capable general purpose models in the future. We have conducted extensive qualitative and quantitative analysis to show that DnD outperforms prior work by providing higher quality neuron descriptions. Specifically, our method on average provides the highest quality labels and is more than 2$\times$ as likely to be selected as the best explanation for a neuron than the best baseline. Finally, we present a use case providing critical insights into land cover prediction models for sustainability applications. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/Describe-and-Dissect.

papers.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
papers.research_question: How do different inductive biases (architecture, task objective, visual training diet) affect the emergent brain alignment of learned visual representations in artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, while architecture and task objective have smaller effects when controlled; many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity despite different representations, suggesting standard linking methods may be too flexible.
papers.conclusion: Dataset diversity is a key factor in developing brain-aligned visual representations, and current model-to-brain linking methods may need to be refined to better capture representational differences.
papers.key_findings:
CNN and transformer architectures achieve near equivalent brain predictivity when trained on the same dataset and task.
Instance-level contrastive learning objectives lead to more brain-predictive representations than non-contrastive self-supervised objectives.
Vision-language alignment (e.g., CLIP) does not consistently yield higher brain predictivity compared to purely visual contrastive learning when controlling for dataset.
Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, with models trained on more diverse datasets (e.g., OpenAI's 400M dataset) performing best.
Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity after feature re-weighting, suggesting that standard linking methods may be too flexible to capture representational differences.
papers.limitation: The two linking methods (classical RSA and voxel-encoding RSA) give different estimates of explained variance, and it is unclear which is more correct.
future_direction: Developing better metrics for dataset diversity and richness.
Refining model-to-brain linking methods to be less flexible and more diagnostic.
Exploring one-to-one mappings between model units and brain neurons, and expanding brain targets to include topographic organization.
papers.abstract: The rapid release of high-performing computer vision models offers new potential to study the impact of different inductive biases on the emergent brain alignment of learned representations. Here, we perform controlled comparisons among a curated set of 224 diverse models to test the impact of specific model properties on visual brain predictivity - a process requiring over 1.8 billion regressions and 50.3 thousand representational similarity analyses. We find that models with qualitatively different architectures (e.g. CNNs versus Transformers) and task objectives (e.g. purely visual contrastive learning versus vision- language alignment) achieve near equivalent brain predictivity, when other factors are held constant. Instead, variation across visual training diets yields the largest, most consistent effect on brain predictivity. Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity, despite clear variation in their underlying representations - suggesting that standard methods used to link models to brains may be too flexible. Broadly, these findings challenge common assumptions about the factors underlying emergent brain alignment, and outline how we can leverage controlled model comparison to probe the common computational principles underlying biological and artificial visual systems.
