RCAV does not account for non-linearity in the initial layers of the model, as it perturbs activations after layer l.
future_direction: Using RCAV to enhance automatic discovery of prediction-relevant concepts.
Conducting a complete comparison of RCAV to other (including non-linear) semantic interpretability methods.
Applying RCAV to scientific discovery, e.g., to assess the importance of specific properties in domains like molecular similarity.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods for image classification assess model trustworthiness by attempting to expose whether the model is systematically biased or attending to the same cues as a human would. Saliency methods for feature attribution dominate the interpretability literature, but these methods do not address semantic concepts such as the textures, colors, or genders of objects within an image. Our proposed Robust Concept Activation Vectors (RCAV) quantifies the effects of semantic concepts on individual model predictions and on model behavior as a whole. RCAV calculates a concept gradient and takes a gradient ascent step to assess model sensitivity to the given concept. By generalizing previous work on concept activation vectors to account for model non-linearity, and by introducing stricter hypothesis testing, we show that RCAV yields interpretations which are both more accurate at the image level and robust at the dataset level. RCAV, like saliency methods, supports the interpretation of individual predictions. To evaluate the practical use of interpretability methods as debugging tools, and the scientific use of interpretability methods for identifying inductive biases (e.g. texture over shape), we construct two datasets and accompanying metrics for realistic benchmarking of semantic interpretability methods. Our benchmarks expose the importance of counterfactual augmentation and negative controls for quantifying the practical usability of interpretability methods.

papers.title: Visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.research_question: Whether large language model (LLM) embeddings of scene captions can characterize brain activity evoked by viewing natural scenes.
papers.core_contribution: LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity, and training deep neural networks to predict these embeddings yields models that are better aligned with brain representations than many state-of-the-art alternatives.
papers.conclusion: The visual system may converge towards representations aligned with LLM embeddings of captions, and these embeddings provide a powerful representational format for studying complex visual information processing in the brain.
papers.key_findings:
LLM embeddings of full image captions predict brain activity across the visual system, especially in higher-level areas.
The success of LLM embeddings derives from their ability to integrate complex contextual information beyond individual words or object categories.
Linear encoding models based on LLM embeddings can capture region-specific tuning properties (e.g., people vs. place selectivity).
Linear decoding can reconstruct accurate scene captions from brain activity using LLM embeddings as a representational format.
Recurrent convolutional neural networks (RCNNs) trained to predict LLM embeddings from images outperform category-trained RCNNs and a wide range of other ANN models in aligning with brain representations, despite being trained on far less data.
future_direction: Future work is needed to assess which other known aspects of visual processing are well captured by LLM embeddings.
papers.abstract: The human brain extracts complex information from visual inputs, including objects, their spatial and semantic interrelations, and their interactions with the environment. However, a quantitative approach for studying this information remains elusive. Here, we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes. We show that LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterise brain activity evoked by viewing the natural scenes. This mapping captures selectivities of different brain areas, and is sufficiently robust that accurate scene captions can be reconstructed from brain activity. Using carefully controlled model comparisons, we then proceed to show that the accuracy with which LLM representations match brain representations derives from the ability of LLMs to integrate complex information contained in scene captions beyond that conveyed by individual words. Finally, we train deep neural network models to transform image inputs into LLM representations. Remarkably, these networks learn representations that are better aligned with brain representations than a large number of state-of-the-art alternative models, despite being trained on orders-of-magnitude less data. Overall, our results suggest that LLM embeddings of scene captions provide a representational format that accounts for complex information extracted by the brain from visual inputs.

papers.title: Concept-Monitor: Understanding DNN training through individual neurons
papers.research_question: How can we automatically monitor and interpret the training process of deep neural networks through the concepts learned by individual neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept-Monitor, a framework to automatically monitor DNN training by tracking neuron concepts in a unified embedding space, and a concept diversity regularizer that improves model accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Concept-Monitor provides an automated, transparent way to monitor and understand DNN training through neuron concepts, and the concept diversity regularizer improves performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In standard training, models progress from learning low-level features (e.g., textures) to high-level concepts (e.g., objects and scenes), and concept diversity increases as training progresses.
Poor training with high learning rate results in low concept diversity and poor performance.
The proposed concept diversity regularizer, which minimizes anchor distance, improves test accuracy and increases the number of interpretable neurons.
In Lottery Ticket Hypothesis pruning, even when rewinding to initialization, the number of interpretable neurons increases, suggesting that pruning encodes concepts by removing harmful connections.
Adversarially trained models rely more on color and texture features and less on high-level object concepts compared to standard models, which may explain their lower clean accuracy but better transfer learning features.
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose a general framework called Concept-Monitor to help demystify the black-box DNN training processes automatically using a novel unified embedding space and concept diversity metric. Concept-Monitor enables human-interpretable visualization and indicators of the DNN training processes and facilitates transparency as well as deeper understanding on how DNNs develop along the during training. Inspired by these findings, we also propose a new training regularizer that incentivizes hidden neurons to learn diverse concepts, which we show to improve training performance. Finally, we apply Concept-Monitor to conduct several case studies on different training paradigms including adversarial training, fine-tuning and network pruning via the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis

papers.title: Insight: Interpretable Semantic Hierarchies in Vision-Language Encoders
papers.research_question: How can we make language-aligned vision foundation models interpretable by decomposing their representations into human-interpretable, spatially grounded concepts?
papers.core_contribution: CFM is a concept foundation model that provides interpretable, spatially grounded concept representations for vision tasks, enabling explanations across classification, segmentation, and captioning.
papers.conclusion: CFM provides a unified concept representation for vision foundation models, yielding human-interpretable, spatially grounded concepts that maintain competitive task performance.
papers.key_findings:
CFM extracts concepts that are more localized, consistent, and pure than existing concept extraction methods.
CFM discovers explicit hierarchical relationships between concepts, improving interpretability.
CFM's concept representations enable competitive performance on downstream vision tasks while providing explanations.
CFM's concept naming is more accurate than baselines, especially when leveraging discovered hierarchies.
CFM enables interpretable open-vocabulary segmentation and steerable captioning through its concept bottleneck.
papers.limitation: Concept naming can be limited for fine-grained concepts, potentially due to the vocabulary not containing relevant names or misalignment between CLIP's text and image encoders.
papers.abstract: Language-aligned vision foundation models perform strongly across diverse downstream tasks. Yet, their learned representations remain opaque, making interpreting their decision-making hard. Recent works decompose these representations into human-interpretable concepts, but provide poor spatial grounding and are limited to image classification tasks. In this work, we propose Insight, a language-aligned concept foundation model that provides fine-grained concepts, which are human-interpretable and spatially grounded in the input image. We leverage a hierarchical sparse autoencoder and a foundation model with strong semantic representations to automatically extract concepts at various granularities. Examining local co-occurrence dependencies of concepts allows us to define concept relationships. Through these relations we further improve concept naming and obtain richer explanations. On benchmark data, we show that Insight provides performance on classification and segmentation that is competitive with opaque foundation models while providing fine-grained, high quality concept-based explanations. Code is available at https://github.com/kawi19/Insight.

papers.title: Labeling Neural Representations with Inverse Recognition
papers.research_question: How can we explain the abstractions learned by neural representations in deep neural networks by identifying compositional concepts that a given representation is best at detecting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces INVERT, a scalable method for labeling neural representations with compositional concepts using AUC similarity, without requiring segmentation masks, and providing statistical significance testing.
papers.conclusion: INVERT is a scalable and effective method for interpreting neural representations, with applications in model auditing and circuit analysis, contributing to more understandable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
INVERT outperforms Network Dissection in accuracy when explaining neurons with known ground truth concepts.
INVERT is computationally more efficient than prior methods like Compositional Explanations of Neurons.
INVERT can identify neurons responsible for spurious correlations by integrating new concepts into the dataset.
INVERT can explain circuits within models by decomposing local explanations into individual neuron contributions.
INVERT enables handcrafting circuits by combining neurons using fuzzy logic operators to detect novel concepts.
papers.limitation: INVERT still relies on a labeled dataset for explanations.
future_direction: Address the dependency on labeled datasets for explanations.
Explore different similarity measures between neurons and explanations.
Investigate new ways to compose human-understandable concepts.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities in learning complex hierarchical data representations, but the nature of these representations remains largely unknown. Existing global explainability methods, such as Network Dissection, face limitations such as reliance on segmentation masks, lack of statistical significance testing, and high computational demands. We propose Inverse Recognition (INVERT), a scalable approach for connecting learned representations with human-understandable concepts by leveraging their capacity to discriminate between these concepts. In contrast to prior work, INVERT is capable of handling diverse types of neurons, exhibits less computational complexity, and does not rely on the availability of segmentation masks. Moreover, INVERT provides an interpretable metric assessing the alignment between the representation and its corresponding explanation and delivering a measure of statistical significance. We demonstrate the applicability of INVERT in various scenarios, including the identification of representations affected by spurious correlations, and the interpretation of the hierarchical structure of decision-making within the models.

papers.title: Open Vocabulary Compositional Explanations for Neuron Alignment
papers.research_question: How to generate compositional explanations for neuron alignment without relying on human-annotated datasets?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for open vocabulary compositional explanations that leverages open vocabulary semantic segmentation models to generate explanations without human-annotated data, offering flexibility and multiple granularity levels.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework addresses the dependency on human annotations in compositional explanations and enables more flexible and open-world neuron analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves comparable performance to human-annotated methods on datasets with annotations.
It provides better flexibility and results on datasets without human annotations.
The framework supports multiple granularity levels and iterative refinement of explanations.
The framework is agnostic to the open vocabulary segmentation model used.
The framework does not require human annotations, thus overcoming a major limitation of previous methods.
papers.limitation: The framework requires technical expertise to implement and interpret the explanations, and the user study design has challenges in evaluating such explanations.
future_direction: Exploring connections and complementarities with other interpretability paradigms.
Improving the usability of compositional explanations to lower the required expertise.
Investigating the effect of template prompts in open-vocabulary segmentation models for explainability.
papers.abstract: Neurons are the fundamental building blocks of deep neural networks, and their interconnections allow AI to achieve unprecedented results. Motivated by the goal of understanding how neurons encode information, compositional explanations leverage logical relationships between concepts to express the spatial alignment between neuron activations and human knowledge. However, these explanations rely on human-annotated datasets, restricting their applicability to specific domains and predefined concepts. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a framework for the vision domain that allows users to probe neurons for arbitrary concepts and datasets. Specifically, the framework leverages masks generated by open vocabulary semantic segmentation to compute open vocabulary compositional explanations. The proposed framework consists of three steps: specifying arbitrary concepts, generating semantic segmentation masks using open vocabulary models, and deriving compositional explanations from these masks. The paper compares the proposed framework with previous methods for computing compositional explanations both in terms of quantitative metrics and human interpretability, analyzes the differences in explanations when shifting from human-annotated data to model-annotated data, and showcases the additional capabilities provided by the framework in terms of flexibility of the explanations with respect to the tasks and properties of interest.

papers.title: Sparse CLIP: Co-Optimizing Interpretability and Performance in Contrastive Learning
papers.research_question: Can interpretability and performance be co-optimized in contrastive learning, challenging the assumption that they are in tension?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse CLIP, a method that enforces sparsity during CLIP training to produce interpretable multimodal features without sacrificing downstream performance, challenging the trade-off between interpretability and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability and performance can be jointly optimized in contrastive learning, offering a promising design principle for future models that need not sacrifice accuracy for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse CLIP maintains competitive performance on zero-shot classification and other downstream tasks while achieving high sparsity (e.g., 0.66% active features).
Sparse CLIP features are multimodal and interpretable, allowing direct concept alignment via top-activated words and images.
Analysis of training checkpoints reveals how concepts emerge and evolve during training, showing early multimodal alignment and concept refinement.
Sparse CLIP enables vision-based steering in vision-language models, allowing controlled suppression or boosting of concepts in generated text.
The work demonstrates that interpretability and performance can be co-optimized, contradicting the common assumption of a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Insights from sparse models do not directly transfer to existing dense CLIP models.
Parameter overhead: the high-dimensional projection layers add significant parameters (e.g., 14% for ViT-L/14).
Memory constraints limit the expansion factor during training (max 72x on 80GB GPUs).
future_direction: Comparing learned concepts across architectures to see if insights transfer.
Investigating whether performance gains stem from added parameters versus sparsity.
Optimizing sparse CLIP training for memory efficiency and throughput.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has become a cornerstone in vision-language representation learning, powering diverse downstream tasks and serving as the default vision backbone in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Despite its success, CLIP's dense and opaque latent representations pose significant interpretability challenges. A common assumption is that interpretability and performance are in tension: enforcing sparsity during training degrades accuracy, motivating recent post-hoc approaches such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). However, these post-hoc approaches often suffer from degraded downstream performance and loss of CLIP's inherent multimodal capabilities, with most learned features remaining unimodal. We propose a simple yet effective approach that integrates sparsity directly into CLIP training, yielding representations that are both interpretable and performant. Compared to SAEs, our Sparse CLIP representations preserve strong downstream task performance, achieve superior interpretability, and retain multimodal capabilities. We show that multimodal sparse features enable straightforward semantic concept alignment and reveal training dynamics of how cross-modal knowledge emerges. Finally, as a proof of concept, we train a vision-language model on sparse CLIP representations that enables interpretable, vision-based steering capabilities. Our findings challenge conventional wisdom that interpretability requires sacrificing accuracy and demonstrate that interpretability and performance can be co-optimized, offering a promising design principle for future models.

papers.title: Brain Mapping with Dense Features: Grounding Cortical Semantic Selectivity in Natural Images With Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we link neural selectivity in the higher visual cortex to specific semantic visual concepts in natural images? The paper introduces a method to identify image regions that drive selectivity patterns in different cortical areas.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BrainSAIL, a method that leverages dense spatial features from pre-trained vision transformers to identify image regions that drive selectivity patterns in the higher visual cortex, enabling fine-grained semantic grounding of neural activity.
papers.conclusion: BrainSAIL provides a powerful tool for dissecting the neural mechanisms underlying semantic visual processing for natural images and paves the way for significant advances in mapping and decomposing high-level visual representations in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
BrainSAIL can accurately localize and disentangle selectivity to diverse visual concepts in cortical regions with known category selectivity.
It can characterize high-level visual selectivity to scene properties and low-level visual features such as depth, luminance, and saturation.
It enables direct comparison of feature selectivity of different brain encoding models across different regions of interest in visual cortex.
The learning-free distillation module effectively denoises dense features, improving open-vocabulary segmentation performance.
BrainSAIL reveals that brain data has semantically coarser attributions compared to CLIP embeddings, likely due to data co-occurrence statistics.
papers.abstract: We introduce BrainSAIL, a method for linking neural selectivity with spatially distributed semantic visual concepts in natural scenes. BrainSAIL leverages recent advances in large-scale artificial neural networks, using them to provide insights into the functional topology of the brain. To overcome the challenge presented by the co-occurrence of multiple categories in natural images, BrainSAIL exploits semantically consistent, dense spatial features from pre-trained vision models, building upon their demonstrated ability to robustly predict neural activity. This method derives clean, spatially dense embeddings without requiring any additional training, and employs a novel denoising process that leverages the semantic consistency of images under random augmentations. By unifying the space of whole-image embeddings and dense visual features and then applying voxel-wise encoding models to these features, we enable the identification of specific subregions of each image which drive selectivity patterns in different areas of the higher visual cortex. This provides a powerful tool for dissecting the neural mechanisms that underlie semantic visual processing for natural images. We validate BrainSAIL on cortical regions with known category selectivity, demonstrating its ability to accurately localize and disentangle selectivity to diverse visual concepts. Next, we demonstrate BrainSAIL's ability to characterize high-level visual selectivity to scene properties and low-level visual features such as depth, luminance, and saturation, providing insights into the encoding of complex visual information. Finally, we use BrainSAIL to directly compare the feature selectivity of different brain encoding models across different regions of interest in visual cortex. Our innovative method paves the way for significant advances in mapping and decomposing high-level visual representations in the human brain.

papers.title: Does VLM Classification Benefit from LLM Description Semantics?
papers.research_question: Does VLM classification benefit from the semantics of LLM-generated descriptions, or is the performance gain due to a noise augmentation effect?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an alternative evaluation scenario to disentangle the effect of semantics from noise augmentation in VLM classification, and introduces a training-free method to select discriminative descriptions that improve classification accuracy and explainability.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates that VLM classification performance benefits from LLM description semantics when descriptions are correctly selected. The proposed evaluation framework distinguishes improvements from genuine semantics versus ensemble effects.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed training-free description selection method outperforms baseline methods (DCLIP, WaffleClip, FuDD) on several datasets with fewer descriptions.
In a classname-free evaluation setup, the selected descriptions show genuine semantic benefit, while LLM-generated descriptions without selection perform poorly.
The method achieves decent classification accuracy even without using the classname (wcls=0), indicating the selected descriptions are inherently discriminative.
Performance gains are attributed to the selection procedure within a local candidate neighborhood, not just the neighborhood restriction itself.
The method provides better explainability by preserving CLIP embeddings, using a manageable number of descriptions, minimizing concept overlap, and avoiding continuous weights.
papers.limitation: The method may be less effective on datasets with noisy backgrounds, such as ImageNet, which can hinder the selection of generally valid descriptions.
papers.abstract: Accurately describing images with text is a foundation of explainable AI. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP have recently addressed this by aligning images and texts in a shared embedding space, expressing semantic similarities between vision and language embeddings. VLM classification can be improved with descriptions generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). However, it is difficult to determine the contribution of actual description semantics, as the performance gain may also stem from a semantic-agnostic ensembling effect, where multiple modified text prompts act as a noisy test-time augmentation for the original one. We propose an alternative evaluation scenario to decide if a performance boost of LLM-generated descriptions is caused by such a noise augmentation effect or rather by genuine description semantics. The proposed scenario avoids noisy test-time augmentation and ensures that genuine, distinctive descriptions cause the performance boost. Furthermore, we propose a training-free method for selecting discriminative descriptions that work independently of classname-ensembling effects. Our approach identifies descriptions that effectively differentiate classes within a local CLIP label neighborhood, improving classification accuracy across seven datasets. Additionally, we provide insights into the explainability of description-based image classification using VLMs.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Interpretable and Testable Vision Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we understand vision models by not only interpreting their learned features but also validating these interpretations through controlled experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a practical, post-hoc method that bridges the gap between concept discovery and causal probing in vision models, enabling both interpretation and controlled testing of learned features.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable both hypothesis formation and controlled testing for vision models, providing a foundation for empirically validated model interpretation that unites explanation with experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on vision transformer activations discover interpretable, monosemantic features corresponding to visual concepts (e.g., cultural symbols, abstract concepts like 'accidents').
CLIP, trained with language supervision, learns abstract semantic features (e.g., country-specific patterns, style-agnostic concepts) that DINOv2, trained with purely visual objectives, does not reliably capture.
SAE-derived features enable precise causal interventions: suppressing a 'blue feathers' feature in a bird image shifts the classification prediction to a similar bird without blue plumage.
SAE features behave as a pseudo-orthogonal basis; suppressing a concept like 'sand' in semantic segmentation affects only the targeted regions without meaningfully altering other predictions.
The method supports patch-level causal edits across different tasks (classification and segmentation) without retraining the original vision transformer or task heads.
papers.limitation:
Discovering interesting SAE units depends on manual browsing of exemplar grids, which is slow, may overlook concepts, and risks cherry-picking.
The work relies on qualitative evaluation through visual inspection, lacking standardized quantitative metrics for measuring interpretability and control effectiveness.
Large interventions on SAE features can push activations off-manifold, and feature correlations/complex interactions complicate clean causal attribution.
SAEs are not guaranteed to surface every concept a model encodes, and low-activation units can be polysemantic or vary across random initializations.
Validation is limited to fine-grained classification and semantic segmentation; broader task coverage and comparison to prior editable concept frameworks (e.g., DN-CBM) are needed.
future_direction: Automating feature discovery and concept-label assignment (e.g., via language supervision).
Developing robust quantitative metrics for semantic alignment, manipulation specificity, and cross-model comparability.
Extending reliable feature control to more sophisticated visual reasoning tasks and understanding feature interactions across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: To truly understand vision models, we must not only interpret their learned features but also validate these interpretations through controlled experiments. While earlier work offers either rich semantics or direct control, few post-hoc tools supply both in a single, model-agnostic procedure. We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to bridge this gap; each sparse feature comes with real-image exemplars that reveal its meaning and a decoding vector that can be manipulated to probe its influence on downstream task behavior. By applying our method to widely-used pre-trained vision models, we reveal meaningful differences in the semantic abstractions learned by different pre-training objectives. We then show that a single SAE trained on frozen ViT activations supports patch-level causal edits across tasks (classification and segmentation) all without retraining the ViT or task heads. These qualitative, falsifiable demonstrations position SAEs as a practical bridge between concept discovery and causal probing of vision models. We provide code, demos and models on our project website: https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/saev.

papers.title: A Closer Look at the Explainability of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
papers.research_question: Why does CLIP exhibit opposite visualization (focusing on background over foreground) and noisy activations in its explainability, and how can these issues be addressed without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that CLIP's explainability issues (opposite visualization and noisy activations) stem from inconsistent self-attention and redundant features, and proposes CLIP Surgery, a method that modifies the inference architecture and features without fine-tuning to produce reliable class activation maps.
papers.conclusion: CLIP Surgery effectively addresses CLIP's explainability problems, enhancing model transparency and enabling improved performance on various downstream tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Raw self-attentions in CLIP build relations among inconsistent semantic regions, leading to opposite visualization where background is highlighted over foreground.
Noisy activations in CLIP's similarity maps are caused by redundant features shared across categories.
The proposed CLIP Surgery, comprising architecture surgery (consistent self-attention and dual paths) and feature surgery (redundant feature removal), significantly improves explainability metrics (e.g., mIoU, mSC) without any training.
CLIP Surgery enables high-quality visual explanations and extends the raw model's capability to open-vocabulary tasks like semantic segmentation, interactive segmentation, and multi-label recognition.
Multimodal visualization with CLIP Surgery reveals that CLIP learns partial context from an image and that the end token and some non-object words are frequently activated.
papers.abstract: Contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) is a powerful vision-language model that has shown great benefits for various tasks. However, we have identified some issues with its explainability, which undermine its credibility and limit the capacity for related tasks. Specifically, we find that CLIP tends to focus on background regions rather than foregrounds, with noisy activations at irrelevant positions on the visualization results. These phenomena conflict with conventional explainability methods based on the class attention map (CAM), where the raw model can highlight the local foreground regions using global supervision without alignment. To address these problems, we take a closer look at its architecture and features. Based on thorough analyses, we find the raw self-attentions link to inconsistent semantic regions, resulting in the opposite visualization. Besides, the noisy activations are owing to redundant features among categories. Building on these insights, we propose the CLIP Surgery for reliable CAM, a method that allows surgery-like modifications to the inference architecture and features, without further fine-tuning as classical CAM methods. This approach significantly improves the explainability of CLIP, surpassing existing methods by large margins. Besides, it enables multimodal visualization and extends the capacity of raw CLIP on open-vocabulary tasks without extra alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/xmed-lab/CLIP_Surgery.

papers.title: Why are Visually-Grounded Language Models Bad at Image Classification?
papers.research_question: Why do visually-grounded language models (VLMs) underperform CLIP models on standard image classification benchmarks, and how can this be improved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the primary reason VLMs underperform CLIP in image classification is insufficient exposure to classification data during training, and shows that integrating such data improves both classification and general VLM capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Classification is a foundational capability for VLMs, and integrating classification data into training improves both classification and general visual understanding abilities.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs significantly underperform CLIP on standard image classification benchmarks.
The performance gap is not due to inference methods, training objectives, or information loss, but rather data scarcity.
There is a strong correlation between class frequency in VLM training data and classification performance.
Fine-tuning VLMs on classification data closes the performance gap with CLIP.
Adding classification data to VLM training improves performance on the ImageWikiQA visual question answering dataset.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to image classification and may not generalize to other VLM tasks.
The proposed method requires additional training data, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Exploring other types of data beyond classification for improving VLMs.
Investigating the role of data in other VLM capabilities.
papers.abstract: Image classification is one of the most fundamental capabilities of machine vision intelligence. In this work, we revisit the image classification task using visually-grounded language models (VLMs) such as GPT-4V and LLaVA. We find that existing proprietary and public VLMs, despite often using CLIP as a vision encoder and having many more parameters, significantly underperform CLIP on standard image classification benchmarks like ImageNet. To understand the reason, we explore several hypotheses concerning the inference algorithms, training objectives, and data processing in VLMs. Our analysis reveals that the primary cause is data-related: critical information for image classification is encoded in the VLM's latent space but can only be effectively decoded with enough training data. Specifically, there is a strong correlation between the frequency of class exposure during VLM training and instruction-tuning and the VLM's performance in those classes; when trained with sufficient data, VLMs can match the accuracy of state-of-the-art classification models. Based on these findings, we enhance a VLM by integrating classification-focused datasets into its training, and demonstrate that the enhanced classification performance of the VLM transfers to its general capabilities, resulting in an improvement of 11.8% on the newly collected ImageWikiQA dataset.

papers.title: Do VLMs Have Bad Eyes? Diagnosing Compositional Failures via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Are entangled or misaligned representations within the CLIP vision encoder the root cause for failures in compositional reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that superposition (entanglement of multiple features in individual neurons) in CLIP's vision encoder is a root cause of failures in compositional reasoning and object binding.
papers.conclusion: The study establishes superposition as a key bottleneck for object-attribute compositionality and motivates future work on disentangling neuron activations to improve CLIP's feature representation.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in CLIP's MLP layers represent multiple features (superposition), which hinders compositional feature representation.
Grad-CAM visualizations show that CLIP fails to bind attributes to objects, attending to multiple unrelated regions when the full conjunction is missing.
Using entropy, the paper identifies feature-selective neurons in CLIP's MLP layers that respond to specific visual attributes.
The paper provides evidence of superposition in neurons, showing that the same neuron can activate for multiple distinct features (e.g., circle and square).
Superposition is correlated with reduced separability in embedding space (smaller cluster-center distance) and higher misclassification rates on compositional tasks.
papers.limitation: This study is limited to the CLIP-ViT-L/14 model, whereas most modern vision-language models (VLMs) adopt variants such as SigLIP and alternative architectures like SAM.
future_direction: Extending analysis to other models like SigLIP and SAM.
Establishing a more direct causal link between weak compositional feature representations and failures in compositional reasoning.
Extending analysis to more complex, feature-annotated datasets.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable performance in integrating visual and textual information for tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering. However, these models struggle with compositional generalization and object binding, which limit their ability to handle novel combinations of objects and their attributes. Our work explores the root causes of these failures using mechanistic interpretability techniques. We show evidence that individual neurons in the MLP layers of CLIP's vision encoder represent multiple features, and this "superposition" directly hinders its compositional feature representation which consequently affects compositional reasoning and object binding capabilities. We hope this study will serve as an initial step toward uncovering the mechanistic roots of compositional failures in VLMs. The code and supporting results can be found https://github.com/Mystic-Slice/Do-VLMs-Have-Bad-Eyes.

papers.title: Navigating Neural Space: Revisiting Concept Activation Vectors to Overcome Directional Divergence
papers.research_question: How can we more precisely estimate the direction of a human-understandable concept in a neural network's latent space, overcoming the directional divergence caused by distractor signals in traditional Concept Activation Vector (CAV) methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces pattern-based Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which more precisely estimate the true concept direction in latent space by focusing on concept signals and ignoring distractor directions, leading to improved performance in concept sensitivity testing and model correction for shortcut behavior.
papers.conclusion: Pattern-based CAVs provide a more precise, robust, and computationally efficient method for estimating concept directions in neural network latent spaces, leading to substantial improvements in downstream interpretability applications like concept sensitivity testing and model correction.
papers.key_findings:
Pattern-based CAVs align significantly better with the true concept direction than filter-based CAVs (e.g., from SVMs) across multiple datasets and model architectures.
Pattern-based CAVs are invariant to feature scaling and more robust to noise and concept labeling errors compared to filter-based CAVs.
In concept sensitivity testing (TCAV), pattern-based CAVs produce more reliable and higher-fidelity sensitivity scores and maps.
Model correction using pattern-based CAVs (via RR-ClArC) more effectively removes shortcut reliance and improves accuracy on biased data while preserving clean data performance.
Visualizations (RelMax) show pattern-based CAVs focus on neurons relevant to the target concept, whereas filter-based CAVs are distracted by noisy or irrelevant neurons.
papers.abstract: With a growing interest in understanding neural network prediction strategies, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) have emerged as a popular tool for modeling human-understandable concepts in the latent space. Commonly, CAVs are computed by leveraging linear classifiers optimizing the separability of latent representations of samples with and without a given concept. However, in this paper we show that such a separability-oriented computation leads to solutions, which may diverge from the actual goal of precisely modeling the concept direction. This discrepancy can be attributed to the significant influence of distractor directions, i.e., signals unrelated to the concept, which are picked up by filters (i.e., weights) of linear models to optimize class-separability. To address this, we introduce pattern-based CAVs, solely focussing on concept signals, thereby providing more accurate concept directions. We evaluate various CAV methods in terms of their alignment with the true concept direction and their impact on CAV applications, including concept sensitivity testing and model correction for shortcut behavior caused by data artifacts. We demonstrate the benefits of pattern-based CAVs using the Pediatric Bone Age, ISIC2019, and FunnyBirds datasets with VGG, ResNet, ReXNet, EfficientNet, and Vision Transformer as model architectures.

papers.title: CE-FAM: Concept-Based Explanation via Fusion of Activation Maps
papers.research_question: How can we provide concept-based explanations for image classifiers that simultaneously reveal what concepts the classifier learns, which image regions are associated with them, and how these concepts contribute to the final prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel concept-based explanation method (CE-FAM) that identifies concept regions and their contributions by fusing activation maps, leveraging Vision-Language Model knowledge without requiring annotated datasets.
papers.conclusion: CE-FAM provides a comprehensive and human-interpretable concept-based explanation for image classifiers by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between concept labels, their spatial regions, and their contributions, outperforming existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
CE-FAM outperforms existing methods (CLIP-Dissect, WWW) in concept region accuracy (NRA, Hit Rate) across various image classifiers and datasets.
The method is effective in a zero-shot setting for unseen concepts, as it learns to mimic VLM embeddings without requiring a predefined concept set during training.
Representing concepts through a weighted fusion of activation maps is more effective than associating a concept with a single neuron, especially for higher-level concepts and Transformer-based models.
Using multiple layers and a similarity loss during training improves the accuracy of the identified concept regions.
The proposed Normalized Region Accuracy (NRA) metric provides a fair evaluation of concept regions by normalizing against ideal and random baselines.
papers.limitation:
The expressiveness of concepts is constrained by the performance of the Vision-Language Model (VLM), making it difficult to predict finer-grained concepts.
Selecting an appropriate concept set is crucial; an excessively large set may introduce noise from irrelevant concepts.
Broader applicability of the method beyond the evaluated settings (models, datasets) remains unexplored.
Establishing a quantitative metric for validating concept contributions is difficult, hindering effective evaluation.
future_direction: Extending evaluations to other settings (classifiers, datasets) and optimizing the framework.
Improving the selection of concept sets to be both necessary and sufficient for explanations.
Clarifying the definition and evaluation of concept contributions.
papers.abstract: Although saliency maps can highlight important regions to explain the reasoning behind image classification in artificial intelligence (AI), the meaning of these regions is left to the user's interpretation. In contrast, conceptbased explanations decompose AI predictions into humanunderstandable concepts, clarifying their contributions. However, few methods can simultaneously reveal what concepts an image classifier learns, which regions are associated with them, and how they contribute to predictions. We propose a novel concept-based explanation method, Concept-based Explanation via Fusion of Activation Maps (CE-FAM). It employs a branched network that shares activation maps with an image classifier and learns to mimic the embeddings of a Vision and Language Model (VLM). The branch network predicts concepts in an image, and their corresponding regions are represented by a weighted sum of activation maps, with weights given by the gradients of the concept prediction scores. Their contributions are quantified based on their impact on the image classification score. Our method provides a general framework for identifying the concept regions and their contributions while leveraging VLM knowledge to handle arbitrary concepts without requiring an annotated dataset. Furthermore, we introduce a novel evaluation metric to assess the accuracy of the concept regions. Our qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate our method outperforms existing approaches and excels in zero-shot inference for unseen concepts.

papers.title: Local Concept Embeddings for Analysis of Concept Distributions in Vision DNN Feature Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we capture the distribution of concepts in DNN latent spaces to better understand sub-concepts and concept confusion, which are missed by existing single-vector concept embedding methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a local concept embedding (LoCE) framework that captures the distribution of concepts in DNN latent spaces, enabling the analysis of sub-concepts, concept confusion, and outliers, which are missed by global single-vector methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed local concept embedding (LoCE) method provides a novel and effective tool for analyzing the distribution of concepts in DNN latent spaces, revealing complexities such as sub-concepts and concept confusion that are not captured by existing global methods.
papers.key_findings:
Concept representations in DNN latent spaces are complex, multi-modal distributions that often exhibit sub-concepts and overlap between different concepts.
Local Concept Embeddings (LoCEs) can capture this distributional information and are competitive with global baselines in concept segmentation tasks.
The distribution of LoCEs can be analyzed using techniques like Gaussian Mixture Models and hierarchical clustering to identify sub-concepts and measure concept confusion.
LoCEs enable concept-level outlier detection and information retrieval, providing debugging insights.
The method is robust to input noise and works across diverse vision architectures (CNNs and ViTs).
papers.limitation:
The image-wise LoCEs may still mix sub-concepts that co-occur within a single image, and instance-wise LoCEs would require more costly instance segmentation labels.
The method's concept segmentation performance, while competitive, can be lower than global baselines due to its local, context-sensitive nature.
future_direction: Extending the approach to instance-wise LoCEs using instance segmentation labels.
Exploring different loss functions (e.g., Dice loss) for optimizing LoCEs.
Applying the distributional analysis framework to other modalities and model architectures.
papers.abstract: Abstract Insights into the learned latent representations are imperative for verifying deep neural networks (DNNs) in critical computer vision (CV) tasks. Therefore, state-of-the-art supervised Concept-based eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (C-XAI) methods associate user-defined concepts like “car” each with a single vector in the DNN latent space (concept embedding vector). In the case of concept segmentation, these linearly separate between activation map pixels belonging to a concept and those belonging to background. Existing methods for concept segmentation, however, fall short of capturing implicitly learned sub-concepts (e.g., the DNN might split car into “proximate car” and “distant car”), and overlap of user-defined concepts (e.g., between “bus” and “truck”). In other words, they do not capture the full distribution of concept representatives in latent space. For the first time, this work shows that these simplifications are frequently broken and that distribution information can be particularly useful for understanding DNN-learned notions of sub-concepts, concept confusion, and concept outliers. To allow exploration of learned concept distributions, we propose a novel local concept analysis framework. Instead of optimizing a single global concept vector on the complete dataset, it generates a local concept embedding (LoCE) vector for each individual sample. We use the distribution formed by LoCEs to explore the latent concept distribution by fitting Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), hierarchical clustering, and concept-level information retrieval and outlier detection. Despite its context sensitivity, our method’s concept segmentation performance is competitive to global baselines. Analysis results are obtained on three datasets and six diverse vision DNN architectures, including vision transformers (ViTs). The code is available at https://github.com/continental/local-concept-embeddings .

papers.title: Multimodal Neurons in Pretrained Text-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: Can the crossmodal generalization ability of language models be traced to individual neurons? Does translation between modalities occur in the projection layer or deeper within the transformer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in a vision-language model with a frozen text transformer, multimodal neurons emerge in the transformer MLPs that convert visual representations into corresponding text, and that translation between modalities occurs inside the transformer, not in the projection layer.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal neurons exist in text-only transformer MLPs and consistently translate image semantics into language. Translation between modalities happens inside the transformer, not in the projection layer.
papers.key_findings:
Image prompts cast into the transformer embedding space do not encode interpretable semantics; translation between modalities occurs inside the transformer.
Multimodal neurons can be found within the transformer MLPs, and they are active in response to particular image semantics.
Multimodal neurons causally affect output: ablating them can remove concepts from image captions.
Multimodal neurons are selective for specific visual concepts across inputs, as measured by IoU with object segmentations.
The decoded text from multimodal neurons agrees with image semantics, as measured by CLIPScore and BERTScore.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single multimodal model (LiMBeR-BEIT) with separately learned vision and language components.
The knowledge of the structure of vector spaces representing information from different modalities remains incomplete, and how concepts encoded by individual units are assembled from upstream representations is not investigated.
future_direction: Investigate the phenomenon of multimodal neurons in other vision-language architectures and models aligning other modalities.
Explore whether similar neurons emerge when the visual encoder is replaced with a raw pixel stream or a pretrained speech autoencoder.
Build a more mechanistic understanding of information processing within transformers to explain their ability to generalize to non-textual representations.
papers.abstract: Language models demonstrate remarkable capacity to generalize representations learned in one modality to downstream tasks in other modalities. Can we trace this ability to individual neurons? We study the case where a frozen text transformer is augmented with vision using a self-supervised visual encoder and a single linear projection learned on an image-to-text task. Outputs of the projection layer are not immediately decodable into language describing image content; instead, we find that translation between modalities occurs deeper within the transformer. We introduce a procedure for identifying "multimodal neurons" that convert visual representations into corresponding text, and decoding the concepts they inject into the model's residual stream. In a series of experiments, we show that multimodal neurons operate on specific visual concepts across inputs, and have a systematic causal effect on image captioning.

papers.title: SPARC: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders for Cross-Model and Cross-Modal Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we learn a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities to enable direct comparison of how different models represent identical concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARC, a framework that learns a unified latent space across diverse models and modalities via Global TopK sparsity and cross-reconstruction loss, enabling direct comparison of concept representations and improving concept alignment (Jaccard similarity 0.80 vs 0.22 for prior work).
papers.conclusion: SPARC provides a powerful framework for cross-model and cross-modal interpretability by learning a unified latent space, enabling direct comparison of concept representations and facilitating applications like attribution and retrieval without manual alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SPARC achieves a concept alignment Jaccard similarity of 0.80 on Open Images, more than tripling the alignment compared to USAE (0.22).
Global TopK enforces identical activation patterns across all input streams, eliminating mixed activation patterns and ensuring all neurons are either active across all streams or dead across all streams.
Cross-reconstruction loss provides semantic alignment, ensuring the meaning of activations is transferable between streams.
SPARC enables practical applications like text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval without requiring manual alignment.
SPARC generalizes to ten diverse pretrained models (including vision and language encoders) and maintains positive cross-stream reconstruction scores.
future_direction: Exploring shallow nonlinear mappings (e.g., two-layer MLPs) for encoders and decoders.
papers.abstract: Understanding how different AI models encode the same high-level concepts, such as objects or attributes, remains challenging because each model typically produces its own isolated representation. Existing interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) produce latent concepts individually for each model, resulting in incompatible concept spaces and limiting cross-model interpretability. To address this, we introduce SPARC (Sparse Autoencoders for Aligned Representation of Concepts), a new framework that learns a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities (e.g., vision models like DINO, and multimodal models like CLIP). SPARC's alignment is enforced through two key innovations: (1) a Global TopK sparsity mechanism, ensuring all input streams activate identical latent dimensions for a given concept; and (2) a Cross-Reconstruction Loss, which explicitly encourages semantic consistency between models. On Open Images, SPARC dramatically improves concept alignment, achieving a Jaccard similarity of 0.80, more than tripling the alignment compared to previous methods. SPARC creates a shared sparse latent space where individual dimensions often correspond to similar high-level concepts across models and modalities, enabling direct comparison of how different architectures represent identical concepts without requiring manual alignment or model-specific analysis. As a consequence of this aligned representation, SPARC also enables practical applications such as text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval. Code and models are available at https://github.com/AtlasAnalyticsLab/SPARC.

papers.title: Toward a Holistic Evaluation of Robustness in CLIP Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the robustness of CLIP models across multiple dimensions including visual factors, out-of-distribution detection, calibration, retrieval, 3D awareness, and vision-language interaction.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a holistic evaluation of CLIP models across visual factors, safety, retrieval, 3D awareness, and vision-language interaction, revealing insights such as the role of visual encoder architecture in 3D robustness and the shape bias in CLIP.
papers.conclusion: The comprehensive evaluation reveals important insights into CLIP's robustness and provides guidance for future improvements in CLIP models.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP models are more robust than ImageNet models on six out of ten visual factors, but training distribution affects this robustness.
CLIP models exhibit a shape bias, which weakens after fine-tuning on ImageNet.
CNN-based CLIP models are more robust to 3D corruptions and show better correspondence matching than ViT-based CLIP models.
Fine-tuning CLIP models can hurt calibration, but methods like LP-FT and WiSE-FT recover it with temperature scaling.
LLaVA models, which use CLIP vision encoders, can outperform CLIP on ambiguous image categories, especially with stronger language models.
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models have shown significant potential, particularly in zero-shot classification across diverse distribution shifts. Building on existing evaluations of overall classification robustness, this work aims to provide a more comprehensive assessment of CLIP by introducing several new perspectives. First, we investigate their robustness to variations in specific visual factors. Second, we assess two critical safety objectives--confidence uncertainty and out-of-distribution detection--beyond mere classification accuracy. Third, we evaluate the finesse with which CLIP models bridge the image and text modalities. Fourth, we extend our examination to 3D awareness in CLIP models, moving beyond traditional 2D image understanding. Finally, we explore the interaction between vision and language encoders within modern large multimodal models (LMMs) that utilize CLIP as the visual backbone, focusing on how this interaction impacts classification robustness. In each aspect, we consider the impact of six factors on CLIP models: model architecture, training distribution, training set size, fine-tuning, contrastive loss, and test-time prompts. Our study uncovers several previously unknown insights into CLIP. For instance, the architecture of the visual encoder in CLIP plays a significant role in their robustness against 3D corruption. CLIP models tend to exhibit a bias towards shape when making predictions. Moreover, this bias tends to diminish after fine-tuning on ImageNet. Vision-language models like LLaVA, leveraging the CLIP vision encoder, could exhibit benefits in classification performance for challenging categories over CLIP alone. Our findings are poised to offer valuable guidance for enhancing the robustness and reliability of CLIP models.

papers.title: NeuroCartography: Scalable Automatic Visual Summarization of Concepts in\n Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we scalably summarize and visualize the concepts learned by deep neural networks by automatically discovering and grouping neurons that detect the same concepts?
papers.core_contribution: NeuroCartography is an interactive system that scalably summarizes and visualizes concepts learned by neural networks by automatically clustering neurons that detect the same concepts and embedding neurons to show concept associations.
papers.conclusion: NeuroCartography provides a scalable way to summarize and visualize concepts in deep neural networks, enabling interesting discoveries about how concepts are encoded and related.
papers.key_findings:
NeuroCartography discovers neuron groups that represent coherent, human-meaningful concepts.
The system can reveal concept cascades and backbone concept pathways for related classes (e.g., different dog breeds).
It can identify isolated concepts, such as watermarks, that are not specific to any image content.
The scalable techniques (neuron clustering and embedding) operate in time linear to the number of neurons.
A large-scale human evaluation shows high agreement on the coherence of discovered neuron groups.
papers.limitation:
Cannot handle poly-semantic neurons (neurons that respond to multiple unrelated concepts).
Concepts need to be manually labeled.
The Neuron Projection View presents all neurons in the same plot even though some concepts' abstraction levels could be very different.
future_direction: Tackling poly-semantic neurons.
Integrating NeuroCartography into more applications (e.g., model compression).
Extending support to other neural network models (e.g., ResNets).
Automatic labeling of concepts.
Providing users the ability to select layers to investigate.
papers.abstract:
Existing research on making sense of deep neural networks often focuses on
neuron-level interpretation, which may not adequately capture the bigger
picture of how concepts are collectively encoded by multiple neurons. We
present NeuroCartography, an interactive system that scalably summarizes and
visualizes concepts learned by neural networks. It automatically discovers and
groups neurons that detect the same concepts, and describes how such neuron
groups interact to form higher-level concepts and the subsequent predictions.
NeuroCartography introduces two scalable summarization techniques: (1) neuron
clustering groups neurons based on the semantic similarity of the concepts
detected by neurons (e.g., neurons detecting "dog faces" of different breeds
are grouped); and (2) neuron embedding encodes the associations between related
concepts based on how often they co-occur (e.g., neurons detecting "dog face"
and "dog tail" are placed closer in the embedding space). Key to our scalable
techniques is the ability to efficiently compute all neuron pairs'
relationships, in time linear to the number of neurons instead of quadratic
time. NeuroCartography scales to large data, such as the ImageNet dataset with
1.2M images. The system's tightly coordinated views integrate the scalable
techniques to visualize the concepts and their relationships, projecting the
concept associations to a 2D space in Neuron Projection View, and summarizing
neuron clusters and their relationships in Graph View. Through a large-scale
human evaluation, we demonstrate that our technique discovers neuron groups
that represent coherent, human-meaningful concepts. And through usage
scenarios, we describe how our approaches enable interesting and surprising
discoveries, such as concept cascades of related and isolated concepts. The
NeuroCartography visualization runs in modern browsers and is open-sourced.

papers.title: CLIP-Adapter: Better Vision-Language Models with Feature Adapters
papers.research_question: Can feature adapters, as an alternative to prompt tuning, achieve better few-shot adaptation of vision-language models like CLIP?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CLIP-Adapter, a simple and efficient method for few-shot learning that fine-tunes lightweight feature adapters with residual connections, outperforming prompt tuning methods like CoOp.
papers.conclusion: CLIP-Adapter demonstrates that fine-tuning lightweight feature adapters is a highly effective alternative to prompt tuning for few-shot adaptation of vision-language models, achieving superior performance with a simple and efficient design.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP-Adapter consistently outperforms zero-shot CLIP, linear probe CLIP, and CoOp on 11 image classification datasets across various few-shot settings.
CLIP-Adapter is more parameter-efficient and has faster training and inference times compared to CoOp.
The residual connection in CLIP-Adapter dynamically blends original and adapted features, preventing overfitting and improving generalization.
Using only the visual adapter yields better performance than using only the text adapter or both together.
The optimal residual ratio α varies with dataset characteristics, reflecting the semantic gap between pretraining and downstream data.
future_direction: Extend CLIP-Adapter to more vision-language applications and tasks.
Combine CLIP-Adapter with cache models and enhanced prompts to further improve CLIP's capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large-scale contrastive vision-language pre-training has shown significant progress in visual representation learning. Unlike traditional visual systems trained by a fixed set of discrete labels, a new paradigm was introduced in \cite{radford2021learning} to directly learn to align images with raw texts in an open-vocabulary setting. On downstream tasks, a carefully chosen text prompt is employed to make zero-shot predictions.~To avoid non-trivial prompt engineering, context optimization \cite{zhou2021coop} has been proposed to learn continuous vectors as task-specific prompts with few-shot training examples.~In this paper, we show that there is an alternative path to achieve better vision-language models other than prompt tuning.~While prompt tuning is for the textual inputs, we propose CLIP-Adapter to conduct fine-tuning with feature adapters on either visual or language branch. Specifically, CLIP-Adapter adopts an additional bottleneck layer to learn new features and performs residual-style feature blending with the original pre-trained features.~As a consequence, CLIP-Adapter is able to outperform context optimization while maintains a simple design. Experiments and extensive ablation studies on various visual classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Code is released at t https://github.com/gaopengcuhk/CLIP-Adapter.

papers.title: Perceptual Grouping in Contrastive Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How well do vision-language models understand where objects reside within an image and group together visually related parts? How can we endow these models with perceptual grouping while retaining their generic and transferable nature?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a minimal set of modifications (max pooling aggregation and specific pre-training) to contrastive vision-language models that enables them to learn perceptual grouping, leading to state-of-the-art zero-shot segmentation without training on any segmentation data.
papers.conclusion: Perceptual grouping can be achieved in vision-language models with simple modifications, leading to improved localization and robustness while retaining zero-shot recognition capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Existing vision-language models (CLIP, ALIGN) fail to localize objects and group semantically related content within images.
The proposed CLIPpy model, with max pooling and DINO pre-training, achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised segmentation and zero-shot semantic segmentation.
CLIPpy shows improved robustness to spurious correlations in datasets like Waterbirds, matching or surpassing specialized supervised methods.
papers.limitation:
CNN-based architectures (EfficientNet-B5) show limited improvement in localization compared to ViT architectures.
The model is trained on a smaller dataset (CC-12M) compared to some baselines (e.g., ALIGN trained on 1.8B pairs).
future_direction: Apply Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) to refine segmentation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot image recognition suggest that vision-language models learn generic visual representations with a high degree of semantic information that may be arbitrarily probed with natural language phrases. Understanding an image, however, is not just about understanding what content resides within an image, but importantly, where that content resides. In this work we examine how well vision-language models are able to understand where objects reside within an image and group together visually related parts of the imagery. We demonstrate how contemporary vision and language representation learning models based on contrastive losses and large web-based data capture limited object localization information. We propose a minimal set of modifications that results in models that uniquely learn both semantic and spatial information. We measure this performance in terms of zero-shot image recognition, unsupervised bottom-up and top-down semantic segmentations, as well as robustness analyses. We find that the resulting model achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of unsupervised segmentation, and demonstrate that the learned representations are uniquely robust to spurious correlations in datasets designed to probe the causal behavior of vision models.

papers.title: CEIR: Concept-based Explainable Image Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we learn high-quality, interpretable image representations without label dependency by projecting images into a human-comprehensible concept space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CEIR, a novel image representation learning method that projects images into a human-interpretable concept space using a Concept Bottleneck Model and a VAE, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering performance while providing concept-based explanations.
papers.conclusion: CEIR provides a novel approach to learning interpretable image representations by leveraging human concepts, achieving strong performance on clustering tasks and offering a pathway for open-world concept mining and label generation.
papers.key_findings:
CEIR achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering performance on benchmarks like CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and STL10.
The method generates human-interpretable concept-based explanations for learned representations without requiring labels.
CEIR can extract relevant concepts from open-world images without fine-tuning, enabling automatic label generation and manipulation.
The concept-based latent representations are robust and capture both high-level and fine-grained semantic information.
The performance gain is attributed to the concept bottleneck layer and the VAE's ability to compress and enhance salient concepts.
papers.limitation: The method's performance depends on the quality of the generated concept reference set.
future_direction: Incorporate more advanced self-supervised methods like contrastive learning to derive more robust representations.
Explore the potential of CEIR's concept-based representations for domain generalization or adaptation tasks.
Investigate discerning causal from spurious concepts associated with images.
papers.abstract: In modern machine learning, the trend of harnessing self-supervised learning to derive high-quality representations without label dependency has garnered significant attention. However, the absence of label information, coupled with the inherently high-dimensional nature, improves the difficulty for the interpretation of learned representations. Consequently, indirect evaluations become the popular metric for evaluating the quality of these features, leading to a biased validation of the learned representation rationale. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach termed Concept-based Explainable Image Representation (CEIR). Initially, using the Concept-based Model (CBM) incorporated with pretrained CLIP and concepts generated by GPT-4, we project input images into a concept vector space. Subsequently, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) learns the latent representation from these projected concepts, which serves as the final image representation. Due to the capability of the representation to encapsulate high-level, semantically relevant concepts, the model allows for attributions to a human-comprehensible concept space.
