This not only enhances interpretability but also preserves the robustness essential for downstream tasks. For instance, our method exhibits state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering performance on benchmarks such as CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and STL10. Furthermore, capitalizing on the universality of human conceptual understanding, CEIR can seamlessly extract the related concept from open-world images without fine-tuning. This offers a fresh approach to automatic label generation and label manipulation.

papers.title: MaskInversion: Localized Embeddings via Optimization of Explainability Maps
papers.research_question: How can we generate a localized embedding for a specific image region using a frozen pre-trained vision-language model by optimizing an embedding token to match a query mask via explainability maps?
papers.core_contribution: MaskInversion is a method that learns a localized embedding for a query image region by optimizing an embedding token to match the region's mask via explainability maps, without fine-tuning the frozen pre-trained vision-language backbone, and includes a gradient decomposition strategy for efficiency.
papers.conclusion: MaskInversion provides an effective way to generate localized embeddings for specific image regions without modifying pre-trained models, enabling a range of region-based vision-language applications.
papers.key_findings:
MaskInversion outperforms baseline methods on referring expression retrieval, class retrieval, and localized captioning across multiple datasets.
The method scales well with the size of the backbone model, achieving state-of-the-art performance with larger CLIP variants.
The proposed gradient decomposition strategy reduces runtime when processing multiple masks per image.
MaskInversion works effectively with approximate masks derived from bounding boxes and SAM, making it practical for real-world applications.
The learned localized embeddings can be used as drop-in replacements for global image embeddings in various downstream tasks like classification, captioning, and image generation.
papers.limitation:
The method's effectiveness depends on the availability and quality of explainability methods compatible with the foundation model; models with suboptimal explainability may not benefit fully.
Foundation models like CLIP are often trained on low-resolution images (e.g., 224x224), which limits the ability to focus on small objects and fine-grained details.
papers.abstract: Vision-language foundation models such as CLIP have achieved tremendous results in global vision-language alignment, but still show some limitations in creating representations for specific image regions. % To address this problem, we propose MaskInversion, a method that leverages the feature representations of pre-trained foundation models, such as CLIP, to generate a context-aware embedding for a query image region specified by a mask at test time. MaskInversion starts with initializing an embedding token and compares its explainability map, derived from the foundation model, to the query mask. The embedding token is then subsequently refined to approximate the query region by minimizing the discrepancy between its explainability map and the query mask. During this process, only the embedding vector is updated, while the underlying foundation model is kept frozen allowing to use MaskInversion with any pre-trained model. As deriving the explainability map involves computing its gradient, which can be expensive, we propose a gradient decomposition strategy that simplifies this computation. The learned region representation can be used for a broad range of tasks, including open-vocabulary class retrieval, referring expression comprehension, as well as for localized captioning and image generation. We evaluate the proposed method on all those tasks on several datasets such as PascalVOC, MSCOCO, RefCOCO, and OpenImagesV7 and show its capabilities compared to other SOTA approaches.

papers.title: Explaining the Impact of Training on Vision Models via Activation Clustering
papers.research_question: How can internal representations of vision model encoders be extracted and visualized to understand learned semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neuro-Activated Vision Explanations (NAVE), a method for extracting and visualizing internal representations of vision model encoders, demonstrating its ability to align with image semantics and its utility for model inspection.
papers.conclusion: NAVE is a valuable tool for post-hoc model inspection and improving transparency in vision models, effectively extracting and visualizing learned concepts.
papers.key_findings:
NAVE extracts semantically meaningful concepts from vision model encoders without fine-tuning.
NAVE performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods on object localization tasks.
Training strategies, such as supervised vs. self-supervised learning, significantly impact the encoder's representation capabilities.
ViT-small models trained on ImageNet1k outperform larger ViT-base models on object localization.
NAVE reveals that artifacts in ViTs primarily affect the background and that shortcuts in training data can degrade model performance.
papers.limitation: The use of k-means clustering introduces variability due to initialization.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Neuro-Activated Vision Explanations (NAVE), a method for extracting and visualizing the internal representations of vision model encoders. By clustering feature activations, NAVE provides insights into learned semantics without fine-tuning. Using object localization, we show that NAVE's concepts align with image semantics. Through extensive experiments, we analyze the impact of training strategies and architectures on encoder representation capabilities. Additionally, we apply NAVE to study training artifacts in vision transformers and reveal how weak training strategies and spurious correlations degrade model performance. Our findings establish NAVE as a valuable tool for post-hoc model inspection and improving transparency in vision models.
